News.title: Rush hour travel chaos with ‘major disruption’ after Lewes train crash & ‘damaged wires’ on second London route
News.content:
DOUBLE WOE Rush hour travel chaos with ‘major disruption’ after Lewes train crash & ‘damaged wires’ on second London route

COMMUTERS are facing rush hour chaos this morning with “major disruption” affecting the rail network after a train crash in Lewes.

Dozens of passengers managed to escape a train after being trapped in overturned carriages following the horror in Lewes, East Sussex, just before 4pm yesterday.



Further disruption has now been sparked by damage to the overhead electric wires between London St Pancras International and Bedford.

Trains running between the two stations may be cancelled, severely delayed or revised, National Rail said.



Commuters are advised to check if their Thameslink tickets are valid with other providers ahead of travelling to Sheffield, Derby, Nottingham and Leicester.

Major disruption along the route is expected to continue until around midday.

Meanwhile, following the Lewes derailment trains are currently unable to run through the area as the emergency services and rail accident investigators remain on scene.

Major disruption is expected to continue for several days to come with the route completely closed off to trains.



The derailment is affecting routes between Ore, Eastbourne, Seaford and Brighton, and also between Ore, Eastbourne and London Victoria.

Rail replacement buses will be running between Haywards Heath and Lewes, calling at Cooksbridge and Plumpton.

Passengers travelling today have been advised to allow an extra hour to make their journey as the rail network faces serious disruption.

The Lewes derailment is affecting Southern Rail services while the disruption between London St Pancras and Bedford is affecting Thameslink services.

Following yesterday’s horror train crash there was “major disruption” across the entire Sussex coastal network during peak hours.



A “do not travel” warning remains in place from Southern Railway.

Network Rail has confirmed the stretch between Lewes and Haywards Heath will remain closed indefinitely while complex investigations and infrastructure repairs are carried out.

Trains that normally run between London Victoria and Hastings / Ore will be either running between London Victoria and Brighton or cancelled.

Busy routes including both ways from Brighton to London were all affected yesterday.

Cops, paramedics, and fire crews were scrambled to the crash after the train derailed at around 3.54pm.



The rear three carriages left the track and rolled onto their sides, trapping around 40 of the 150 passengers, with one sliding partially down the embankment.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Twenty people in total went to the hospital for treatment, including two who suffered serious injuries and were sent to a major trauma centre.

Eighteen people were taken by ambulance, while a further two made their own way as temperatures climbed to 38C in London.

News.title: Nigel Farage BEATS Count Binface in Clacton by-election – but refuses to attend result due to ‘threats’
News.content:
NIGEL Farage has stormed the Clacton by-election after comfortably beating his main rival Count Binface.

But the Reform leader refused to attend the official result this morning after claiming “an organised campaign” planned to disrupt his speech.



Mr Farage hoovered up a decisive 22,239 to Count Binface’s 9,455, equalling a 12,784 majority.

He had triggered the by-election amid an ongoing row into his finances including a £5million gift he failed to declare.



Ahead of the official result this morning, Mr Farage claimed an “overwhelming victory” to his supporters that dwarfed his 8,405 majority in 2024.

He said: “In doing so, we have beaten the candidate for the uniparty: Count Binface.”

But he told activists he would not be attending the count at the town hall and alleged that agitators were planning to disrupt it.

He said: “I am damned if I am going to stand on a stage, having won a resounding victory, and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies.

“I will not, sadly, be attending the count.”

A Reform spokesman added: “Essex Police advised Nigel not to attend the count tonight due to a credible threat against him.”



Yet the force appeared to dispute the claims, saying: “We have a proportionate and robust policing operation to ensure the safety and security of all participants in the count.”

Instead the Reform leader addressed cheering crowds of grassroots members at so-called “Farage Fest” in Clacton.

He had been facing a Commons ethics probe over his failure to declare a £5million donation from a crypto tycoon in the months before he became an MP.

Mr Farage had said he would “let the people of Clacton” be his judge rather than the “the Establishment in Westminster”.

The other main parties refused to take part and instead swung behind comedy candidate Count Binface.



Yesterday Clacton constituents chose from the largest pool of candidates in history, with the ballot paper stretching onto three pages.

Mr Farage was always the overwhelming favourite to retain the Essex seaside seat that is fertile electoral ground for Reform.

But upon his expected return as an MP today the Standards Commissioner is expected to resume the investigation into whether he broke the rules.

If found to have committed a serious breach, he could even face another by-election if a recall petition is triggered.

Warning the Standards Commissioner not to take such action, he told The Sun this week: “If I get the result I want, if Standards decide that they want to do it again, well, I think they’d look rather silly.”



He has argued he did not need to declare the £5million as it was gifted to him before he became an MP when he had no intention of returning to frontline politics.

Mr Farage has said the cash was intended to pay for his extensive security protection given the level of threats against him.

Asked if he would still have taken the money from Christopher Harborne if he knew of the subsequent hassle, he said: “Oh yes. Ann Widdecombe was 78 years old.

“She was murdered. She had nothing apart from CCTV.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Reform has suffered a dip in the opinion polls in recent weeks and been leapfrogged by Labour for the first time in around 15 months.



Mr Farage has insisted the “Burnham Bounce” will soon fizzle out and expects to reclaim his lead soon.

News.title: Hundreds of tourists rescued by boats fleeing resorts in Greece as ‘wall of flame’ wildfire rages & threaten beaches
News.content:
HUNDREDS of terrified tourists have been evacuated from beaches as a “wall of flames” menaced two popular resorts.

Petrifying infernos threatened multiple busy beaches, sparking 500 holidaymakers – some in their swimwear – to urgently flee into the sea via emergency boats in Greece.



Water-bombing planes, helicopters and more than 200 firefighters battled for hours to stop the flames spreading across the Halkidiki peninsula, south of the city of Thessaloniki.

Local media say a 3km “wall of flames” that roared up to 30 metres high was closing in on the resorts.



Desperate tourists – some with small children in their arms – were taken out to sea while crews tackle the blaze on Thursday.

Wearing protective face masks and holding their pets, residents also boarded the dinghies and small boats in the coastal region of Siviri as flames consumed nearby forests and thick gray smoke filled the clear skies.

Sophia, a homeowner in the region who only gave her first name, said: “We are on the beach and looking for a way to get away,

“From where we are, we can see that flames have reached the town and the houses.”



The region is dominated by flammable pine forests where the blaze is thought to have erupted, with firefighters saying strong winds made battling the blaze harder.

Within hours of erupting, the fire bore down on homes around the popular resorts of Siviri and Fourka, which were packed with summer travellers.

Dozens queued on a pontoon at Fourka waiting to flee as smoke blotted out the sky over the resorts, according to images broadcast by ERT.



Cars frantically trying to leave Fourka and Siviri caused traffic jams in the area.

Two injured firefighters were rushed to hospital.

Greece’s civil protection agency initially sent evacuation warnings by phone to people in the two resorts.



After extensive action, the blaze was later brought under control, according to the regional civil protection chief.

Crews remain on scene, alert for any potential flare ups.

Prior to the blaze Halkidiki authorities had banned the public from entering the region’s pine forests.

The Greek authorities had also issued a maximum five alert for fires for much of the Greek mainland.

Already this month, two crew from a helicopter helping to battle a forest fire near Athens died when their aircraft collided with another helicopter in mid-air.



The fire destroyed 110 square kilometres (42 square miles) of forest.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Earlier this month wildfires raged across Greece with a large fire tearing through the west of Athens, prompting evacuations.

The fire at the capital city gutted homes and burnt through farmland and pine forest, forcing emergency evacuations by land and sea.

News.title: What Brits remember from their childhood revealed – & it’s not big birthdays or expensive presents
News.content:
BLAST FROM PAST What Brits remember from their childhood revealed – & it’s not big birthdays or expensive presents

THE little things Brits remember most from childhood revealed – and it’s not birthdays or presents.

Brits are more likely to treasure family film nights, dinners around the table and long car journeys than big birthdays or expensive presents, research has found.



A study of 2,000 adults found 85 per cent believe their strongest childhood memories were made during small, unplanned moments rather than major occasions.

Family holidays topped the list at 43 per cent, followed by watching films together (32 per cent), family meals (26 per cent), car journeys (16 per cent) and playing games (14 per cent).



The latest research suggests it is often the ordinary experiences rather than the major milestones that stick with us.

More than three quarters (78 per cent) said who they shared an experience with was more important than where they were or what they were doing.

It comes after previous Samsung research revealed just how much of everyday life Brits are now documenting.

The average adult takes 1,040 photos and 312 videos every year, while 37 per cent capture more pictures and clips than they did five years ago.

Holidays (53 per cent) and family occasions (52 per cent) were the moments people were most likely to photograph or film.

And that growing bank of pictures appears to play an important role in keeping memories alive.



More than three quarters (76 per cent) said taking photos and videos helps them appreciate simple experiences more, while 81 per cent said it makes them feel closer to the people who matter most.

More than a quarter (28 per cent) regularly revisit childhood pictures or videos, sparking feelings of nostalgia (48 per cent), happiness (39 per cent), connection (33 per cent) and comfort (29 per cent).

The latest research was commissioned by Samsung to mark the launch of the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold8 Series, including the Galaxy Z Fold8 and Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra.

Annika Bizon, Mobile Experience VP of Product and Marketing for Samsung UK and Ireland, said: “Our research is a reminder that it’s often the everyday moments that matter most.

“From daily routines and family film nights to holidays and unplanned moments, the new Galaxy Z Fold8 and Galaxy Z Fold8 Ultra are designed to adapt to whatever comes your way.”

News.title: Woman, 75, dies following burglary at home as man, 81, hospitalised with cops launching urgent appeal for information
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

BURGLARY DEATH Woman, 75, dies following burglary at home as man, 81, hospitalised with cops launching urgent appeal for information

A 75-YEAR-OLD woman has died after a suspected violent burglary as an 81-year-old man was hospitalised.

Police have launched an urgent appeal, urging the public to come forward with information that could help their investigation.

Cops rushed to a home in Tollington Park, Finsbury Park at 9.20pm on Tuesday night, responding to reports of an aggravated burglary.

Paramedics from the London ambulance service also attended.





A 75-year-old woman and an 81-year-old were treated at the scene before being rushed to hospital.

The man was discharged the next day, but the woman died in hospital on Wednesday.

A post mortem is set to take place.

The crime scene on Evershot Road remains secured as cops gather evidence.

Detective Chief Inspector Ben Massink said: “We’re at an early stage of this investigation and awaiting a post-mortem examination to determine how the woman died, with my team working hard to pursue all lines of enquiry.”

He stressed that “no detail is too small” to present to police.

Massink added: “We thank those who have already come forward to provide witness accounts, and appeal for anyone with information or doorbell footage to come forward.

“We believe a number of residents in the area will have key information that could help inform our investigation.”



Superintendent Mark Hambleton said: “Our thoughts remain with the woman’s family and friends at this unimaginably difficult time.

“We recognise the concern this will cause locally and can reassure the community that officers are working tirelessly to determine what happened.

“There will be an increased police presence in place while enquiries continue and we thank the public for their understanding at this time.”

Anyone with information is asked to call police on 101, quoting CAD7757/12AUG, or contact Crimestoppers anonymously on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Huge £20,000 reward issued for information to locate man who disappeared 18 years ago aged 16 from his home
News.content:
FIND HIM Huge £20,000 reward issued for information to locate man who disappeared 18 years ago aged 16 from his home

A HUGE £20,000 reward has been offered by detectives searching for a man who vanished from his home 18 years ago as a teenager.

Alex Sloley was just 16 years old when he was reported missing from Islington in August 2008.



Alex’s disappearance sparked an extensive Metropolitan Police investigation that continues to be regularly reviewed for fresh leads despite it occurring nearly two decades ago.

Cops have disclosed that Alex was a victim of exploitation who was being coerced into criminality by local gangs at the time he went missing.



Investigating officers now want to hear from anyone who was similarly exploited by gangs in North London around 2008 and may hold crucial information.

Police have released two potential e-fits of Alex that could show what he looks like aged 34.

Detective Chief Inspector Sarb Kaur said: “We are continuing our efforts to find Alex and support his family who have spent the past 18 years desperately wanting answers.

“We are aware that at the time he went missing, Alex was a victim of exploitation and was being coerced into criminality by gangs in the area.

“We are looking to speak with anyone who believes they were exploited by gangs in North London around 2008 and may have seen Alex or have information to contact us.

“You will not be in trouble, but you may hold key information which could help us piece the jigsaw together.



“A £20,000 reward is on offer to anyone who provides information which could lead us to Alex.

“Over time allegiances can change and we hope that the offer of this substantial reward could help someone with information to come forward.”

The Met Police first received a report from Alex’s family on 8 August 2008 after they had not seen or heard from him.



An investigation was immediately launched, with officers gathering statements from Alex’s family and friends while reviewing CCTV from the surrounding area.

At the time he disappeared, Alex was described as being around 5ft 5ins tall, of medium build, and with striking blue eyes.

Repeated public appeals made over the years have yielded multiple reported sightings, but detectives hope the substantial reward will finally provide the breakthrough needed to locate him.



Cops urged anyone with information to come forward immediately and “do the right thing” despite the age of the case.

DCI Kaur added: “Over the years following the appeals we have made, our officers have reviewed hundreds of reports from people who believe they’ve seen Alex in London.

“Unfortunately, this information is yet to provide investigating officers with the information needed to find him.

“Alongside this appeal, we are continuing to put Alex’s image out there, both at the time he went missing and how he may look now at the age of 34, in case anyone has seen him and can contact us.

“We remain committed to this investigation which I believe can be solved.”



Anyone who has any information can contact the investigation team directly, via phone or text message on 07860 369 603.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Alternatively, information can be provided via 101 or submitted online.

Information can also be provided anonymously to independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.

News.title: Burnham came to power promising radical change – the signs are that it won’t be for the better
News.content:
Growing pains

ONE of Andy Burnham’s key slogans since becoming Prime Minister is “growth in every postcode”.

Whatever that means.



Yesterday’s quarterly GDP figures show there is still a very long way to go.

Despite the promises, growth has basically flat-lined for over two years.



Tax rises have squeezed incomes and businesses, while giant welfare bills have become a massive drag on the economy.

That has left the construction industry in ruins, shattering any hopes that the Government can build the 1.5million new homes it pledged.



More than one million young people are not in work, training or education as a result of Labour’s National Insurance and minimum wage increases.

What do Burnham and his Chancellor John Healey plan to do about either?

The signs are not good.

More taxes ALWAYS mean less growth. Yet Burnham is planning a wealth whack on individuals and property that will drive away entrepreneurs.



Closer ties with the dying EU won’t deliver growth either.

The ongoing Iran War also threatens to blow a huge hole in Healey’s plans at a time when he MUST ramp up defence spending.

The autumn, with no heatwaves or World Cup to boost spending, could see a painful economic slowdown ahead of Healey’s first Budget.

Burnham came to power promising radical change. The signs are that it won’t be for the better.

Hard Labour

YVETTE Cooper finally admits what most of the country may have decided a long time ago: Labour hasn’t been very good at being in government.



Turning on the man who made her Foreign Secretary, Cooper says Sir Keir Starmer’s hands-off style of management meant their first two years in power were wasted.

Certainly, there have been precious few upsides and plenty of disasters. Welfare up, taxes, spending and debt all up, inflation and unemployment both up and defence spending down.

The Chagos Islands giveaway, the endless U-turns. The Peter Mandelson scandal.

The only question is: Will Burnham prove to be any better?

Dawn of the dud

LABOUR truly is the party of the sneering metropolitan elite.



In response to a post on the struggles of the betting industry — which employs thousands and supports dozens of charities — Dawn Butler MP posted: “lol.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Laughing in the faces of ordinary punters who choose to spend hard-earned money on a harmless flutter is typical of a party that has lost all connection to its working-class roots.

Butler’s attitude reflects many within Labour’s ranks for whom the first instinct is always that Nanny Knows Best.

News.title: When Andy Burnham promised Brits growth in every postcode, did he really mean more illegal migrants?
News.content:
ARE you playing your part? Are you doing your fair share? The Prime Minister wants to know.

It turns out that going to work every day to put a roof over your own family’s head isn’t enough any more. And neither is paying thousands in taxes to fund other people’s families, too.



No, according to Andy Burnham, we all need to do more for the country by accepting our “fair share” of illegal migrants into our local neighbourhoods.

Mr Burnham says middle-class families need to “play their part” when it comes to asylum seeker accommodation, instead of leaving the burden to fall on poorer parts of the country.



He told the country this week: “We cannot have a situation where it’s only the poorest communities in the country that receive all of the dispersal of refugees and asylum seekers.

“I do believe all parts of the country need to work to play their part.”

No10 then doubled down, with a staffer insisting that the PM “feels the current system is unfair, and as a point of principle, he wants to see a redress of the distribution.

“He acknowledges that it would cost more money to do it more fairly, but that is what we need to do”.

Sorry, Prime Minister, but we don’t all have to play our part. We never asked for these people to come here and we don’t want them here.

And it’s not a “point of principle” for us all to have to endure the arrival of thousands of undocumented fighting-age men from far-flung places into our local hotels and residential roads to hang around on street corners, take illegal work and sexually harass teenage girls.



What the PM said is wrong on so many levels.

First, Mr Burnham appears to think that better-off people need to follow poor people who have “accepted” these illegal migrants into their areas.

They absolutely have not.

Illegal migrants have been imposed against their very clearly expressed wishes, and often in the face of opposition from local councils, too.

Apparently Mr Devolution doesn’t like local people power when it comes to asylum seeker accommodation.



Or has he somehow managed to miss all the protests outside asylum hotels in Epping, Crowborough, Canary Wharf, Bristol, Liverpool and Manchester, to name but a few?

The PM also assumes that the middle classes aren’t playing their part already when it’s their taxes which foot the bill for the many billions of pounds spent on migrant accommodation.

Many better-off areas are already sharing the burden, including my own local high street, where the only hotel now only houses asylum seekers.

Only 17 local authorities out of 361 have so far been spared the arrival of illegal migrants in their areas, which hardly suggests most Britons have dodged that particular bullet.

When Andy Burnham promised us “growth in every postcode” on his first day in No10, I don’t think most of us thought he meant that sort of growth.



What was most illuminating from Andy Burnham’s comments, however, was his inadvertent admission that having illegal migrants in your area isn’t necessarily a good thing.

Apparently it’s a burden that we all need to share rather than a blessing.

Who would’ve guessed that all these young men paying people smugglers are not in fact fine, upstanding engineers and doctors desperate to pick up litter and help little old ladies across the road to show their gratitude to us for giving them refuge?



And let’s face it, by calling on us all to share the burden, Andy Burnham was also admitting that he can’t and won’t solve the boats crisis. And he’s not even going to bother to pretend that he will.

Fewer than 300 migrants crossed the Channel on dinghies in December 2018 when the boats crisis first emerged.

It was such a big story at the time that then Home Secretary Sajid Javid had to cut short his family’s Christmas holiday to come home to deal with it.

Eight years later, we see 230 migrants arriving on just one boat in one day and the PM decides to hold an emergency Cobra meeting to discuss . . . the weather and whether to ban disposable barbecues.

Perhaps the only answer is for us all to follow in the footsteps of the Oxfordshire village of Piddington, where the 400 local residents have voted to hold a referendum on seceding from the United Kingdom to prevent 1,250 illegal migrant men from being housed just a few hundred yards away in Bicester barracks.



Meanwhile, all the MPs, charity workers, civil servants, human rights lawyers, BBC and Guardian staff who insist every arrival is a desperate refugee deserving of our sympathy can happily take all these young men into their local communities.

Or, better still, into their own homes.

We’ve seen one illegal immigrant landing on Britain’s shores every 14 minutes since Labour came to power two years ago.

And even though numbers have fallen since last year, most of the illegal boat migrant arrivals — largely fighting-age men from countries with alien cultures — are still here years later.

Indeed, some 200,000 illegal migrants have arrived here since 2018.



And we are still paying for most of them to the tune of some £4billion a year.

It’s not only better-off folk who don’t want illegal migrants in their streets. NO ONE wants them.

We don’t want them in four-star hotels or two-star hotels. We don’t want them in flats, barges or former Army barracks. We don’t want them, full stop.

Spreading asylum seekers around a few more postcodes, shuffling them from inner city sink estates to leafy villages, isn’t the solution to this problem.

The solution is to stop allowing more illegal boat arrivals into our country and to detain and deport the ones who are already here.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The one thing Andy Burnham is right about is that the current system is unfair — but it’s unfair to all British people.

The only “point of principle” he should be caring about when it comes to illegal migrants isn’t which postcode they live in but that people who have no right to live in Britain should not be here at all.

News.title: Clacton by-election result live: Nigel Farage refuses to attend as he beats Count Binface to return as MP
News.content:
Reform UK leader Nigel Farage has won the Clacton by-election. He is the first successful Parliamentary candidate in over 40 years to miss his victory declaration, instead partying with supporters at an invite-only 'Farage Fest'

Clacton by-election result live: Nigel Farage refuses to attend as he beats Count Binface to return as MP

Nigel Farage has been successfully re-elected as the MP for Clacton.

He will become the first successful Parliamentary candidate in over 40 years to miss his victory declaration.

The under-fire Reform UK leader picked up 22,239 votes in the Clacton by-election, ensuring he will return as the constituency's MP. His main rival, parody candidate Count Binface, was backed by thousands of voters with a turnout of just over 44.4 percent.

The Reform UK leader, who has been locked in a humiliating showdown with Count Binface for more than a month, spent the night partying with activists at an invite-only 'Farage Fest' nearby. He told supporters Essex Police had told him of an "organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result that will take place in a few hours' time". A speech scheduled for later this morning has also been cancelled.

It is the first time a victorious candidate has missed the election count since imprisoned IRA hunger striker Bobby Sands did so in 1981.

Despite Mr Farage's comments the count continued, with staff told there was "no issue" with continuing. Binface, who was present, told The Mirror he was "flattered" by how hard Reform had campaigned in order to beat him.

The vote - expected to cost the taxpayer more than £250,000 - was triggered by the Reform chief quitting as an MP earlier this summer. He was facing a Commons probe into the failure to declare a £5million gift he received from Thai-based crypto billionaire, Christopher Harborne, ahead of the 2024 general election.

News.title: Stourbridge fires live: Child among 10 injured as Andy Burnham issues wildfire update
News.content:
A total of 11 wildfires have broken out in the West Midlands, with a child injured in Stourbridge and six homes gutted by by the flames that are still raging this morning

News.title: Met Office maps show heavy rain in 10 UK regions on Friday
News.content:
Met Office maps show heavy rain in 10 UK regions on Friday

It's set to be a 'thundery' end to the country's fifth heatwave, which has brought 38C temperatures, more wildfires, deepening drought fears, and concerns for nurses collapsing on baking hot wards

View 3 Images Heavy rain will give Scotland a very wet start on Friday

Thunderstorms are set to soak most of the UK on Friday as forecasters believe up to an inch rain will fall.

‌



The latest Met Office forecast for Friday (August 14) shows showers will cover most of the country, with heavy rain expected in multiple areas. Weather maps show 10 regions of the country will get wet at some point.

‌



It’s a ‘thundery’ end to the country’s fifth heatwave of the summer, and a huge contrast from just 24 hours earlier, when Brits saw the hottest day of the year with 38.1C recorded in Kew Gardens, London.

‌



Rain will be a welcome relief for some as most of England and Wales is in drought, and wildfires have raged across parts of the country in a record-breaking summer.

The Met Office said: “Hot and sunny in the southeast. Increasingly humid for Wales and western/northern England with variable cloud and possible afternoon thunderstorms.

View 3 Images It will be dry for most at 2pm, aside from heavy rain in the Yorkshire Dales

‌



“Fresher, albeit rather cloudy, conditions for Northern Ireland and Scotland after early heavy and thundery rain clears the east.”

This evening’s forecast is: “Thunderstorms pushing eastwards overnight, with heavy downpours particularly possible over eastern England.

“Warm and muggy in the southeast, but fresher than recent nights elsewhere. A few showers for northern Scotland.”

‌



Weather maps released overnight show a wet start for most of Scotland, where an inch of rain could fall in central parts of the country at 5am. By 8am, that band of rain moves out to the North Sea, but scattered showers are present across the country.

It will be dry for the vast majority at lunchtime, although some rain will hit north Wales and Northern Ireland.

There will also be some heavy isolated rain expected in northern England in early afternoon, around the Yorkshire Dales.

‌



View 3 Images By 11pm, heavy rain will return for some areas

Those clouds will move eastwards, bringing a lot of precipitation to the north east of England, East Yorkshire, and the East Midlands in the evening.

As the evening progresses, those areas will see more heavy rain, while the south west and East Anglia will see lighter showers.

News.title: Tourists evacuated in Greece by boat as wildfires rage near  Halkidiki beaches
News.content:
Tourists evacuated in Greece by boat as wildfires rage near Halkidiki beaches

Heatwaves across have contributed to tinderbox conditions and weather forecasters have predicted winds of up to 100km/h on Friday - wildfires could spread quickly

View 4 Images Tourists flee beaches after wildfires breakout in Greece

Tourists have fled resorts and been evacuated by small boats as wildfires ravaged a region of northern Greece.

‌



Hundreds of tourists were evacuated from beaches in the area, while water-bombing planes, helicopters and firefighters battled to stop the blaze on Thursday, August 13.

‌



Heatwaves across Europe this summer have contributed to tinderbox conditions in Spain, France and Greece. Unprecedented amounts of land have been scorched.

‌



In the northern Greek region of Halkidiki, the area's dense pine forests helped the raging fire. Authorities banned the public from entering the region's pine forests.

View 4 Images Firemen work to extinguish a wildfire near the village of Siviri, northern Greece (Image: Getty)

Homes and popular resorts were destroyed within hours of the fire breaking out and the country's civil protection agency sent evacuation warnings by phone to people in the two resorts.

‌



As the blaze approached from inland, flames charred holiday apartments and their sea-facing balconies.

Fire service officials and ERT public television said more than 480 tourists in bathing costumes were evacuated by sea in small boats and coast guard and fire brigade vessels.

View 4 Images People evacuated on small boats, with some taken to a ship waiting at sea (Image: Getty)

‌



People wearing face masks, some holding children or pets, boarded dinghies and boats in the seaside town.

A fire service spokesman said the evacuation had to be by sea as the flames were getting close to the beaches.

Some were moved to nearby beaches, while about 200 tourists were taken to a ship waiting at sea.

Article continues below

View 4 Images People evacuate on small boats during a wildfire near the village of Siviri, northern Greece, on August 13, 2026 (Image: Getty)

A three-kilometer-long wall of flames up to 30 meters high was closing in on the resorts, according to reports.

Weather forecasters have predicted winds of up to 100km/h on Friday, posing the threat that wildfires could quickly spread.

News.title: 'No cosmetic surgery is worth risking a life - and the warnings must be heard'
News.content:
'No cosmetic surgery is worth risking a life - and the warnings must be heard'

"The Mirror has repeatedly exposed the dangers surrounding poorly regulated cosmetic tourism and called for stronger safeguards. Those warnings must be heard"

View Image Voice of the Mirror has its say...

Hayley Dowell travelled to Turkey for cosmetic surgery and never returned to her husband and three children.

‌



Her inquest has heard that she had intended to undergo liposuction and a tummy tuck, only to be offered a discounted Brazilian butt-lift minutes before surgery and given just five minutes to make the decision. That raises profoundly serious questions about how major medical procedures are being sold to British patients abroad.

‌



Hayley died after suffering a fat embolism linked to liposuction. Her death should serve as a stark warning that cosmetic surgery, wherever it is carried out, is surgery. It carries risks that cannot be reduced to a price list or a last-minute offer.

‌



The Mirror has repeatedly exposed the dangers surrounding poorly regulated cosmetic tourism and called for stronger safeguards. Those warnings must be heard.

People considering treatment overseas deserve clear information, proper consent and rigorous standards of care. No cosmetic procedure is worth risking a life.

Water joke

Households have every right to be furious at the prospect of yet another water bill rise.

‌



For years, customers have paid more while pipes leak, sewage pours into rivers and seas, and executives pocket huge rewards. Now five firms could be allowed to reach into billpayers’ pockets again to fund another £3.4billion of spending.

Andy Burnham is right. Customers cannot be treated as a blank cheque for an industry that has badly failed the country.

Thames Water alone is drowning in more than £20billion of debt, yet somehow found £1million for its finance chief’s sign-on payment. Investment in crumbling infrastructure is desperately needed. But ordinary families should not endlessly be forced to pay for corporate failure.

‌



The water companies created this mess. They must shoulder far more of the cost.

Forever bonds

Good friends really can be good for your health.

A huge global study suggests that strong adult friendships help protect us from stress, boost self-esteem, and improve mental and physical well-being.

Article continues below

Family bonds matter too, but the message is wonderfully simple: friendships made and nurtured throughout life can make us healthier and happier.

News.title: Having great friends through adulthood is key to lifelong good health
News.content:
Having great friends through adulthood is key to lifelong good health

A study of 205,000 people in 22 countries finds quality social connections in adulthood appear even more important than positive family ties in childhood for health

View 4 Images Having good friends appears one of the biggest determinants of health (Image: Getty Images)

Strong friendships through adulthood are vital for lifelong health, a global study shows.

‌



Good social connections then appear to be even more important than positive family ties in childhood according to the research into 205,000 people in 22 countries. Experts say relationships protect against stress, boost self-esteem and help people manage their emotions in a positive way.

‌



The study published in the Journal of Mental Health involved participants from countries including the UK, United States, Australia, Argentina, Brazil, Germany, Spain and India. Study lead author Dr Veli Durmu, of Kutahya Health Sciences University in Turkey, said: "I found that people who were more satisfied with their friendships and relationships also tended to report better mental and physical health.

‌



View 4 Images Previous research has shown the number and quality of personal ties influence mental and bodily well-being from birth onwards. (Image: Getty Images)

"While these findings suggest that childhood relationships matter, they do not tell the whole story. People's social environments continue to change throughout life, and friendships, partnerships and other relationships may strengthen or modify the influence of earlier experiences."

Previous research has shown the number and quality of personal ties influence mental and bodily well-being from birth onwards.

‌



View 4 Images Participants were asked the extent to which they agreed or disagreed that they were content or satisfied with their friendships and relationships. (Image: Getty Images)

Dr Durmu analysed data from 204,907 adults aged 18 and over from the Global Flourishing Study to determine what factors help humans to flourish throughout life. It covers countries in Europe, the Americas, Asia, Oceania, the Middle East, and Africa.

Participants were asked the extent to which they agreed or disagreed that they were content or satisfied with their friendships and relationships.

‌



Childhood connections with mothers and fathers were scored on a scale from "very good" to "very bad". Those taking part in the survey also had to rate their mental and physical health from "poor" to "excellent".

View 4 Images Friendships in adulthood appear crucial for health (Image: Getty Images/Image Source)

People who reported the highest contentment with friendships and for satisfaction with relationships also tended to report better overall mental and physical health. A similar, although weaker, pattern emerged among participants who reported very good childhood relationships with their parents.

‌



The research team attempted to take into account income, education and other factors. Being married, having sufficient money, and identifying with a religion was associated with better mental and physical health scores.

Mental health scores were lower among people in their mid-thirties to late forties compared with those aged 18 to 34, but higher among those aged 65 and above.

People living in Indonesia scored highest for contentment with friendships and relationships, and lowest among those in Japan.

Article continues below

Dr Durmu said: "These findings show why social connections should be considered an important part of overall health and well-being. With this in mind, public health planning and prevention strategies should include the impact on mental and physical wellbeing of how people connect with others and with their families."

News.title: Horrifying moment toddler is dragged along street after getting caught in bus doors
News.content:
Horrifying moment toddler is dragged along street after getting caught in bus doors

The incident took place just months after a schoolboy was trapped in the automatic doors of a bus and dragged 350 metres before the bus driver noticed

View 3 Images The boy's legs became trapped and the bus pulled away from the pavement (Image: 9News)

Terrifying footage has capture the moment a toddler was dragged along a street after his legs got stuck in a bus door.

‌



The boy, believed to be aged between three and five, boarded the bus with a man in Melbourne, Australia at around 5pm on June 5.

‌



Around 15 minutes later, the pair tried to disembark but the doors began to close.

‌



CCTV footage released this week showed the moment the doors shut before the child was off the bus.

View 3 Images Authorities are working work to identify the pair (Image: 9News)

His legs became trapped and the bus pulled away from the pavement.

‌



The man, believed to be the boy's parent or guardian, tried to pull him from the moving vehicle.

Passengers, in complete shock, shouted for the bus driver to stop.

Authorities are working work to identify the pair.

‌



Public Transport Users Association spokesperson Tony Morton said the incident demonstrates the transport network must have stronger structural safeguards.

"This appears to be a case where things have just not really been attended to properly, and there's been a lapse in some of the basic safety there," he told Australian news outlet 9News.

View 3 Images The man desperately clung to the boy (Image: 9News)

‌



The state's bus safety regulator has issued a call for the man, witnesses or anyone who helped the pair to come forward.

Bus operator described the incident as distressing.

It said it has reinforced safety protocols with all drivers.

Article continues below

Just months earlier, a 12-year-old boy was dragged along a road in Melbourne after his bag and right arm became caught in the automatic bus doors.

He was dragged for about 350 metres down the street before the bus driver noticed.

News.title: Dad charged with murder to face trial over death of nine-year-old daughter
News.content:
Dad charged with murder to face trial over death of nine-year-old daughter

Christopher Rice, 35, of Wakefield, appeared at Forfar Sheriff Court for a second time after being charged with murder following the death of his nine-year-old daughter Minnie Merriman

View 2 Images (Image: Police Scotland/PA Wire)

A dad charged with murder following the death of his nine-year-old daughter in Arbroath is facing trial after appearing in court for a second time.

Minnie Merriman, from West Yorkshire, was found injured just after midnight on August 3 at the Elliot industrial estate in the Angus town, while her family were camping in the area.

She was taken to Ninewells Hospital in Dundee, where she later died. Her father Christopher Rice, 35, of Wakefield, West Yorkshire, appeared at Forfar Sheriff Court last week charged with murder.

View 2 Images Forensic officers at Elliot Industrial Estate Arbroath (Image: Daily Record)

He made a further appearance in private at the same court on Thursday. He did not enter a plea and was fully committed and remanded in custody.

The date of his next court appearance is yet to be confirmed.

Minnie’s family previously paid tribute to her in a statement released through Police Scotland.

They said: “We are devastated with the loss of our beloved, absolutely incredible, beautiful and brave Minnie Moo. Our family asks that our privacy is respected at this extremely difficult time.”

Article continues below

There was a police presence in the area for a number of days following the incident while further investigations were carried out.

Floral tributes were also left at the scene. It is understood West Yorkshire Police supported Police Scotland’s investigation.

News.title: Farage's by-election victory won't stop questions about finances
News.content:
Nigel Farage did not turn up to savour his victory in the by-election he triggered himself.

Overnight he told a rally of Reform UK supporters he had been advised there was an "organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result" and wanted to avoid being "demeaned and humiliated by nobodies".

When the official result did come in hours later, it confirmed the Reform UK leader had indeed won this by-election convincingly with 22,239 votes, but without any serious opposition after the other main parties did not put up candidate.

Farage's allies say he has been both emboldened and re-energised by this race, and it is not difficult to work out why.

He is clearly popular in the constituency, his party has had a commanding lead in national opinion polls for much of the past 18 months, and he has achieved something remarkable in turning his upstart organisation into a mass-membership movement with a serious chance of getting into government.

But today's result won't stop the Metropolitan Police investigation into donations to Reform UK, questions about Farage's friendship with a convicted fraudster, or the parliamentary investigation into why he did not register a Â£5m gift from a billionaire donor.

And given Farage triggered this race and the result was entirely predictable, what was the point of it all?

When he made his surprise announcement last month that he was resigning to run for a seat he already represented, the Reform leader said "the people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions" - and he wanted to "fight to continue the political revolution that Reform has started".

Could he have predicted that continuing his "revolution" would descend into a bizarre electoral battle involving a record 34 candidates, a 90cm long ballot paper, with his most prominent challenger being a man dressed as a bin?

Labour say Farage has been trying to "dodge scrutiny", and the Conservatives argue he triggered this race because he was having a "hissy fit".

One thing the Reform UK leader could have anticipated is the cost. In a constituency with the most deprived neighbourhood in England, the council estimates taxpayers will need to fork out Â£250,000 for the organisation of this by-election. Reform UK has offered to foot the bill, but that is not allowed under electoral law.

Now the election is over, Farage is likely to face renewed scrutiny on those outstanding questions about his finances.

News.title: NHS service admits data breach due to pager use
News.content:
The sensitive medical data of transplant patients from across the UK was routinely sent over an unencrypted pager network, an NHS service has admitted.

A BBC investigation found NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT) sent the names, dates of birth and types of organs being offered or needed to members of hospital transplant teams who were using pagers, unaware they were not encrypted.

In 2019, then-Health Secretary Matt Hancock announced the NHS in England should stop using pagers by 2021, but some parts of the organisation have continued doing so.

NHSBT said it was "deeply sorry" and has reported the data breach to the Information Commissioner. It added it has now stopped sending patient data in this way.

Pagers are small battery operated radio receivers - popular in the 1980s and 1990s - that can receive short text messages, numbers to call, or alerts.

They are a one-way communication system and only able to receive messages, not send them, which was why they largely fell out of public use as more and more people started carrying mobile phones.

News.title: Final day of heatwave for many before weekend cooldown
News.content:
Kew Gardens in London reached 38.1C on Thursday, making it the UK's hottest day of 2026 so far, and the fifth hottest UK day on record.

It is also the second time this year that the temperature has reached 38C, after Lingwood, Norfolk recorded 38.0C on 26 June.

This is only the second time that 38C has been reached twice in the same year - the previous occasion being 2022.

Though the Met Office amber warning for extreme heat that covered large swathes of England on Thursday expired at midnight, high temperatures will linger in central and eastern parts of England on Friday.

Long spells of sunshine will lift temperatures to 29-34C (84-93F) across large parts of the Midlands, Lincolnshire, East Anglia and the south-east.

For many places it will mark a third consecutive day above official heatwave thresholds.

The heat will ease elsewhere.

Somewhat cooler conditions will begin to move into northern and western parts of the UK, although temperatures will generally remain above the norm for the time of year - widely reaching the low to mid-20s Celsius.

Many places will be dry with a mix of cloud and sunny spells although a few showers are possible, and these could be heavy and thundery in some places.

News.title: 'Two out of four, baby' - Hunt wins 200m as she eyes historic quadruple
News.content:
Britain's Amy Hunt charged to 200m glory to secure her second gold medal of the European Championships - but the sprinter has her sights set on a historic quadruple in Birmingham.

The 24-year-old wants to "be iconic" and become the first athlete to win four European gold medals in the same tournament.

And after triumphing in the 100m on Monday, she added another gold to her collection with a season's best time of 22.19 seconds in the 200m final on Thursday.

Hunt reeled in rival and compatriot Asher-Smith down the back straight to cross the line first.

"Two out of four, baby!" Hunt told BBC TV.

"This is becoming a magical week and one I will remember for the rest of my life."

Hunt is set to compete in the women's and mixed 4x100m relay events later and says there will be "no celebrations and no champagne until Sunday night".

"I have got a debt to the ladies," she said.

"We have got to come out here and make sure we show them who the best sprinting nation is in Europe."

Asher-Smith was beaten to silver by just 0.01 seconds by Ireland's Rhasidat Adeleke, who set a new national record.

"It unfolded exactly how I thought it would," two-time European 200m silver medallist Nethaneel Mitchell-Blake said on BBC Radio 5 Live.

"I knew Dina would run a blistering bend and then say 'Amy, come and catch me'. And that's what Amy has done."

News.title: How a major oil slick started washing up on Iran's beaches
News.content:
Verified videos show a major oil slick washing up on Iran's Qeshm Island, which analysts have said comes from a ship hit by a strike in the Strait of Hormuz.

BBC Verify has also analysed satellite imagery suggesting the oil spill originated from an attack on a vessel in Omani waters on 3 August. A week later, the apparent fuel leakage from the Minoan Pioneer bulk carrier had spread across a large area of the strait.

Environmental experts say the spill threatens wildlife, protected ecosystems and fishing communities around Qeshm, which is home to mangrove forests, nearby coral reef habitats and nesting sites for critically endangered Hawksbill turtles.

Iranian media initially reported the origin of the pollution was under investigation and Iran's foreign ministry spokesman said on Thursday its source was a "foreign bulk ship".

A local environmental protection official has since said the spill has been "almost completely cleaned up". BBC Verify has not been able to independently confirm this.

News.title: Mangione lawyers to meet federal prosecutors amid reports of plea deal
News.content:
Attorneys for Luigi Mangione, who is accused of killing United Healthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York, are meeting federal prosecutors on Friday amid US media reports of a potential plea agreement.

Mangione faces two federal charges of stalking resulting in death, each carrying a maximum sentence of life in prison. It was not immediately clear which charges are under discussion.

"There's a conference scheduled for 11 am on Friday, and that's all we can say at this time," Jamie McDonald, the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), said this week.

Mangione also faces a separate state trial over Thompson's death. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges in both cases.

Discussion of a plea deal does not guarantee one will be reached, and such arrangements can fall apart before they are finalised.

Deals must also be approved by the court, and a separate hearing is typically scheduled for the defendant to enter a new plea.

Federal prosecutors brought the stalking charges against Mangione, alleging he travelled between states and carried out electronic surveillance with the intention of killing or harming Thompson. Prosecutors allege those actions resulted in Thompson's death.

A federal judge threw out two other charges in January, including that of murder through use of a firearm, which had carried the possibility of the death penalty.

Mangione's attorneys, the SDNY, and Manhattan District Attorney's office did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

His attorneys have previously argued he should not be tried in both state and federal court. At the moment, the judges presiding over both cases have allowed the trials to proceed.

But if Mangione pleads guilty in his federal case, it could open the door for his attorneys to argue the state case runs afoul of double jeopardy â a constitutional protection that prevents an individual from being prosecuted twice for the same crime.

New York's state constitution has its own prohibition on double jeopardy, which, if invoked here, could have a knock-on effect on Mangione's upcoming state trial.

"If a federal prosecution has been completed on a matter, the state cannot prosecute the matter on those same facts," said Mitchell Epner, a white-collar attorney.

There is still little clarity on what happens to the state case in that scenario.

Mark Chutkow, a white-collar defence attorney at the Dkyema law firm, said it is "kind of a live issue".

Chutkow the judge in the state trial would have to determine whether the charges overlap enough to trigger New York's double jeopardy statute, while Manhattan prosecutors may argue their case is distinct enough to proceed.

Mangione's state trial is scheduled to begin on 8 September, while the federal trial is listed for January 2027.

News.title: Count Binface receives nearly a quarter of votes in Clacton's by-election
News.content:
Count Binface, the self-styled intergalactic space warrior, has received nearly 10,000 votes in the Clacton by-election, his best performance yet.

The much-photographed election veteran was the main rival to Reform UK leader Nigel Farage in an election race caused by Farage resigning, only to run again - which sparked a mass boycott by the other main UK parties.

Farage has re-won his seat, receiving more than 22,000 votes in Clacton, on the Essex coast.

Binface received 26.9% of the vote while Farage won 63.3%. Binface had his highest share yet with 9,455 votes, having lost to no fewer than three prime ministers, and one who later became prime minister, in previous attempts.

But how many votes has he previously received? And where does he fit into the British tradition of spoofing politicians?

News.title: BBC Verify speaks to woman who filmed ICE agent pointing gun at her
News.content:
A video showing a US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agent pointing his gun at a woman has been viewed by millions after she shared the moment on Instagram.

Carolina Molina says she was out delivering business cards in Falls Church, Virginia, when she saw ICE agents, who then surrounded her car.

The US Department of Homeland Security said she "attempted to harm officers by weaponising her vehicle". Molina denies this.

BBC Verify assesses the dashcam footage shared by Molina. Jake Horton reports.

Produced by Tom Joyner. Graphics by Mark Edwards.

News.title: Ice cream man hit with noise complaint over van's music
News.content:
An ice cream man has been hit with a noise complaint by someone who did not like the loud chimes from his van.

Mark Edwards was contacted by the council after a Tonyrefail resident complained about the van's music being played in the evening.

He said he had been serving the area for more than 20 years without a complaint and was determined "not to let one individual spoil it for everybody else". He has agreed with customers to beep his horn in each street so they know he is there.

Rhondda Cynon Taf council said it received a noise complaint in June relating to music being played after 20:00 BST, which it investigated and found to be valid.

Edwards, from Trebanog, said he was taken aback when he found a letter from the council on the van's dashboard: "Twenty-odd years and I have never had anything like this at all. It's unbelievable."

He said his employer told him to stop operating in the area because continuing to use the chimes could result in a fine, but he did not want to stop serving customers, so came up with the alternative plan.

"I thought 'I'm not going to let one individual to spoil it for everybody else', so have come to an arrangement with my customers in the area.

"They know roughly what time I'm there and I toot the horn in each street, and they all come out and enjoy it. They're not going to beat me."

The council said the law required a 19:00 cut-off time for ice cream van operators to use their chimes, but it did not "prevent them from trading after this time".

It added that Edwards had been sent a letter reminding him of these requirements and that it considered the matter closed.

News.title: Top grades rise again as students get A-level, T-level and BTec results
News.content:
Hundreds of thousands of students in England, Wales and Northern Ireland have opened their A-level, T-level and BTec results on Thursday morning.

The percentage of top A-level grades edged up again, and a record number of students found out they had secured a place at university.

The cost of going to university has been in the spotlight this year, with mounting pressure on the government to reform student loan repayments, and there has been a renewed focus on technical education under Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

But the chief executive of Universities UK, which represents more than 140 vice-chancellors, urged students to not "let politicians make your decision for you".

The percentage of A* and A grades at A-level increased to 28.5% across England, Wales and Northern Ireland this year, up from 28.3% last year.

About 40% of 18-year-olds in England receive A-levels every summer.

Around 250,000 grades for vocational and technical qualifications were also released to students in England.

These include BTec National, Cambridge Technical, Cambridge Advanced National and T-level results.

Almost 20,000 students completed a T-level in 2026, with a pass rate of over 90%.

Launched in 2020, T-levels are two-year technical courses that are taken after GCSEs. They focus more on practical subjects than academic ones, but are an equivalent qualification to three A-levels.

AS-levels, which will count towards students' final A-level results next summer in Wales and Northern Ireland, have also been released.

This year, the pass rate for National 5, Higher and Advanced Higher exams in Scotland rose across the board.

News.title: Son of 102-year-old says father died after being 'pushed off stage'
News.content:
Robert said: "He just asked them to turn the music down."

He said his father turned around to come back down off the stage when he was pushed, and that resulted in a broken hip.

"[That's] the most upsetting part. He wasn't going to live forever but it's not a nice way, obviously in pain," he said.

"We want to see justice, of course.

"They must have known he was an old man. It makes you wonder what the world is coming to.

"It has obviously made it difficult. It would've been nice if he'd gone quietly in his sleep.

"He was in hospital, suffering, for a week-and-a-half. It's not nice.

"I feel sad - even though he could be difficult because of his age and dementia, still, you get used to him being around," he said.

Robert, a retired civil engineer, said his father used to visit the Crow's Nest.

"What happened is not nice. The pub has changed a lot over the years. It has become a youngsters' pub," he said.

Robert said he grew up in the home in the the Llanyrafon neighbourhood where his father had lived since 1960.

He said his dad had a career as a design draughtsman and had lived alone since his wife died 40 years ago.

"Me and my brother would visit our father regularly, and clean the house and buy him food.

"His eyesight had deteriorated and he had been diagnosed with dementia two or three years ago."

Robert said: "He's well-known around here, although a lot of his generation are gone," he added.

He said his father would visit the pub two or three times a week, where he would drink beers, and described how he became a familiar face to some locals.

"I suppose he became a pub character," he added.

News.title: Couple tie the knot on 'magical' solar eclipse day
News.content:
Wednesday's full eclipse may be something many of us remember for a long time: the special glasses, the colanders, and the eerie shadowing of the sun.

And for one couple, it was especially unforgettable as they got married during the once-in-a-generation event.

Jerry and Jamie Bone, from Gosfield, Essex, planned their big day around the astronomical phenomenon - the first total solar eclipse visible over mainland Europe since 1999 - and tied the knot in Alpheton, near Sudbury, Suffolk.

Jamie said they had realised a few years ago the eclipse would take place in 2026, and decided it would be the "perfect" day to get married.

News.title: Bonnie Tyler's classic hit spiked in streams during solar eclipse
News.content:
Born Gaynor Hopkins in a council house in Neath, Tyler grew up with a love for music before she was discovered by talent scout Roger Bell in a Swansea club.

Tyler released her first single, Lost in France in 1977, but it was the release of Total Eclipse of the Heart five years later which changed her life.

The ballad spent two weeks at UK number one and four weeks in the US.

The iconic love song's music video surpassed 1.2 billion views on YouTube and has had over a billion streams on Spotify.

Spotify previously said it had paid out more than $1.4 million for streams of Tyler's catalogue in 2025.

The music platform said Total Eclipse of the Heart was one of a few "celestial" songs that saw a streaming spike in the UK on 12 August.

According to Spotify, the biggest increases in UK streams during the eclipse were:

Evolfo, Moon Eclipsed the Sun (+12,817%)

Chris Staples, Dark Side of the Moon (+2,805%)

Pink Floyd, Eclipse (+594%)

Delta Goodrem, Eclipse (+104%)

Bonnie Tyler, Total Eclipse of the Heart (+94%)

Bill Withers, Ain't No Sunshine (+17%)

Shannon Carragher, senior editor at Spotify, said: "It is always fascinating to see how major cultural events instantly reflect in what the UK is listening to.

"Cultural phenomena like the solar eclipse naturally bring people together and we instinctively look for the perfect soundtrack to share that moment."

Ahead of the solar eclipse, Tyler's McVitie's Jaffa Cakes TV advert also resurfaced - it was originally broadcast in 2023 when there was a partial lunar eclipse.

The nostalgic advert came after research revealed almost half (49%) of Brits did not understand how eclipses occurred.

In the video, Tyler uses a Jaffa Cake as a prop to describe the different types of eclipse.

She said: "There are three types of eclipse. You've got the lunar eclipse, the solar eclipse, and then there's the total eclipse of the heart.

"When the earth is situated between the moon and the sun it creates a shadow, and when it looks like someone has just taken a bite out of the moon. That's a partial lunar eclipse."

The grammy-nominated star had a string of other hits, including Holding out for a Hero and also represented the UK at the Eurovision Song Contest in 2013.

She was named in the Queen's last Birthday Honours list in 2022 and was awarded an MBE for her services to music by Prince William the following year.

Tyler died "unexpectedly" on 8 July, aged 75, at a Portugal hospital, "as a result of the illness that she was being treated for", her family said in a statement released on the star's official website, external.

At the time, tributes poured in from a host of friends and stars including Catherine Zeta-Jones, Bryan Adams and Rod Stewart.

Tyler's funeral service will take place on 17 August at 12:00 BST at St Mary's Church in Swansea.

It has since been confirmed that her coffin will be brought to her Mumbles home on 15 August at 15:30 BST.

People are invited to "pay their respects" by lining Newton Road at 15:15 BST.

News.title: Honeytrap thieves jailed for killing men they had drugged
News.content:
A couple who drugged men seeking sexual services in order to steal from them have been jailed for killing two men and poisoning others.

Adina Mihai and Madalin Dumitru admitted the manslaughter of Gary Mouat, 37, from Oxfordshire, and Malcolm King, 80, from Gloucestershire, in 2025 and 2024 respectively.

On the first day of their trial in June, the pair also each admitted two further counts of administering poison to surviving victims.

Mihai, 31, and Dumitru, 30, were both sentenced to 17 years in prison at Oxford Crown Court.

Mihai, who posed as a sex worker, and her partner Dumitru, arranged to meet men paying for services she had advertised online at their homes.

The court heard four had their alcoholic drinks spiked with the powerful sedative gamma-butyrolactone (GBL) so the pair could steal from them.

Two men died as a result, while two others - who cannot be named due to reporting restrictions - survived.

News.title: Big Issue says vendors struggling as sales hit by heatwaves
News.content:
Big Issue vendors are struggling to sell magazines in the UK's extreme heat, which is having an "immediate" impact on their earnings, Big Issue's managing director says.

Sales of the British news and entertainment magazine are down on average 20% year on year in weeks where heatwaves have been declared, Catherine Parsons said.

During June's record-breaking temperatures, the worst-hit West Midlands and Wales saw 34% and 33% fewer sales respectively.

George Anderson, who sells the Big Issue near the BBC's Broadcasting House in London, says it is a struggle when footfall is lower and people would rather be near the aircon.

"People are uncomfortable, they don't want to hang around in the heat and chat," he told the BBC on the hottest day of the year.

"I manage it as best I can, and so far so good, but my sales are definitely down which can be quite tough."

Big Issue is sold by people experiencing homelessness or financial instability.

But Parsons said sellers are losing out on vital income due to the heatwaves.

"For most of us, extreme heat is an inconvenience. For Big Issue vendors, it means earning significantly less and making difficult decisions about rent, food and other essentials," she said.

In the week of 22 June, when the UK's June temperature record was broken and temperatures hit 37.7C (99.9F), Big Issue sales fell by an average of 22% compared to the same week the previous year, their figures show.

The latest spell of extreme heat marks the UK's fifth heatwave this year, with the Met Office warning this summer is on course to be the UK's hottest since records began.

Parsons said Big Issue teams were working to support vendors and had been handing out sunscreen, caps and water bottles.

"But in the most extreme temperatures, it's simply unsafe for vendors to be out and selling, and when the heat forces them to cut their working day short, the financial impact is immediate."

News.title: Did the eclipse damage your eyes?
News.content:
An eye surgeon says that fewer people have been seeking treatment for eye damage than after the UK's last total solar eclipse in 1999.

Millions across the UK on Wednesday witnessed the most significant solar eclipse in 27 years - which saw more than 90% of the Sun covered by the Moon.

Speaking to the BBC, Mr Alexander Ionides from Moorfield Eye Hospital said hospitals were "inundated" with worried patients in 1999, but said it seemed warnings about looking directly at the sun with the naked eye were "getting through".

He added that symptoms of eye damage can include a spot in the centre of your vision, which may appear grey or yellow. Symptoms can develop within hours, but sometimes take days to develop.

The by-election campaign in Clacton, with a man with a bin on his head a favourite among the record 34 candidates, was not short of a few surprises.

But news that Nigel Farage has reclaimed his seat will come as a shock to no one.

The Reform UK leader will hail today's result in Clacton as a victory against the establishment after taking 62.8 per cent of the vote, with his chief rival, Count Binface, in a distant second with 26.71 per cent.

But while he may have won the battle for the constituency of Clacton, he still risks losing the fight for the country.

Mr Farage’s approval rating has plummeted to the lowest since the 2024 general election, while Labour has leapfrogged Reform in the polls to lead for the first time since March 2025, helped by the boost in support since Andy Burnham became prime minister.

In fact, his ‘stunt’ by-election may actually have made his situation worse - and left his return to parliament potentially short-lived.

open image in gallery Farage enjoys a pint in the sun on polling day ( PA )

One of the strangest elections in recent years began when Mr Farage dramatically quit as an MP, just two years into the job, at the start of the summer.

Facing at least one probe over unregistered donations of cash and support, he accused his Westminster opponents of using sleaze investigations as a “political tool” against him and insisted he had done nothing wrong.

At the time, he declared: “I’ve decided that the people of Clacton should be the judges of my actions. This will be a people versus the establishment by-election.”

The problem for Mr Farage, of course, is that the people of Clacton are not the only judges.

open image in gallery Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has pledged her party will stand if there is another by-election in Clacton ( PA Wire )

That baton falls, initially at least, to Daniel Greenberg, the Parliamentary Commissioner for Standards. The by-election has not halted his investigation into a £5m donation from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, which Mr Farage has struggled to explain. It merely paused it.

And the probe is expected to restart within hours now the result is known.

If the commissioner finds Mr Farage has broken strict parliamentary rules, he can trigger a series of steps that lead to a recall petition in Clacton. The signatures of just 10 per cent of voters would be enough to launch another by-election - and see Mr Farage fighting for his parliamentary career all over again.

Second time around, the voters of Clacton could start to tire of the Farage saga.

When The Independent visited the town last week, locals said they felt they had been made the butt of a joke that does little to serve their community.

Mr Farage will also face stiffer competition in any future by-election.

On Thursday the Reform leader’s main opponent was comic candidate Count Binface, after all the major parties boycotted what was described by former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer as a “desperate political stunt”.

However, Tory leader Kemi Badenoch has already pledged that her party will stand a candidate next time around. She wrote an open letter to the residents of Clacton earlier this week, telling them that they deserved better, and promising them that if there is another election, a Tory will be on the ballot paper.

open image in gallery Count Binface signage in Kirby Cross, ahead of a by-election triggered by Reform UK party leader ( Reuters )

No matter how the parliamentary process ends, the scrutiny that Mr Farage is facing will also not go away.

If anything, his shock decision to call a by-election has probably intensified it. That matters for the Reform leader, because he has made clear just how much he dislikes the attention on his affairs.

When he quit as an MP, he extraordinarily publicly confirmed reports in this publication that he had discussed walking away from politics altogether as pressure grew over his undeclared donations.

That press conference followed weeks of speculation about his future.

The usually headline-grabbing Reform leader had seemingly been sent underground over the previous few weeks by questions about the £5m donation. He even cancelled a high-profile appearance on the BBC's flagship Sunday morning political programme at the last minute, leaving Laura Kuenssberg to tell startled viewers: “His team told us, he’s changed his mind”.

That was followed by weeks of silence from the ex-Ukip leader.

At the same time, tensions were building behind the scenes within Reform. They bubbled over when not one but two senior Reform figures, including the party's former chairman Dr David Bull, went public with their call for Mr Farage to temporarily step back from political life.

It is in that context then that his decision to risk it all by quitting as an MP and forcing an election should be seen.

With the Clacton by-election, Mr Farage bet the house in a bid to win the war.

But he may find that he has merely survived the first skirmish.

Nigel Farage won the Clacton by-election.

The Reform UK leader pre-empted the official declaration by telling supporters he had won “fairly convincingly” and the result on the hottest day of the year was an “overwhelming endorsement” of him.

Speaking at an event organised by Reform UK in Essex on the same night as the count, the party’s leader celebrating surpassing the 21,225 votes he received just over two years ago.

Mr Farage said: “The verdict is now in, and it is a convincing, overwhelming win with more votes than we got in the General Election of 2024.

“In doing so we have beaten the candidate for the ‘uni-party’. Yes there were Liberal Democrats, Labour, Conservative canvassers out canvassing for Count Binface. What an upside-down world it is, where Count Binface is now the candidate of the establishment.”

He added: “Today the voters in Clacton have stuck up two fingers to the entire political establishment.”

However he said he would not attend the official declaration of the result at Clacton Leisure Centre as Essex Police had told him about an “organised campaign to disrupt and degrade the result”.

open image in gallery Count Binface gestures while standing with other candidates after Reform UK party leader Nigel Farage was declared the winner for the Clacton by-election, triggered by the resignation of Farage, in Essex, Britain, 14 August 2026 ( Reuters )

A Reform UK spokesperson later said: “Essex Police advised Nigel not to attend the count tonight due to a credible threat against him.”

However, it is understood Essex Police did not tell Mr Farage, or any other candidate, not to attend the count.

A spokesperson for Essex Police said: “We have a proportionate and robust policing operation to ensure the safety and security of all participants in the count.”

Results

Mr Farage won with 22,239 votes, with Count Binface in second place on 9,455 votes. Mr Farage secured a 12,784 majority, 62.82% of the vote.

This is up from his 8,405 vote majority, 46.2%, when he won at the 2024 general election. The result was declared shortly after 6am.

Turnout was 44.37%, down by just over 14%.

A total of 32 of the record-34 candidates lost their deposit.
