World.title: Northern Lights travel bucket list: Unique trips and experiences to book in 2026-2027
World.content:
For people around the world, seeing the Aurora Borealis – better known as the Northern Lights – is high on many a travel bucket list.

 

Typically visible in regions near the Earth’s poles, the spectacular phenomenon occurs when electrically charged particles from the Sun reach Earth and interact with its magnetic field and atmosphere, creating vivid ribbons of green, red, blue and purple light across the night sky.

Do you have the Northern Lights on your travel bucket list? Here’s some of the top trips and experiences to book in 2026 and 2027.

Best places and time to see the Northern Lights

While you can see “the world’s greatest light show” in both polar regions, the viewing is “better in the northern hemisphere”, said Bucket List Travels. In the so-called “Aurora Belt”, it appears with the “most intense light and greatest colour variations”.

Top destinations to see the Northern Lights include Iceland, Finland, Norway, Sweden, Lapland, Alaska and the Yukon in Canada.

It’s well known that the Aurora Borealis is an “elusive spectacle” and “sightings can’t be guaranteed”, said Exodus Adventure Travels. However, during prime weather conditions, you are “more likely to catch a glimpse” between the months of September and March when the skies are at their darkest.

Spectacular hotel stays

Hotel Rangá in south Iceland is a popular place to stay for guests seeking to see the Northern Lights or to go stargazing, due to its own advanced on-site observatory and remote location. By turning off the external lights, the hotel provides “optimal conditions to view the night sky” and travellers can also relax in geothermal hot tubs while starbathing.

The Kakslauttanen Arctic Resort, a wilderness retreat in Finland, offers “infinite stars” with guests sleeping under the Northern Lights in its iconic glass igloos.

Another property to offer “sky views from the comfort of your bed” is Aurora Village Ivalo in Finnish Lapland, which has a range of igloo cabins available.

The Santa Claus Express, Finland

Autumn and late winter are the best times to spot the Northern Lights, and if you’re lucky you could combine seeing them during certain journeys on the Santa Claus Express in Finland.

One of the most magical rail journeys in Europe, this Finnish overnight sleeper train takes travellers from Helsinki and Turku all the way north into the Arctic Circle to Rovaniemi, through frozen lakes and snow-dusted woods.

Horse riding on the Northern Lights Trail in Iceland

Horse riding holiday company Saddle Travel has a four-day trip on the "Northern Lights Trail" in Iceland. Starting from £1,179 (€1,375) per person, guests can spend around four hours per day for three days riding Icelandic horses on volcanic mountain slopes, before relaxing in thermal swimming pools and watching snow fall from the outdoor hot tub in a cosy winter wonderland.

Aurora360 flight Travel Yukon/Neil Zeller

Yukon's Aurora360 experience: Fly through the Northern Lights

One of the world's rarest Northern Lights experiences is returning to the Yukon, with an exclusive Aurora360 flight taking to the skies in February 2027. It offers travellers the opportunity to witness the Aurora Borealis from 30,000 feet aboard a private Air North charter aircraft.

Unlike traditional Northern Lights holidays, the Aurora360 flight lifts guests above cloud cover, dramatically increasing the chances of witnessing the dancing lights in all their brilliance. With every passenger guaranteed a window seat, the flight provides an unrivalled perspective of the aurora.

Canada As You Like It offers a seven-night Yukon's Northern Lights Resort & Spa Aurora360 holiday from £7,735 (€9,021) per person, including return international flights, two nights in Vancouver, four nights at Northern Lights Resort & Spa, one night in Whitehorse, and an exclusive Air North Aurora360 flight.

Reykjavík and the Northern Lights, Iceland

Travellers on this five-day trip with Newmarket Holidays can explore Iceland’s capital Reykjavík before heading out of the city to search for the Aurora Borealis. There’s also the option of a dip in the mineral-rich warm waters of the Blue Lagoon, and a Golden Circle tour to see Þingvellir, the dramatic open expanse where Iceland's ancient assemblies came to set the laws of the land.

Available from October 2026 to March 2028, it costs from £1,056 (€1,231) per person and includes return flights from various airports in the UK.

Havila Voyages is confident guests will see the Northern Lights Havila Kystruten

Havila Voyages’s Northern Lights ‘promise’

Norway-based cruise operator Havila Voyages is so confident that passengers will see the Northern Lights on its sailings that it’s made this promise: “If the lights don’t show up, your next voyage is on us – free of charge.”

For passengers that book on a 12-day round voyage between 1 October and 31 March, Havila Voyages promises that the magical Aurora Borealis will “make an appearance”. However, “if nature plays shy" and the lights "don’t grace the skies", passengers will receive a complimentary six-or seven-day voyage, Havila Voyages said.

World.title: Scientists map how spacecraft design could affect astronauts’ mental health
World.content:
Scientists have mapped how different features of a space habitat could affect astronauts’ mental, emotional and social well-being, in a new study.

 

Researchers from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and the University of Colorado Boulder in the United States examined links between features such as lighting, privacy and the layout of living spaces, and experiences including anxiety, homesickness, fatigue and relationships between crewmates.

The idea is to give engineers a clearer way to consider astronauts’ mental health when designing habitats for long-duration space missions.

“The awareness has been there for some time that living in space is difficult,” Mich Lin, a lead author of the study and a PhD candidate in the Human Systems Lab and the Engineering Systems Lab at MIT, said in a press release.

“We’ve come a long way from the human in a tin can. As our priorities shift toward long-duration exploration missions, making sure a crew is safe, healthy, happy, and productive becomes even more important,” she added.

In extreme environments, habitats are usually built primarily for survival. Submarines, Antarctic bases and spacecraft must protect people from immediate physical dangers, often with very limited space.

Spaceflight can put astronauts under considerable psychological strain. Isolation and confinement can affect sleep, mood, cognitive performance and relationships within a crew, while living without normal day-night cycles can disrupt the body's circadian rhythm.

But as humans prepare for longer missions to the Moon and eventually Mars, astronauts could spend months or even years confined with the same small group of people, far from family and friends and with little opportunity to leave their surroundings.

How much can design help?

Researchers carried out an extensive, iterative review of scientific literature on habitability in space and other extreme environments to find evidence linking physical surroundings with behavioural health.

They used the research to build a map containing 68 factors and 167 connections showing how aspects of an environment could influence behavioural health and performance.

They focused on 14 emotions and experiences that could be affected by habitat design, including anxiety, autonomy, curiosity, fatigue, nostalgia and kinship.

They then mapped how different design factors could contribute to these outcomes.

Lighting, for example, can affect sleep and circadian rhythms. The amount of privacy available to crew members could influence stress and autonomy, while the arrangement of shared spaces, corridors and entrances can shape how often people interact with one another.

Meanwhile, access paths, stairs and entrances can contribute to friendships and social cohesion because they influence how often people naturally encounter one another.

Researchers also suggest looking at features that can help astronauts develop a stronger attachment to where they live in order to reduce homesickness. These could include greater privacy and spaces that crew members can reconfigure or personalise.

“The connection between habitat and behavioural health has not been made in this format before,” Lin said. “So we made those connections for the first time.”

The research team says the same approach could also be applied on Earth, including to submarines, oil rigs, Antarctic expeditions and other environments where people spend long periods isolated and confined.

Researchers have also made the findings available through an interactive website called the Human-Environment Connection and Interaction Atlas (HECIA), where designers can explore the different connections.

However, the researchers stress that the tool and the ideas behind it are not a one-size-fits-all guide to designing extreme habitats. The appropriate design will depend on each habitat’s particular specifications and constraints.

World.title: Trump orders Navy to return to older system of launching jets off aircraft carriers
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has ordered the US Navy to remove the advanced system used to launch fighter jets from its newest type of aircraft carrier and return to using older steam catapults that he has long said he prefers.

 

The memo issued on Thursday directs the Pentagon and the Navy to present Trump with plans to remove the Electromagnetic Aircraft Launch System, also known as EMALS, within two months. It also says the Ford-class carrier’s electromagnetic weapons elevators should be replaced.

According to the directive, the new mandate would likely cost billions of dollars and revert the Navy’s most advanced ships to a system that takes more sailors to operate and is more difficult to maintain.

The move follows years of Trump's criticism of the new, magnetically driven catapult technology that launches fighter planes off the carriers' decks even as some tech experts believe some of the key advantages of the system are its ability to launch aircraft at faster speeds while being easier to maintain, requiring fewer sailors to operate and using less space aboard the ship.

It also comes at a time when the Navy is having difficulty staffing its ships with enough sailors and the US military is attempting to secure financing from Congress for more equipment.

Trump’s memo directs the fourth Ford-class carrier, the USS Doris Miller, to be the first ship to include the new changes. That will leave the USS Gerald R. Ford, as well as the forthcoming USS John F. Kennedy and USS Enterprise, untouched.

Trump's ire with the latest tech dates back to 2017

During his first term, Trump, in an interview with Time magazine, claimed the new system is “not good” and “doesn’t have the power” of the older steam systems.

“You’re going to goddamned steam,” Trump said at the time. The topic has frequently come up since then at rallies and other events.

While the US president is looking to roll back the latest technology, the newest Chinese aircraft carriers employ electromagnetic catapults, and France said it plans to use the system on its new carrier.

However, redesigning an already finalised ship for such a major system change will not be an easy task. EMALS aboard the USS Ford cut the number of sailors needed to operate the catapults from about a dozen to two earlier this year.

Trump’s memo that mandates the removal of the system also noted that one of the issues facing shipbuilding is the Navy’s constant design changes, “which have resulted in cost growth, delays, and cancellations.”

According to General Atomics, the company that makes EMALS, the decision not to proceed with the system on the USS Doris Miller “warrants careful reconsideration".

General Atomics said the work on Doris Miller’s catapults and arresting gear was already halfway complete and said, "Changing course now would introduce significant cost, schedule, and integration risks.”

The move comes as Congress will weigh the necessary budget and funding bills that the Trump administration has said they need to fund the Pentagon and the Iran war.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth estimated last month that the war’s cost grew to $37.5 billion (nearly €32.6 billion) as Republicans prepared a $95 billion package (€82.7 billion) to fund the military, along with other White House priorities.

Hegseth said the supplemental war funding is an “urgent, necessary” injection of money, and with Trump’s proposed $1.5 trillion (around €1.31 trillion) defense budget a generational investment in the military.

The House narrowly adopted both, but the Senate still must act when it returns in September.

World.title: Black Forest coolcation: tourism in Germany surges in 2026
World.content:
Most tourists in Germany come from the country itself. The trend towards travelling to all kinds of regions, from the Baltic Sea to the Alps, has continued in recent years. According to the Federal Statistical Office, hotels, guesthouses and campsites recorded 223.8 million overnight stays in the first six months of this year, a new record for Germany.

 

And the growing number of guests booking holiday flats online is not even counted. Germans also top the rankings for online bookings of holiday rentals, followed by visitors from the Netherlands, Poland and the United States.

Hiking through the gorges of the Black Forest AP Photo

Southern Europe turns to the Black Forest

Regionally, however, there are some striking trends. The Black Forest is particularly popular in Spain and Italy. That has less to do with its delicious Black Forest gateau, which has long since made a name for itself internationally, and more with the search for cooler climes.

With the 1,493 metre Feldberg and the picture-postcard Titisee, the Black Forest, like Scandinavia or Scotland, is regarded in this era of climate crisis as a "coolcation", in other words as a particularly cool holiday destination. The fact that summer 2026 in south-west Germany, as in neighbouring France, was marked by heatwaves has so far done little to dent that image.

According to Schwarzwald Tourismus GmbH, the number of visitors from Spain coming to the Black Forest has risen particularly sharply, by 64 percent since 2015. The State Statistical Office of Baden-Württemberg counted 199,000 overnight stays by Spanish guests last year.

Italians are close behind, with 194,000 overnight stays in the Black Forest.

The famous fairy-tale brothers Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm grew up in the 19th century not far from the Black Forest and collected stories from all over Germany. The slightly eerie atmosphere of "Hansel and Gretel" and "Little Red Riding Hood" draws visitors not only at Halloween, but can also be relived on a summer walk through the forest in its more mystical corners.

World.title: White House says it’s losing $19B-$26B a year in revenue as countries dodge tariffs
World.content:
The Trump White House said in a new report on Thursday that countries are routing their exports through third countries to avoid US tariffs, estimating that there are tax revenue losses of $19 billion to $26 billion (around €16.5 billion to €22.6 billion) annually.

 

Peter Navarro, the White House trade adviser, told reporters on a conference call that China is laundering its exports through more than 40 countries, though he claimed that the issues raised in the report were really more about other nations enabling the avoidance of tariffs.

“For years, the great transshipment scam has let communist China launder its exports,” Navarro said.

The report comes ahead of a planned September visit by Chinese leader Xi Jinping, who President Donald Trump described in flattering terms during his own visit to Beijing in May.

White House trade counselor Peter Navarro speaks with reporters following a video interview with Real America's Voice News, Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026, AP Photo

In response to increasing duties in 2018, China sent its goods to countries like Mexico and Malaysia for packaging and limited assembly, a practice known as transshipping, according to the research. Although Beijing was able to continue expanding its manufacturing sector in ways that could pose a threat to American firms and jobs, this trend gave the impression that US imports from China had decreased.

Beijing has described its relationship with Washington as one of “strategic stability", yet its government policies that support exports of manufactured goods have destabilised the auto, metals and electronics sectors in America, Europe, Japan and elsewhere.

New trade frameworks to penalise tariff evaders

Navarro stated that other countries, like India, might potentially transship to evade new duties and that the Trump administration's new trade frameworks would include clauses guaranteeing that trading partners who participate in the practice will face consequences.

The Trump administration has levied high tariffs on much of the world in hopes of protecting US manufacturers, hitting allies and rivals alike with import taxes. At the same time, those tariffs have created new inflationary pressures at home.

The report includes a range of estimates for the scale of transshipments to avoid tariffs, citing government and private sector numbers to estimate roughly $34.2 billion to $303 billion of goods (some €29.7bn–€263bn) transshipped each year.

It used a central figure of $75 billion worth of goods being transshipped to estimate how much in tax revenues have been lost.

According to Navarro, US Customs and Border Protection has begun using artificial intelligence in a pilot programme to halt transshipments in order to address the issue.

An importer's imports may be subject to retroactive tariffs stretching back about a year if it is discovered that the importer faked the provenance of a commodity, Navarro warned.

Trump's tariffs during his second term have faced an array of legal challenges, with the Supreme Court overturning some of them in February.

The US continues to import more than it exports to the rest of the world, but the trade imbalance so far this year at $371 billion (about €322bn) is running about $189 billion (€164bn) lower than it did during the same period last year.

World.title: Four dead, thousands stranded as record rain lashes Japan
World.content:
Unprecedented rainfall in Japan's Chiba prefecture has stranded thousands of passengers at Tokyo's Narita airport and prompted authorities to issue the highest-level rain warning for the first time.

At least four people have died in eastern Japan as heavy rain flooded roads, cut power and left thousands of travelers stranded overnight at Tokyo's Narita airport, authorities said Friday.

More than 36 centimeters (14 inches) of rain fell in 24 hours in parts of Chiba prefecture, which borders Tokyo, triggering landslide warnings and power outages for nearly 25,000 households.

Japan facing 'unprecedented' rain during busy holiday week

The downpour struck during one of Japan's busiest holiday weeks, prompting the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) to issue its highest-level heavy rain warning for the region for the first time.

A JMA official on Thursday said this was "shaping up to be an unprecedented level of heavy rain."

"This case was an extremely unusual situation, even ​by Japan's historical weather standards," Chiba Governor Toshihito Kumagai told reporters early Friday. "I have responded to many disasters in the past, but ⁠I ​have never experienced a case like this."

Several roads in the Chiba Prefecture were inundated Image: Kyodo/REUTERS

The Chiba Prefecture Disaster Management Office said those confirmed deaths included a man in his 60s or 70s found on a flooded road and a 66-year-old woman found in her submerged car.

A third victim was a man of unknown age found collapsed in the street, and a fourth was a person whose age and gender have not been determined, AFP reported. A fifth person is feared dead and a sixth remains unaccounted for. Soldiers have been deployed to help with relief efforts.

Thousands stranded at Narita airport

More than 6,000 people were stranded overnight at Narita, one of Tokyo's two major international airports. Many train services to and from the airport were also canceled into Friday afternoon.

"I never thought I'd spend the night at the airport but it is what it is and we are learning," a traveler told Japanese public broadcaster NHK. "We're never going to forget this trip."

Hundreds more were stranded at Chiba station after train services were suspended. Several people spent the night in shelters. NHK footage also showed cars submerged up to their headlights in Kashiwa city.

Hundreds were stranded at the Chiba Metro Station as weather authorities issued their highest-level heavy rain warning for the region Image: Philip Fong/AFP

Major highways in Chiba, including routes connecting Narita to central Tokyo, remained closed Friday, according to highway operator NEXCO East, forcing drivers onto alternate routes. Some train services connecting Narita to Tokyo had resumed early Friday.

An airport spokesperson said all flights were scheduled to operate normally, and Japan Airlines said some delays were possible, but no cancellations were expected.

The level-5 heavy rain warnings issued Thursday were downgraded to level 4 by Friday morning.

Scientists warn that human-driven climate change is making extreme weather events more frequent and intense.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: Romania shuts nuclear plant, Hungary dams dry Danube River
World.content:
Romania has shut down its only nuclear plant in a rare move prompted by the lack of cooling water from the Danube River. Hungary, meanwhile, is racing to dam the Danube, trying to keep its Paks plant online.

Romania shut down its lone nuclear power plant on Thursday, a rare move amid the drought that has caused record lows on the Danube River and other major waterways in Europe.

The Danube is the sole source of cooling water for the Cernavoda plant, which usually generates around one-fifth of Romania's electricity.

The power station has only been shut down once before, in 2023, again as a result of drought and a hot summer.

Meanwhile, Hungary was scrambling to dam the Danube, as it tries to keep its Paks nuclear power plant at least running at the minimal levels that it has maintained in recent days, which are far below capacity.

Attempts to divert more water to Cernavoda earlier this month didn't prevent a shutdown Image: Alex Nicodim/Anadolu/picture alliance

What did the operator and authorities in Romania say about the shutdown?

Romania's Nuclearelectrica company had already shut one of the two reactors at Cernavoda last month.

On Thursday, it said it needed to shut the second "because of the significant and ongoing drop in the water level of the Danube River."

The company tried earlier this month, with help from the Navy, to improve the plant's chances of staying operational.

Most memorably, it blew up a rocky outcrop exposed by the low water levels and strategically deposited the rocks on the riverbed in a bid to direct more water to Cernavoda.

But ultimately, continued dry weather and sinking water levels prompted the total shutdown.

"We do not foresee a restart within the next 10 days," the plant director, Romeo Urjan, told the AFP news agency.

Romania's Energy Ministry said it was procuring alternative power sources, including from wind power but also from energy imports, to try to ensure adequate supplies. Still it appealed to the public to consume responsibly.

It warned that as a last resort, large industrial users would have to face restrictions in the evening hours to save electricity. Carmakers Ford and Dacia had already committed to pausing production until August 19 to save power.

Earlier in August, the Romanian Navy detonated submerged rocks as part of a bid to funnel more water to the power plant Image: Andreea Alexandru/AP Photo/picture alliance

What is Hungary doing to try to prevent a similar shutdown of the Paks plant?

Prime Minister Peter Magyar on Thursday visited Hungary's only nuclear power plant, the Paks facility that is also cooled by the Danube.

"We have begun construction of the low weir that will permanently contribute to raising the Danube's water level," Magyar told reporters at the site, roughly 100 kilometers (about 60 miles) south of Budapest.

Only one of Paks' four reactors is currently operational amid the drought.

Nine days ago, the plant was at risk of a complete shutdown, but the government was able to abort those plans at the last moment as the Danube's levels ended up being a few millimeters higher than forecast.

The unusually low river levels near the Paks plant are hard to miss at present Image: Robert Nemeti/Anadolu/picture alliance

Under normal circumstances, the plant is responsible for around half of Hungary's electricity generation, and about one-third of its consumption.

Before the completion of the weir, authorities plan to deliberately sink two 80-meter-long barges — placed end-to-end and perpendicular to the river's flow — to create an initial damming effect and raise the water level somewhat.

Magyar said that Hungarian soldiers were working round the clock on the construction, and that it should be completed in the next four weeks. He said the project should elevate water levels in front of the Paks plant cooling system by more than a meter.

The project might not be finished long before the summer starts to fade and the rains return, but the low water levels also provide a rare opportunity to undertake such construction projects relatively cheaply and easily.

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: Kennedy Center board approves Trump name on facade, renovation plan
World.content:
The move appears designed to circumvent a judge's ruling that the US president's name should be removed, potentially setting the stage for a new legal fight over the Kennedy Center's name and future.

The board of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts voted Thursday to add President Donald Trump's name to the building's facade, according to US Congresswoman Joyce Beatty.

The board also voted to proceed with a two-year closure of the performing arts venue in the US capital, Washington, D.C., for major renovations.

The decision comes after a federal judge in May ordered Trump's name to be removed from the building, ruling that only Congress can change the institution's name or authorize major alterations.

"This latest development is a transparent effort to circumvent the Court's ruling, and flies in the face of the statutes that Congress passed," Beatty, a Democrat who is also an ex-officio board member, said in a statement. "I will continue to fight for this treasured national monument."

The latest vote revives a dispute that has been unfolding since Trump reshaped the center's leadership after returning to office.

Why was Trump's name on the building in the first place?

Trump became interested in the Kennedy Center's operations after winning the 2024 election. He installed a mostly handpicked board that named him chairman, and his name was added to the building's facade in December.

The move was part of a broader effort to overhaul the institution. At the time, the president also announced a two-year closure of the performing arts venue for renovations that were scheduled to begin in July.

That decision soon faced a legal challenge. In May, Judge Christopher Cooper said, "the Kennedy Center's organic statute makes crystal clear that the Center is to be named for President Kennedy, and it cannot bear any other formal name or public memorial based on the Board's unilateral say-so."

The Kennedy Center dispute became one of several obstacles to Trump's broader efforts to remake prominent Washington landmarks. An appeals court last week halted his planned White House ballroom after he demolished the East Wing.

His Reflecting Pool renovation also faced major problems, though he still plans to build a massive Memorial Arch.

How has the Kennedy Center board justified the move?

"In its meeting today, the board voted to change the front of the building's facade to read 'The John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts Restored and Renovated By President Donald J. Trump,' and renamed the physical site 'the President Donald J. Trump Plaza,'" Congresswoman Beatty said.

According to The New York Times, an inscription underneath the institution's name would read: "Restored and Renovated by President Donald J. Trump."

The newspaper said the wording appears intended to avoid a provision in the federal law governing the Kennedy Center that states "no additional memorials or plaques in the nature of memorials shall be designated or installed in the public areas."

Edited by: Karl Sexton

World.title: US disputes reports of trying conditions on carrier in Gulf
World.content:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called reports of poor conditions and mental health strain aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier in the Middle East "completely misrepresented." Senators want an investigation.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has defended conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln aircraft carrier, which has spent a record-breaking number of days at sea during a period of more than eight months with only brief stops at ports.

Hegseth called recent reporting in two military-focused outlets in the US, the Navy Times and the Stars and Stripes, "completely misrepresented."

The reports had quoted relatives of sailors recounting stories of poor conditions on board and even a thwarted attempt by a crewmember to throw themselves overboard.

The aircraft carrier's crew of around 5,000 provide crucial aerial and naval support to US operations in the Gulf Image: U.S. Navy/Planet Pix/ZUMA/picture alliance

What did Hegseth say about conditions?

The 5,000-person aircraft carrier left San Diego in November for what was scheduled to be a Pacific deployment.

It was subsequently rerouted to the Middle East ready for what the Trump White House called Operation Epic Fury, and has been in the Persian Gulf or the wider region since January amid the war with Iran.

"We make sure every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment," Hegseth told reporters during a visit to Panama on Thursday. "Some deployments are longer than others, and I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody. What they do in those high seas in those austere conditions with less port calls — it's incredible."

Longer deployments at sea, particularly in wartime with higher stress and danger levels and fewer chances for rest and recreation, have always been a challenge for the US Navy.

During the longest period at sea without docking in US military history, the ship had to be restocked on the move, with several non-essential supplies falling by the wayside Image: U.S. Navy/SIPA/picture alliance

Senate calls for inspection visit

A day earlier, Arizona Senator Ruben Gallego said he was calling for an official oversight visit to the USS Abraham Lincoln by a bipartisal Senate Delegation to "investigate the alarming conditions."

"Unlike Donald Trump, I've seen active duty," Gallego said. "They way he's treating our service members as he carries out this illegal war is not just disgusting; it's dangerous. These sailors are owed a sense of when they will go home."

Gallego repeated the call on Thursday, saying Congress "needs to do its job and hold this administration accountable."

Senator Richard Blumenthal also called for the Navy to account for conditions aboard the aircraft carrier, noting "widespread reports of shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns" and other problems aboard the Lincoln.

What if Iran and Oman split control of the Strait of Hormuz? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What did the military media outlets report?

The Navy Times and Stars and Stripes have had their eye on the USS Abraham Lincoln's record-setting deployment for months but both revisited the issue in depth this week. This followed a direct appeal late last week by family members to Acting Secretary of the Navy Hung Cao and other senior officials in town hall meetings.

The deployment has included 40 days of continuous combat operations in the US Fifth Fleet area of operations and 250 consecutive days at sea, including a record-breaking number of days without even a port stop, restocking supplies at sea and by air as best as the crew could.

"We already had an instance where watchstanders had to stop someone from jumping," Stars and Stripes quoted one sailor as saying .

It also noted various supply and service issues affecting morale, like food rationing, water shortages, and a stretch of more than a week when crew could not do laundry.

It said that many of these issues had since improved, as had mail delivery services — but nevertheless reported a situation of deteriorating morale where, as one sailor put it, "All we want is a date home."

The Lincoln made a brief port call in Oman in early July. Stars and Stripes reported, that allowed it to stock up on valuable produce like fresh fruit and vegetables, but sailors were only permitted to disembark into a secure compound within the port. The ship had also briefly docked in Guam in December, but again with limited shore leave. In the interim it spent the longest period at sea without ever docking in US military history.

The Reuters news agency on Thursday cited a US official, who it said was speaking on condition of anonymity, as saying that another aircraft carrier — the USS George Washington — was headed to the region to relieve the Lincoln. The Wall Street Journal in the US carried similar reports on Thursday. The ship departed Vietnam earlier this week.

Both combat aircraft and tactical early-warning aircraft like the E-2D Hawkeye operate from the Lincoln Image: NAVCENT Public Affairs/SIPA/picture alliance

Hegseth, Trump both indicate much longer deployment conceivable

When asked about what the US calls its "blockade" of Iran's ports — with the Lincoln a crucial command and air-superiority component in the operation — Hegseth said that the US could continue to enforce it for as long as it wished.

"Indefinitely the United States Navy can maintain a blockade like that because we'll rotate ships in and out, as we have, and we'll continue to," he said.

President Donald Trump had claimed on Wednesday that the navy had "total control" of the Strait of Hormuz and speculated that he might try to permanently police it.

"The USA has total control over the Strait of Hormuz. I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT!" Trump wrote online. "Our Naval Blockade is being called, by everyone, 'A WALL OF STEEL,' and there is nothing Iran can do about it."

The head of Iran's Basij paramilitary unit, Hossein Taeb, on Thursday disputed Trump's assesment saying the Strait is "under Iran's control and management."

Commercial shipping — whether bound for Iranian ports or for Gulf states, or trying to sail out of the Gulf — has been drastically reduced in volume throughout the conflict, with risks to commercial crews of all stripes from both sides complicating and often halting journeys.

Can Trump end the Iran war and sell it as a victory? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: When the earth moves: 6 major earthquakes of 2026
World.content:
Colombia, Venezuela, Mindanao: Thousands have died in powerful earthquakes this year. Six such events show that the magnitude of the quake is not the only factor determining the scale of the disaster.

Is 2026 a particularly bad year for earthquakes? The number of extremely strong quakes so far this year is not, in fact, unusual. Over the long term, around the world, there are an average of about 15 earthquakes per year registering above magnitude 7 on the Richter scale. By mid-August this year, there had been 10. The devastation some of the quakes have wreaked has, however, been striking.

Venezuela: two quakes in just 39 seconds

On June 24, Venezuela was hit by an earthquake that proved to be by far the deadliest this year. A magnitude 7.2 quake was followed just 39 seconds later by an even stronger one of magnitude 7.5. The north of the country and the capital, Caracas, were the areas worst affected.

Two earthquakes wreaked destruction in Catia La Mar, Venezuela Image: Maxwell Briceno/AFP

According to official figures, more than 6,300 people were killed in the double earthquake. The effects on the impoverished country's infrastructure have also been dramatic. Shortly afterward, a satellite-based assessment by researchers at Oregon State University provisionally concluded that more than 58,000 buildings may have been damaged or destroyed.

Venezuela quakes death toll rises to almost 4,000 To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Philippines: the strongest quake of the year

With a magnitude of 7.8, the earthquake on June 8 off the southern coast of the Philippine island of Mindanao was the strongest of 2026 so far. It occurred at a depth of about 57 kilometers (35 miles), and was felt across large parts of the island.

This university building in General Santos City on Mindanao in the Philippines collapsed during the earthquake in June Image: Daniel Ceng/Anadolu/picture alliance

At least 107 people were killed. But the fact that, despite the very high magnitude of the quake, far fewer people died in the Philippines than in Venezuela demonstrates that the strength of the quake does not necessarily determine the severity of the consequences.

Colombia: hundreds dead, despite the depth

On August 10, a magnitude 7.4 earthquake shook western Colombia. The epicenter was in the Choco region, near San Jose del Palmar. Although the quake occurred at a depth of 100 kilometers (62 miles), the damage it caused was immense.

Pereira, in the foothills of the Andes, was one of the cities worst hit by the earthquake in Colombia Image: Jaime Saldarriaga/AFP

More than 250 people are currently estimated to have died. Landslides and damaged roads are hampering the search for victims buried beneath the rubble, as well as the provision of supplies to remote areas. After Venezuela, this quake is the most consequential so far this year for Latin America.

Tonga: powerful earthquake with little damage

On March 24, the earth shook near the island group of Vava'u in the Pacific kingdom of Tonga. With a magnitude of 7.5, it was one of the strongest globally this year. But because there was no severe damage and no deaths, it received almost no attention from the media.

Tonga is located on the Pacific Ring of Fire and suffers frequent natural disasters, as here, after a volcanic eruption in 2022 Image: New Zealand Defence Force/UPI Photo/Newscom/picture alliance

The quake occurred unusually far below the earth's crust, at a depth of around 230 kilometers (143 miles), meaning that the tremors were significantly weakened by the time they reached the surface. To date, there have been no reports of deaths, or damage to infrastructure.

Japan: strong undersea quake off the Sanriku Coast

On April 20, there was an undersea quake off the northeastern coast of Japan. The US Geological Survey recorded a magnitude of 7.4.

This region, the Sanriku Coast area in Iwate prefecture, achieved terrible notoriety after the catastrophic earthquake and tsunami there in 2011, which also resulted in the Fukushima nuclear disaster. A tsunami warning was issued after this year's earthquake, too, but fortunately the region was spared the devastation of that magnitude 9 quake 15 years ago.

After the earthquake off Japan's Sanriku Coast, people were evacuated as a precaution Image: Haruki Kobayashi/AP Photo/picture alliance

There was no major tsunami this time, but the quake illustrated once again how much Japan is affected by its location on the Pacific Ring of Fire. This 40,000-kilometer (25,000-mile) volcanic belt runs around the edge of the Pacific Ocean where several tectonic plates collide.

Afghanistan: weak, but deadly

The earthquake in the northeastern Afghan province of Badakhsham on April 3 only reached a magnitude of 5.8, which puts it right at the bottom of the list of the strongest earthquakes this year. Despite this, at least 12 people were killed, which is why it counts as one of the most significant quakes of 2026.

Poor building construction contributed to the deaths of several people in a magnitude 5.8 earthquake in Afghanistan in April Image: Saifurahman Safi/Xinhua/IMAGO

In poorer countries, even slight tremors can have deadly consequences. The risks are heightened by inadequate building construction, the difficulty of accessing remote areas and underdeveloped disaster response protocols.

This article has been translated from German.

World.title: Israeli military moves as settlers besiege 3 West Bank homes
World.content:
Israel's military has moved to try to stop a group of settlers from besieging three homes in the occupied West Bank. One was owned by a Palestinian American, prompting an unusually sharp rebuke from the US ambassador.

Israel has sent soldiers to try to protect three homes in the occupied West Bank village of Qusra that have been surrounded by a small group of Israeli settlers for several days.

One of the three homes is owned by a Palestinian American, and the incident prompted an unusually critical reponse from the US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, typically considered an ally of Israel's settler movement.

The case comes amid continued Israeli settlement building, which is considered illegal under international law, in parts of the occupied West Bank, and allegations from critics of the Israeli government that it sometimes turns a blind eye to, or does too little to prevent, settler violence against Palestinians.

What is happening and where?

Starting on Sunday, a group of settlers started gathering around three houses in the village of Qusra.

One of the buildings belongs to Palestinian-American homeowner Loui Ridi. Local officials said the settlers sometimes numbered several dozen. They supposedly threw strones, attempted to bring down a stone wall, and prevented occupants from leaving their homes as their supplies dwindled.

Israel's military moved into the area on Wednesday and moved settlers away from the properties Image: Nidal Eshtayeh/AP/dpa/picture alliance

Ridi's brother, Qusai Abu Rida — who had holed up in the house with his son — said on Thursday morning that they had been moved to another home by the Israeli military but still could not leave the area some 16 kilometers (10 miles) from the Palestinian city of Nablus. Loui Ridi resides in Ohio but owns the property.

Israel's IDF military said its troops had dismantled "two illegal outposts" near the homes, and detained one Israeli. It wasn't immediately clear if the individual was subject to arrest or investigation, or just detention.

The local mayor, Abdel Azim Wadi, said that Israeli forces evacuated seven Palestinian households from their homes to make space for soldiers to take up positions in the village. He said that the settlers remained in other parts of the village, despite being removed from their outposts.

Locals said the village was on effective lockdown.

"No one is allowed to enter. Even food and water are prohibited from reaching those besieged," the Associated Press cited Yasser Ahmad, a resident of a neighboring village, as saying as he watched the operation unfold from one hilltop over.

Qusra is in one of the most violent pockets of the northern West Bank, surrounded by settlements. Its mosque was damaged in attacks last month.

Qusra has been a frequent flashpoint of late; its mosque was set on fire in a settler attack in late July Image: Debbie Hill/UPI/newscom/picture alliance

What did US Ambassador Huckabee say about the incident?

US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee, typically a supporter of the Israeli settler movement — but also critical of settler violence — spoke out in unusually sharp terms against an incident impacting a US citizen in the West Bank.

"The actions of those doing this to this family's home is criminal," he said. "Actions by those who carried out this horrific act of terror meant to intimidate and harass this family are disgusting. No excuse for such thuggish behavior."

However, Huckabee also repeatedly defended both US and Israeli authorities response to the incident, saying the US Embassy in Jerusalem had been "very involved," and that "the IDF and Israel Police have gone at our request to remove the Israeli terrorists doing this."

He later repeated this message, posting video footage seeming to show Israeli security vehicles driving into the area.

The UN Human Rights Office in the occupied Palestinian territory on Thursday called on the Israeli authorities to "immediately" act against the settlers .

"These criminal actions by the settlers, supported or acquiesced to by Israel, the occupying power, are making life unbearable for these Palestinian families, and are clearly aimed at forcing them to leave their homes and land," it said in a statement.

EU foreign policy spokesperson Anitta Hipper called on Israel to take "concrete action to prevent settler violence."

What's the wider issue with West Bank settlement building and settler violence?

Palestinians and some in the Israeli opposition accuse Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government of turning a blind eye to attacks by settlers against Palestinians, as such cases have increased in recent years since the October 7 attacks and amid the war in Gaza.

Israeli government officials tend to describe the violence as the actions of a few fringe youth acting outside the law. The UN's human rights office (OHCHR) said 18 Palestinians have died in the first seven months of this year in attacks involving settlers.

Most of the international community condemns Israeli settlement building in the West Bank as an impediment to a lasting peace and the so-called two-state solution.

More than 500,000 Israelis live — most with but also some without Israeli government authorization and support — in the West Bank, which is home to roughly 3 million Palestinians.

The Palestinians seek the West Bank, captured by Israel in the 1967 Six-Day War, as part of a future state. Many settlers and some members of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's government claim the area should belong to Israel, often citing a mixture historical, religious and security reasons.

Palestinian group watches for Israeli settlers in West Bank To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

World.title: Ukraine's monthly civilian casualties highest since 2022
World.content:
Skip next section Russian drone strike on Ukraine train kills two

08/13/2026 August 13, 2026 Russian drone strike on Ukraine train kills two

A Russian drone strike has hit a passenger train carrying hundreds of people in Ukraine's southern Odesa region, killing two railway workers, Ukrainian officials said.

President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said 340 people were on board when a drone struck and destroyed the locomotive.

Zelenskyy said the locomotive driver and his assistant were killed in the attack.

None of the passengers was injured, according to the head of Ukraine's state railway operator.

Footage released by emergency services showed flames engulfing the damaged front of the train.

Zelenskyy accused the drone operator of knowingly targeting a civilian train, saying it would have been impossible not to recognize the nature of the target.

Russian forces have repeatedly struck Ukraine's railway network during the war, hitting trains, stations and other infrastructure.

Kyiv says the attacks are intended both to disrupt transport and logistics and to target civilian life.

Zelenskyy said Russian forces had also launched more than 130 attack drones overnight, with strikes reported across 11 regions.

He again called for additional air defenses and stronger international pressure on Moscow.

World.title: How Germany's drone defense fails
World.content:
Drone defense is a priority for the German government. The latest dramatic incident involving an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig airport shows there are still substantial shortcomings.

How could a drone laden with explosives fly unhindered into Leipzig/Halle airport, where it remained apparently unnoticed for several hours? After last week's incident, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt spoke of a "hybrid attack scenario" which he suspected came from "foreign powers."

Suspicion has been directed at Russia, also because the drone was said to have been located near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane. The Federal Prosecutor's Office has taken over the investigation.

The fact that the drone was loaded with explosives and able to reach the airport demonstrates a new level of threat. However, drone sightings over airports and ports, industrial sites and military properties have been increasing in Germany. In 2025, Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) recorded more than 1,000 suspicious drone flights.

Last October, drones disrupted air traffic in Munich for several hours, stranding numerous passengers. There is not sufficient drone protection at German airports, warned security expert Nico Lange.

"We do not possess the sensor networks and sensor beams needed to spot all types of drones, especially low-flying, slow drones," he told DW.

Leipzig drone threat prompts security concerns in Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The European Association for Unmanned Aviation has also long pointed out weak points in Germany's drone defense. "That a drone could apparently reach the airport tarmac and be discovered rather by chance, shows where the core of the problem is," said chairperson Gerald Wissel in relation to the latest incident.

The association suggests "the establishment of real-time monitoring of the lower airspace as well as the mandatory tracking of all airspace participants via ADS-L" — a radio communications system that makes drones in an airspace electronically visible.

Coordinated response difficult for state, federal police

Germany has so far done little to address the issue of drone defense. Interior Minister Dobrindt wants to remedy this by setting up new institutions.

In December, he launched the Joint Counter Drone Center (GDAZ) in Berlin. There, information from the federal police, state police, secret service and armed forces is collated around the clock. But the incident at Leipzig airport shows that even a new hub is of little use if a dangerous drone at a large airport cannot be discovered and intercepted.

Drones move quickly, and any response must be decided within minutes. Doing so is made more difficult by Germany's system of divided responsibilities. If a suspicious drone takes off somewhere in the country, it's initially a matter for the state police. Germany has 16 police authorities, one for each of its 16 states. Only when the drone moves over a large airport or railway facility are the federal police allowed to step in.

Europe's defense: Latest drone technology shown in Berlin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Unclear responsibilities

Security experts and opposition politicians in Germany's Bundestag federal parliament have called for clear regulation and consolidation of responsibilities. "The muddle over responsibilities in drone defense is a substantial danger to our domestic security," said Irene Mihalic, lawmaker with the opposition Green Party and herself a former police officer.

Many, including the Greens, suggest the federal police should take the lead when it comes to drone defense. The federal police set up a new special unit for drone defense in December, and Dobrindt now wants to expand the unit following the incident at Leipzig airport.

Originally, 130 staff positions across four locations were planned. In the future, there will be 300 personnel across eight locations, to "be on site quickly and flexibly when needed," according to the Interior Ministry.

Who is allowed to shoot down a drone in Germany?

As so often happens following dramatic incidents, there have also been calls to deploy the Bundeswehr, Germany's armed forces, to take care of drone defense efforts at airports. However, current German law maintains that police are responsible for upholding security in the country.

A Defense Ministry spokesperson warned that protecting its own facilities, with their "tens of thousands of kilometers of fencing," is already a challenge for the Bundeswehr. Adding 24/7 protection of civilian infrastructure "would proclaim a false sense of security that we could never achieve," he added.

In an emergency, the police are allowed to ask the army for assistance. To achieve legal clarity in this regard, Germany amended its air security law in March. For the first time, it allows the Bundeswehr to shoot down drones outside their own premises to prevent "a particularly serious disaster."

From printing to presses to drones To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Airports, train stations still lack protection

There is also lot of catching up to do when it comes to the technical equipment used to defend against drones.

"There were big announcements at airports about positioning drone defense systems. They are more like detection systems," Manuel Atug, a spokesperson for the independent Critical Infrastructure Working Group (Arbeitsgruppe Kritische Infrastruktur) told DW. "So far, they have not intercepted a single drone, and at some airports they have still not yet been put in place."

The German Police Union (GdP) has also lamented the lack of resources for drone defense. "Unsafe train stations, unsafe airports and a police force which has to beg for money, law changes and the latest defense technology are really disconcerting," criticized GdP federal chairman Jochen Kopelke.

An Interior Ministry spokesperson said large airports were steadily being equipped with drone defense technology. "The federal police have already procured a considerable amount of equipment. The eight large airports are prioritized: Frankfurt (Main), Munich, Berlin, Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Cologne/Bonn, Stuttgart and Leipzig/Halle," she said.

The plan is for all of these airports to be equipped with mobile drone defense technology by the end of the year.

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: Marruecos despliega cientos de policías y militares en la frontera ante los llamamientos a una nueva irrupción masiva
World.content:
Este sábado aparece marcado en rojo en el calendario de los responsables del Ministerio del Interior, pero también en el de las autoridades marroquíes. En las redes sociales circulan desde hace días mensajes que alientan a repetir las escenas vividas los pasados 30 y 31 de julio con miles de migrantes entrando de manera irregular en Ceuta a nado, bordeando el espigón de El Tarajal. “La frontera de Ceuta estará abierta el día 15 [de agosto], festivo en España”, rezan algunos mensajes difundidos a través de internet para animar a participar en una nueva irrupción masiva. Ante ello, Rabat ha reforzado el puesto fronterizo de Fnideq (Castillejos en su denominación colonial española) con cientos de miembros de las fuerzas de seguridad apoyados por tropas militares, según se observa en vídeos que circulan desde hace casi una semana en medios digitales del país magrebí. También se han difundido imágenes de la instalación de concertinas y alambradas en las vallas que marcan el límite fronterizo del lado marroquí.

“Se han tomado todas las medidas necesarias para impedir cualquier intento de cruce ilegal e interceptar a cualquier persona que intente participar en él”, aseguró el miércoles Rachid el Jalfi, portavoz del Ministerio del Interior, quien definió el actual despliegue como parte de un “sistema de vigilancia continua” en los pasos de Ceuta y Melilla. El Jalfi instó a los ciudadanos a desoír llamamientos considerados “sospechosos y engañosos”, que suponen “graves riesgos para la seguridad de las personas”. Desde el otro lado de la frontera, el ministro del Interior, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, incidía este jueves en el mismo mensaje en una comparecencia ante la prensa durante su segunda visita a la ciudad autónoma: “Se lo digo a ellos para que no atiendan a las mafias que juegan con su vida. Ninguno de ellos se va a quedar [en Ceuta], ninguno de ellos va a ir a la península, ninguno de ellos va a ser regularizado”.

En el lado español de la frontera, el refuerzo de efectivos también ha sido significativo, según se desprende de los datos facilitados este jueves por el ministro. Desde el inicio de la crisis, el número de policías y guardias civiles desplegados ha pasado de algo más de los 1.100 que componían las plantillas de ambos cuerpos a cerca de 1.600 que hay en la actualidad. Además, 2.000 militares han pasado a realizar funciones de apoyo. Sin embargo, estos esfuerzos no se centran solo en la frontera, sino que con ella también se busca hacer más visible la presencia de agentes en las calles —el ministro ha admitido que devolver la “normalidad” a Ceuta del 29 de julio “evidentemente” llevará tiempo ante las quejas de los vecinos que hablan de inseguridad―, como en agilizar la expulsión de los 5.000 migrantes irregulares que permanecen aún en la ciudad. Marlaska muestra así, una vez más desde que estalló la crisis, su confianza en que Marruecos asumirá buena parte de la responsabilidad de frenar cualquier intento de repetir una entrada masiva este sábado. “Siempre ha sido, es y será extraordinaria y excepcional”, ha afirmado el ministro al ser preguntado por la colaboración entre Madrid y Rabat, incluso cuando se le recordó el anterior incidente grave en la frontera de Ceuta, la entrada de 10.000 migrantes en mayo de 2021.

Como ejemplo de esa disposición a impedir una nueva crisis migratoria, las autoridades marroquíes han asegurado haber detectado numerosos mensajes en las redes sociales para organizar y coordinar un nuevo cruce masivo este sábado hacia las ciudades autónomas españolas. Varias personas han sido detenidas y han sido procesadas tras ser acusadas de lanzar bulos para favorecer a la migración irregular, según informó el portavoz de Interior a la agencia estatal de noticias MAP. No obstante, y en línea con lo anticipado por los Ministerios de Asuntos Exteriores y Justicia de Rabat, Interior reclama a las autoridades españolas que asuman sus responsabilidades y aceleren, por ejemplo, los procedimientos de retorno de los miles de menores marroquíes que irrumpieron en Ceuta ―Marlaska aseguró este jueves que se habían tutelado ya a 1.898― junto con decenas de miles de adultos. El ministerio de Interior marroquí también insiste en la alegación oficial de ese país de que la lucha contra la migración irregular y las redes de trata de personas no puede depender de los esfuerzos de una sola parte y exige una responsabilidad compartida para poder aplicar el mecanismo de “retorno inmediato” o responsabilidad compartida.

Mientras los ministerios de Exteriores e Interior, cuyos titulares son designados directamente por el rey Mohamed VI, mantienen un discurso diplomático institucional en la presente crisis migratoria, el ministro de Justicia, Abdelatif Uahbi, está adoptando un perfil de confrontación política con España. Como uno de los principales líderes del Partido de la Autenticidad y la Modernidad (PAM, centro derecha), el ministro Uahbi está en campaña para las elecciones legislativas que se celebrarán el 23 de septiembre, en las que se perfila como ganador el candidato de esa fuerza política, Fuzi Lekjaa, presidente de la Federación Marroquí de Fútbol y ministro de Presupuestos. El ministro marroquí de Justicia ha criticado a España por haber aceptado a los migrantes irregulares mientras su país, según ha afirmado, se ha esforzado por impedir su salida. En una entrevista con la agencia Efe, Uahbi declaró: “Nosotros impedimos la salida de los inmigrantes, no solo de los marroquíes, sino también de otros, pero cuando llegan a España son aceptados y se regulariza su situación”.

Sin embargo, EL PAÍS y otros medios constataron durante los primeros días de la crisis que en la frontera de Castillejos las fuerzas de seguridad marroquíes se inhibieron ante el paso de decenas de miles de migrantes irregulares hacia Ceuta. Una fuente gubernamental de Rabat justificó esta actuación a Efe tres días más tarde, en que las fuerzas de seguridad no se enfrentaron a la multitud para evitar daños. Pese a todo ello y a las voces discrepantes de la oposición, pero también en su propio Gobierno, Marlaska insiste una y otra vez desde el estallido de la crisis en que “la cooperación y coordinación” con Rabat ha sido “de una complicidad fuera de toda duda”. El mismo jueves que estalló la crisis, el entorno del ministro recuerda que este recibió una llamada telefónica de su homónimo marroquí, Abdelouafi Laftit, para intercambiar información sobre lo que estaba pasando en Ceuta.

Tras el despliegue de la barrera marítima en el espigón de El Tarajal y ahora otra similar en el dique sur de Melilla ―con una altura en superficie de entre 30 y 70 centímetros únicamente, pero que faculta a las fuerzas de seguridad a devolver en caliente a los migrantes en aplicación de la reciente sentencia del Tribunal Supremo―, los esfuerzos de Interior se centran no solo en el límite fronterizo. El mismo día de la entrada masiva, Interior envió cerca de 350 agentes para apoyar a las plantillas de ambos cuerpos en la ciudad, que aquel día se vieron desbordadas. En el caso de la Policía Nacional, se desplegaron cinco equipos (225 agentes) de las Unidades de Intervención Policial (UIP, los conocidos como antidisturbios), cuya misión principal ahora es el control de las playas donde se han asentado muchos migrantes, así como vigilar otros puntos sensibles.

Para hacer visible la presencia policial en las calles ―en los últimos días, los jueces de Ceuta han enviado a prisión a nueve de los migrantes llegados en la entrada masiva y han expulsado a otros dos por la comisión de diversos delitos―, Interior ha doblado los turnos de los policías de seguridad ciudadana. Ahora se les refuerza con 45 miembros de la Unidad de Prevención y Reacción (UPR) procedentes de la península. A ellos se suman seis de la Unidad Central de Expulsiones y Repatriaciones (UCER) que llegaron a la ciudad horas después de estallar la crisis migratoria para apoyar en las labores de filiación de los migrantes, y los 20 de la Brigada Central de Extranjería y Fronteras que se incorporan para agilizar las expulsiones. También hay seis miembros de la Comisaría General de Información, encargados de la lucha antiterrorista, aunque el ministro este jueves ha negado que la situación creada haya supuesto un incremento de la amenaza yihadista. “Estamos vigilando, estamos monitorizando a todas las personas que han entrado”, añadió.

Por su parte, la Guardia Civil envió 60 agentes para reforzar la vigilancia fronteriza y otros 160 para realizar labores de seguridad ciudadana. Para el control de la línea costera, el instituto armado ha enviado buceadores del Grupo Especial de Actividades Subacuáticas (GEAS) y el buque Duque de Ahumada, el más grande del instituto armado, con una dotación de 12 guardias civiles. El Servicio Aéreo se ha reforzado con un helicóptero. Desde la semana pasada, a los agentes del instituto armado destinados en Ceuta, pero también en Melilla, no se les autorizan nuevas “vacaciones, permisos ni licencias” ante “la situación operativa derivada del incremento de la presión migratoria irregular”.

World.title: Las palabras de Albares activan el temor a la devolución entre los migrantes llegados a nado a Ceuta
World.content:
“Ya han llegado a un acuerdo”, escribe Siraj en su teléfono. Tiene 16 años y lleva casi dos semanas en Ceuta, desde que el 30 de julio cruzó a nado desde Marruecos. El mensaje va dirigido a un amigo que, como él, permanece en la ciudad autónoma. Le cuenta lo que acaba de escuchar: el ministro de Asuntos Exteriores, José Manuel Albares, ha hablado en conferencia de prensa. No ha pasado ni media hora desde su intervención, pero el mensaje ya corre de móvil en móvil. En los grupos de WhatsApp y las redes sociales de los jóvenes que llegaron a nado, la noticia se propaga como un reguero de pólvora. Para muchos, esas palabras confirman el peor de sus temores.

Hasta entonces, algunos se aferraban a una última posibilidad: que su país de origen no colaborase con España y que, por tanto, su devolución estuviese llena de obstáculos. Albares cerró esa puerta. “Hasta la última persona que ha entrado irregularmente en España volverá a Marruecos”, advertía el ministro. Y añadía que esa es la “voluntad expresa” de Rabat. Su contundencia y la confirmación de la cooperación con Marruecos han hecho saltar todas las alarmas entre quienes temen ser devueltos. El titular de Exteriores explicaba también que mantiene conversaciones diarias con su homólogo marroquí, Naser Burita, y aseguraba la “total disposición de Marruecos” para facilitar el retorno de sus ciudadanos a su país “sin pedir ninguna contrapartida”.

Siraj no quiere volver a Marruecos. Su deseo es quedarse en España y estudiar tecnología, pero la esperanza empieza a flaquear. Lleva toda la semana madrugando para plantarse frente a la Jefatura de Policía de Ceuta a la espera de que algún día le tomen los datos y pueda acceder así al sistema de protección de menores. Pero ese día no llega. Cada jornada transcurre de la misma manera: horas al sol, sentado en la calle junto a cientos de menores, mientras cuatro policías custodian la entrada para impedir que se acerquen a la puerta. Al final, Siraj regresa a la casa de un familiar que le ha dado refugio, siempre con las manos vacías. “Si me echan esta vez, intentaré estudiar en Marruecos y volver a España de forma legal, porque ahora mismo parece que no le importamos a nadie y no quiero desperdiciar mi futuro”, dice.

Multitud de menores migrantes esperan para su filiación frente a la Jefatura Superior de la Policía Nacional en Ceuta este lunes. Reduan (EFE)

En el polígono de El Tarajal, donde cientos de migrantes que llegaron a nado duermen en condiciones infrahumanas, un grupo de unas quince personas conversa en voz baja, visiblemente preocupado. “¿Es verdad lo que dicen?”, preguntan a una trabajadora de una ONG que ha acudido a curarles las heridas. Uno de ellos le enseña la pantalla de su teléfono: una captura de una noticia publicada en Instagram por un medio de comunicación árabe. En ella, el ministro de Justicia de Marruecos, Abdelatif Wahbi, asegura que su país “mantiene su determinación de recuperar a sus niños y menores que se encuentran en España”.

Las palabras del ministro dan forma a un temor que hasta ahora muchos preferían no mirar de frente. “Marruecos no está dispuesto a abandonar a sus niños, sus jóvenes y sus adolescentes”, afirma Wahbi. Pero ellos no han entrado a nado por el mar para regresar. Han llegado hasta aquí para escapar. Ahora, la advertencia de Albares llega después de dos semanas de espera en condiciones precarias: durmiendo hacinados sobre colchones, cuando los hay, o directamente sobre el suelo; protegidos apenas por una manta que durante el día utilizan para intentar resguardarse del sol. El hambre, la sed y el calor empiezan a pesar. Y, con ellos, crece también la certeza de que la posibilidad de ser devueltos a Marruecos ya no es un temor lejano, sino una amenaza cada vez más real.

“¿Y qué harán con los niños?”, pregunta una madre que huyó de Marruecos para escapar de un marido que la maltrataba. Cuenta que él ya le arrebató a su hijo mayor y que no puede permitir que le quiten también a la pequeña con la que llegó a nado hasta Ceuta. A su lado, la niña, con el pelo revuelto, mira a su alrededor con la misma angustia que su madre. “Si vuelvo a Marruecos, mi marido me mata”, dice la mujer.

Un padre de familia se acerca, visiblemente nervioso. “¿Crees que me separarán de mi familia?”, pregunta. La inquietud se extiende entre quienes escuchan. Nadie sabe qué responder. A las declaraciones de Albares se suma la presencia constante de policías y militares en las calles de Ceuta, una imagen que se repite a cada paso y que, para quienes esperan, resulta cada vez más difícil de ignorar. Mohamed, de ocho años, y su madre dormían hasta hace poco en la calle, frente a una casa. El pequeño cuenta que sentía terror cada vez que veía a los soldados pasar.

Y no son solo los más pequeños quienes viven con miedo. Hamza, de 26 años, duerme donde puede, siempre en la barriada de El Príncipe. Cuenta que estas últimas noches apenas ha pegado ojo. “He pasado mucho frío y no me he atrevido a dormir por miedo a que llegara la policía”, dice. En Ceuta, la espera ya no transcurre solo entre el hambre, el calor y el cansancio. También se duerme con miedo a que, al despertar, haya llegado el momento de volver.

World.title: 16 pueblos españoles que piden manga larga cuando cae la tarde
World.content:
Vielha (Lleida). La gran baza de los pueblos seleccionados radica, sobre todo, en la posibilidad de tener que taparse para descansar, algo que se ha convertido en todo un lujo durante la canícula. Es un requisito que cumple Vielha, a la vera de los ríos Garona y Nere, con su casco histórico construido a la manera aranesa, a golpe de piedra, pizarra y madera. Sus mínimas descenderán hasta los 12ºC la noche del domingo; las máximas alcanzarán picos de 33ºC en las horas centrales del jueves y viernes, pero bajarán a los 24ºC (y con probabilidad de lluvias) el lunes, según la Aemet. La capital del Valle de Arán se presenta como un buen campamento base para conocer este territorio del Pirineo catalán, con sus 33 núcleos de población, sus algo más de 10.000 habitantes y sus iglesias románicas. Es recomendable acercarse a la cascada Saut deth Pish, probablemente la más bonita de la zona. Más información: visitvaldaran.com/descubre-la-val-daran/pueblos/vielha/.

World.title: Illegal gambling ads on Meta target vulnerable gamblers: BNR
World.content:
Unlicensed gambling sites are running adverts on Facebook and Instagram that target vulnerable people who have signed themselves onto the national register barring them from gambling, an investigation by radio station BNR has found.

More than 100,000 people in the Netherlands have registered with Cruks, the self-exclusion scheme set up when online gambling was legalised, which requires every licensed casino, arcade and betting site to turn them away.

BNR found that searching Facebook for terms such as “Cruks”, geen Cruks or zonder Cruks (without Cruks) – surfaces a stream of adverts from casinos that hold no Dutch licence, promising large bonuses and offering routes around the register.

The adverts follow a consistent pattern, BNR reported: they suggest Cruks is restricting the user, then point them towards unlicensed alternatives. One features an AI-generated woman who tells viewers that international casinos do not consult the Dutch register and invites them to play the same day.

The accounts placing them carry names such as Betrouwbare Spelsites (reliable gaming sites). Users who encounter the adverts on Facebook go on to see them on Instagram and Threads.

Addiction specialists told BNR they were concerned that people registered with Cruks were being singled out, because seeing gambling adverts can trigger strong urges in addicts.

Meta removed adverts

Meta pulled a large number of the adverts from its public ad library after BNR put questions to the company, and the accounts that were identified were taken offline.

In a written response, Meta said it takes enforcement seriously and that advertisers must comply with the law. It declined to tell BNR what it earns from the adverts.

An estimate published in May by two gambling industry bodies KVA and VNLOK put Meta’s annual revenue from illegal gambling adverts aimed at the Netherlands at between €7.3 million and €13.6 million.

The figure is modelled from publicly available advertising data rather than confirmed by Meta, and the report states that it is not suggesting Meta knowingly allows the adverts.

VNLOK took Meta to court in June in an attempt to force it to act faster, and complained to the European Commission that the company is not meeting its obligations under the EU’s Digital Services Act.

The cabinet set out plans in June for a complete ban on online gambling advertising and bonuses. Junior justice minister Claudia van Bruggen has said the rise in gambling addiction, particularly among young people, is deeply worrying.

If you are concerned about your own or someone else’s gambling, OpenOverGokken, the national gambling helpline run by regulator the Kansspelautoriteit, can be reached free on 0800 24 000 22, day or night.

World.title: Man admits bomb attack on D66 office, calls it protest
World.content:
The man who set off a firework bomb at the D66 headquarters in The Hague in May has admitted the attack, telling a court it was a protest against Dutch asylum policy and what he called the dismantling of the country.

The 37-year-old, identified as Berry van D., appeared at a preliminary hearing at The Hague district court on Thursday. He is accused of causing an explosion with terrorist intent.

About 30 people, most of them members of the party’s youth wing, were inside the building when the firework bomb went off shortly after 9pm. No one was hurt.

Van D. said he had not known anyone was there because he had seen no lights on and that he never intended to hurt anyone.

Prosecutors said he acted alone and told the court he had a political message and wanted to silence people who think differently, ANP reported.

Van D. was arrested about an hour after the blast in the Grote Marktstraat, the city’s main shopping street, carrying two knives. NOS reported that he has a previous conviction for setting fire to city buses in Tilburg, where he had worked as a driver.

He told the court he had turned to violence because voting and peaceful demonstration had achieved nothing.

Psychiatric assessment

Thursday’s hearing was procedural and no trial date has been set yet. Van D. will be transferred to a forensic psychiatric clinic to assess whether he can be held responsible for his actions.

NOS reported that Van D. presents himself on social media as a supporter of the anti-immigration PVV, and described D66 leader Rob Jetten being sworn in as prime minister in February as a black day for the country.

The office on the Lange Houtstraat was also attacked in September last year, when rioters from an anti-immigration demonstration smashed its windows.
