The military industry has the priority to apply cutting-edge technologies and also make breakthrough innovations, Lu Guangshan, chairman of the Avionics System Co under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, was quoted by Shanghai Securities News as saying.

"For example, virtual reality headsets were first used in helmets for fighter jets and my company has developed six civilian industries such as virtual reality, drones, robotics and smart wearing," Lu said.

Military companies are encouraged to work with local governments to promote their advantageous expertise and develop a large number of new high-tech industries, Long Hongshan, chief engineer at the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense, told a news conference last week.

These new industries will play a vital role in promoting local economic growth and creating new employment opportunities, Long said.

Currently, 30 percent of products made by China's military companies are for military purposes and the other 70 percent for civilian purposes, he said.

In the future, high-tech industries will cover half of the military-related economy, Long added.

World.title: Dangerous stunts get thumbs-down from video platforms
World.content:
Multiple social media and video streaming platforms will limit who can view videos that depict dangerous stunts - and may even prohibit such material - in an effort to discourage imitators.

In November, daredevil stunt climber Wu Yongning fell to his death while scaling a skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan province. Wu, 26, had more than 1.3 million followers on social media who regularly devoured his breathtaking videos and photos. He climbed with no protective gear.

Last month, Wu's account on Sina Weibo stopped updating, leading followers to worry about his well-being.

On Friday, Wu's girlfriend confirmed on social media that the "rooftop daredevil" had fallen and died.

"Today is Dec 8. It makes me think of Nov 8, the day that you left us, left this world," she wrote.

Wu's family also confirmed his death to Jiefang Daily, a newspaper in Shanghai.

Meipai, Kuaishou, Xiaohuoshan and other video platforms on which Wu posted content, expressed their condolences, according to ThePaper.cn. Platform representatives told the news outlet that China currently has no law regulating extreme stunt videos, but each platform will update its content policy to discourage imitators.

Kuaishou said Wu's account had been restricted - meaning that only the uploader can see it - in September because of its depictions of dangerous acts.

Xiaohuoshan said it will ban video livestreams of dangerous stunts because live interactions between the performer and the audience could be a distraction and lead to catastrophic results.

The platform also said it will respect the desires of Wu's family in dealing with the videos.

All of Wu's stunt videos on the three platforms had been restricted or taken down as of Monday. A cellphone video of Wu performing his last stunt and falling to his death on Nov 8, has also been taken down.

Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Taiwan's New Party vows to help improve relations
World.content:
Delegation to Beijing reaffirms support for one-China, rejection of agitators

Top political adviser Yu Zhengsheng met with a Taiwan delegation representing the island's New Party in Beijing on Monday to discuss the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations and how to achieve the "great rejuvenation" of the Chinese nation.

Yu praised the New Party's unbroken stance upholding the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, since the party's establishment, as well as its peaceful approach to relations.

The 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which was held in October, further clarified the guidelines and policies addressing Taiwan, Yu said.

In his opening address to delegates during the congress, Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Central Committee of the CPC, called the one-China principle the political foundation of cross-Straits relations, and said that attempts to move toward "Taiwan independence" in any form will be defeated.

Taiwan will share development opportunities on the Chinese mainland, and its residents will enjoy the same treatment as mainland people as they pursue studies, start businesses, seek jobs or come to live on the mainland, Xi said in the address.

Yok Mu-ming, chairman of the New Party and head of the Taiwan delegation, said the party has firmly upheld the one-China principle and promoted peace.

The delegation also met on Monday with Zhang Zhijun, head of the State Council's Taiwan Affairs Office.

Zhang and Yok agreed that the one-China principle must be upheld going forward, expressed firm opposition to separatist activities and vowed to make efforts toward peaceful relations.

Both sides agreed to establish and improve mechanisms of communication, share opinions on major issues in the relationship and promote exchanges and communication in all fields - especially between youth. They further agreed to create a constructive and convenient environment for the development of Taiwan youth on the mainland.

Zhang said cross-Straits relations have faced challenges because the island's Democratic Progressive Party has refused to clearly express support for the one-China principle, which led to the mainland suspending official communications with the island.

He said that a "Taiwan independence" force had recently stirred up the island, proposing the removal of Chinese mainland elements in a variety of fields.

"Its aim is to cut the historical ties between Taiwan and the mainland, reduce public awareness that Taiwan people are part of the Chinese nation and limit many cultural influences on the island," he said.

Some people advocating "Taiwan independence" have pushed for amending the law, and have proposed changing the island's constitution. "This shows that separatist activities and the group supporting 'independence' pose the most serious threat to the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations," Zhang said.

He warned that people from both sides should be vigilant and firmly oppose such activities.

luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Former Chongqing political official facing corruption investigation
World.content:
Sun Zhengcai, the former secretary of Chongqing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of accepting bribes, according to the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Monday.

According to the procuratorate, Sun has been placed under "coercive measures", which may include summons by force, bail, residential surveillance, detention and arrest.

The investigation is underway, the procuratorate said in a statement released on Monday.

In July, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection launched an investigation into Sun for "serious violations of Party discipline".

The CCDI said in a news release that Sun betrayed Party principles and ignored the Party code of conduct and rules.

He was found to have seriously violated the CPC's eight-point code on frugality and maintaining close ties with the masses, seeking pomp, ostentation and privileges, according to the CCDI.

The CCDI said he was guilty of nepotism and seeking benefits in selection of officials. He was found by the CCDI to have leaked confidential Party information and seriously breached Party rules on integrity.

Moreover, he abused power and used his job to gain benefits for others, then accepted their huge bribes in return, either paid in cash or properties, the CCDI said. He was found to seek substantial benefits for his relatives' businesses and accepted valuable gifts, the CCDI said.

The anti-graft inspectors also accused Sun of bureaucracy and sloth in work and degradation and power-for-sex trades, according to the CCDI.

Sun totally deviated from the Party spirit and political requirements of senior officials, the CCDI said in the statement, adding that his misconduct betrayed the trust of the CPC Central Committee and the public, inflicting huge harm to the Party and the country with "extremely bad" social influences.

The CCDI transferred the criminal evidence involving his case to judicial authorities for further investigation.

In September, the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee expelled Sun from the Party and dismissed him from public office.

China Daily - Xinhua

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018887/Lost, Looted, Crumbling: The Vanishing Temple Murals of Yu County
World.title: Lost, Looted, Crumbling: The Vanishing Temple Murals of Yu County
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018887/Lost, Looted, Crumbling: The Vanishing Temple Murals of Yu County
World.content:
A Chinese county known as the home of over 400 temple murals dating back to the Ming dynasty (1368–1644) is facing a heritage restoration crisis, with many of its murals stolen, destroyed, or marred by thieves.

In an investigation published Wednesday, Shanghai-based news outlet The Paper visited 16 fortified villages in Yu County in the northern Hebei province and found that many of the area’s temple murals had been stolen, destroyed during temple collapse, or weathered beyond recognition. Remaining fragments often bore looters’ cut marks.

A major cultural relic hub, the county served as a military and commercial crossroads during the Ming and Qing dynasties (1644–1911) and is home to more than 1,600 registered cultural heritage locations, including numerous fortified villages. The accompanying temples feature murals depicting Taoist, Buddhist, and folk religious elements.

Danhou Village — inscribed on China’s official list of traditional villages in 2016 — is one of the county’s most popular tourist destinations. The village’s Guandi Temple was once home to extensive murals, but only fragments remain today.

When The Paper visited, the temple was under renovation for leaking roofs, missing wooden components, and cracked walls after years of neglect. Work began in April and is projected to be completed by the end of the year.

Of the 16 villages The Paper visited, only those officially considered “traditional villages” or protected sites received restoration and care. The report noted that overall neglect of the fortified villages stems from their abandonment, as villagers have mostly lived outside the sites since the 1980s, leaving the buildings to decay.

A member of the county’s cultural relics management office told The Paper that he recently inspected a temple on a visit to his hometown.

“I went there around noon, and the wall was still standing,” he said. “But at around 2 p.m., I got a call saying the western wall of that temple had collapsed. If I had gone any later, I might have been buried under it.”

Another obstacle to upkeep is funding. Under China’s cultural relics law, their owners or users must preserve them, with government subsidies provided where possible. But in Yu County, most low-level relics are owned by villages that can’t afford maintenance, placing the burden on the county.

The cultural relics worker described how every village has an appointed relic steward, but with no subsidy budget, the role falls to village cadres as an additional duty. With heavy workloads and no stipends, protection relies on individual goodwill.

Yet government investment has been considerable. Over a decade ago, Yu County built a 12,000-square-meter museum for 10,000-plus movable relics, free to the public, costing the county nearly 4 million yuan ($600,000) annually. In 2023, state and provincial funds for restoration projects totaled 14.6 million yuan.

Despite the investment, Yu County’s neglected relics expose gaps in China’s heritage architecture protection, a problem that it has been working to solve in recent years.

In July 2024, the Finance Ministry created a lottery-funded program for unlisted ancient buildings. Upon submitting a proposal, local authorities whose heritage architecture and restoration projects are deemed to serve the public good are given priority. The program will run through 2027.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Murals at an ancient temple in Yu County, Hebei province, June 20, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018886/The Forgotten Legacy of China’s Greatest Explorer
World.title: The Forgotten Legacy of China’s Greatest Explorer
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018886/The Forgotten Legacy of China’s Greatest Explorer
World.content:
During the opening decades of the 15th century, a eunuch from China’s imperial court led seven epic voyages across Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean, pushing westward as far as the Red Sea and the shores of East Africa.

The expeditions were astonishing feats of engineering and navigation. Setting sail decades before Christopher Columbus or Vasco da Gama, Zheng spent years crossing the oceans at the head of a vast fleet of 200 ships. Some of the vessels measured up to 70 meters long — three times the size of Columbus’ ships.

For many, Zheng deserves to rank among history’s greatest explorers. Yet, much about the voyages — and Zheng himself — remains shrouded in mystery. He barely features in the official records left by China’s Ming dynasty (1368–1644), with court historians dismissing his expeditions as impressive, but ruinously expensive. Even the place and date of Zheng’s death are unknown.

The Ming court’s assessment still colors views of Zheng centuries later. Today, the great admiral is well known in China, with generations of schoolchildren learning about his amazing treasure ships that brought giraffes, lions, zebras, and other exotic beasts back from Africa. But the voyages tend to be presented as a historical curiosity that had little lasting impact.

Zou Zhenhuan is on a mission to change that. The 69-year-old — now a distinguished professor at Shanghai’s Fudan University — has spent decades studying Zheng He, and his research has played a significant role in shifting perceptions of the explorer and his legacy. His latest book, “Monsoon Asia and Africa: Cultural Exchange and Zheng He’s Voyages,” is his most comprehensive look at the subject yet.

For Zou, Zheng’s voyages were far more influential than often assumed. Far from a flash in the pan, they opened up a new era of maritime trade between Asia and Africa, as merchants took advantage of the navigational technologies and sea routes pioneered by Zheng. He even believes they helped pave the way for the European Age of Discovery that followed.

In this interview, Zou, who is also a research fellow at the Shanghai Research Institute of Culture and History, explains why Zheng He is often so misunderstood — and why his voyages should be seen as a harbinger of globalization. The text has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: You have studied Zheng He for more than 20 years. What drew you to this subject in the beginning?

Zou: My interest in Zheng He began in my boyhood. What captivated me most was his extraordinary perseverance — seven voyages spanning more than two decades. Such marvelous experiences are enough to stir the imagination. As the Portuguese poet Luís de Camões wrote in “Os Lusíadas,” the true and marvelous deeds of brave men surpass all fantasy and legend. I was a sickly boy, but I harbored an intense hero complex, and Zheng He’s exploits answered it perfectly.

It was this interest that led me to study Zheng He once I became a historian, and it is this same interest that has sustained my research for so many years.

Sixth Tone: After all these years of research, what kind of person is Zheng He in your mind?

Zou: As my research has deepened, the image of Zheng He in my mind has grown ever richer. Take his religious faith, for example. Many people might assume Zheng He was simply a Muslim. He was indeed born into a Muslim family; his grandfather and father both made the hajj to Mecca. But he was also a devout Buddhist who was accepted as a disciple by an eminent monk, receiving the Dharma name “Fushan,” and supervising the construction of the Great Bao’en Temple in Nanjing. At the same time, Zheng He was also an adherent of Confucianism. Historical records describe him as “endowed with the talent to govern and versed in the teachings of Confucius and Mencius.”

The most famous material testimony to Zheng He’s plural faith is the trilingual stele he erected in the kingdom of Ceylon (present-day Sri Lanka) during his second voyage in 1409. The stele, commonly known as the Galle Trilingual Inscription, is carved in three scripts: the Chinese text praises the Buddha and records a list of offerings; the Tamil text glorifies the Hindu god Shiva; and the Persian text extols Allah. Paying tribute to the deities of three great religions on a single stone tablet is, in my view, the most vivid expression of Zheng He’s cosmopolitan, all-embracing spirit.

Sixth Tone: It seems “plurality” is a keyword when it comes to Zheng He.

Zou: Exactly. Zheng He was a man of all-around talent. To begin with, he possessed exceptional organizational and managerial abilities — commanding a fleet of more than 27,000 men was in itself an enormously complex feat of systems engineering.

He also had the metaphysical learning of a Confucian scholar and was equally adept at practical, technical matters: during the voyages he spread the Chinese calendar, rituals, weights and measures, and architectural techniques to other countries, and with superb diplomatic skill he mediated disputes between Siam and Malacca, and between Annam and Champa.

Plus, he even displayed outstanding military talent: on his very first voyage he defeated Chen Zuyi, a pirate chief who commanded tens of thousands of followers in the Strait of Malacca, wiping out more than 5,000 pirates.

Sixth Tone: When I was reading your book, what impressed me most was Zheng He’s nautical technology — especially his precise understanding and ingenious use of the Indian Ocean monsoons.

Zou: That’s right. The fleet’s seven expeditions were deeply embedded in the monsoon, which is the main reason I titled the book “Monsoon Asia and Africa.”

The regions the fleet traversed — East Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Indian Ocean — are among the areas of the world where the monsoon phenomenon is most pronounced. And in an era without modern propulsion, the monsoon was the “engine” that drove this enormous armada on its long voyages.

The fleet usually departed China in winter, between October and March, riding the northeast monsoon southward. By the time it reached the Indian Ocean, the summer southwest monsoon would be blowing, allowing a smooth voyage home. The whole round trip took about a year and a half.

To visit more places efficiently, Zheng He would dispatch detached squadrons along the way; after completing their missions, these squadrons would regroup at designated rendezvous points in accordance with the monsoon patterns.

But here’s the thing: the monsoon and the compass could carry the fleet forward, but they could not tell the crew exactly where they were on the open sea. To do this, the fleet mastered a refined technique known as “guoyang qianxing,” or star-observation navigation, using an instrument called the “qianxing,” or star-measuring, board to determine a ship’s latitude according to stars’ altitude above the horizon. Zheng He’s fleets also compiled these observations into dedicated star charts, creating a reusable navigational database.

One could say that Zheng He’s fleet fused three techniques — the monsoon patterns, star-observation navigation, and the magnetic compass — into a single, world-leading navigational system for its time. I believe these sea routes, nautical technology, and geographical knowledge helped lay the intellectual and technical foundations for the arrival of European explorers more than half a century later. However, this topic needs further research.

Sixth Tone: Since you mention the European explorers who came later, I have to raise a common critique: that unlike the explorers who launched Europe’s Age of Discovery, Zheng He’s expeditions — for all their grandeur — were a mere flash in the pan that left no lasting imprint. How do you see it?

Zou: This view is indeed very common. I would point out that Zheng He’s seven voyages were not merely official acts of diplomacy by the Ming court; they also facilitated exchanges of goods, species, and technologies between Asia and Africa on an unprecedented scale.

The exotic animals the fleet brought back from foreign lands — giraffes, lions, ostriches, zebras — and the rare plants and fruits such as pepper, sappanwood, and durian greatly enriched China’s native stock of species. Wherever it went, the fleet shared nautical and astronomical knowledge with local peoples, deepening mutual learning among the civilizations of Asia and Africa.

The most representative example of all this is blue-and-white porcelain. Zheng He’s fleet carried large quantities of porcelain into the Islamic world, while the cobalt pigment needed to produce blue-and-white ware, known as “Sumali blue,” originally came from Persia. This pattern of “bringing finished products out and importing raw materials in” was itself a cross-cultural dialogue of technology and aesthetics.

As the Ming dynasty’s most sought-after export in overseas markets, blue-and-white porcelain was among the important gifts carried on every mission. Pieces dating from the period of Zheng He’s voyages have been unearthed at Fustat in Egypt, at Aydhab in Sudan, at Aden on the Arabian Peninsula, and elsewhere.

The huge overseas demand, in turn, stimulated a massive increase in early Ming porcelain production: according to historical records, in 1433 alone the court ordered the firing of 443,500 pieces in a single decree.

What does this tell us? It shows that nearly a century before Columbus set sail, Zheng He’s fleet had already opened up the east-west sea routes of the Indian Ocean and built a regional network of trade and cultural exchange. I call this the “Zheng He exchange.”

Sixth Tone: That concept readily brings to mind the “Columbian exchange” — the massive exchange of people, plants, animals, and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia that opened up after Columbus’ voyages.

Zou: I did indeed borrow the theoretical framework of the “Columbian exchange,” but my concept points to an earlier wave of civilizational interaction — one that unfolded between Asia and Africa. In many respects, Zheng He was a key catalyst on the eve of globalization.

Of course, while the “Zheng He exchange” and the “Columbian exchange” share many similarities, their purposes were fundamentally different. Zheng He’s voyages never established colonies overseas, and they were extremely restrained in their use of force.

As you mentioned, many Chinese people feel rather regretful about this, believing it caused China to miss a golden opportunity to dominate the globe. Liu Cixin’s short science-fiction story “Xiyang” (“The Western Ocean”) expresses exactly this sentiment through an alternate-history framework: in the story, Zheng He’s fleet sails farther west from the East African coast, rounds the Cape of Good Hope, and eventually reaches Europe, defeats the combined Anglo-French forces, and conquers the European continent, turning China into an empire on which the sun never sets.

But in my view, Zheng He radiates the light of pacifism and cultural pluralism — and that is precisely where his example can offer inspiration for our own time.

(Header image: A statue of Zheng He in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, 2024. 500px Essential)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018882/An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.title: An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018882/An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.content:
“My contact lenses are comfortable even after wearing them all day. Do you want to try them?”

So says a young woman in glasses with transparent lenses, in response to a friend who says her contacts are painful. She then takes a contact box out of a black handbag, offers it, and says, “You can blink without worry.”

The endorsement seems genuine enough — except neither woman is real.

This , featuring the popular AI actress Fang Taozi endorsing colored contacts, has recently sparked controversy in China over whether an AI character can vouch for a product’s quality.

Released in late July on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, by domestic contact lens brand Nutnutlook, the ad was taken down without comment last week.

In response, Chinese netizens criticized the  for using an AI avatar instead of a human actress. “What makes me uncomfortable is that someone without eyes now has the right to speak about eyes,” one user commented.

“AI doesn’t even know what it feels like to actually wear the product,” another wrote.

Neither the company behind the AI actress, Guangzhou-based World Media Film and TV Culture, nor the contacts brand has responded to the controversy.

The fictional 20-year-old Fang Taozi was unveiled in the AI short drama “The Laid-off Girl” in June this year. The series, which tells the story of a small-town girl moving to a fictional city to pursue a modeling career, has been viewed more than 320 million times on Douyin.

In the months following the series’ release, directed by popular content creator Fei Feifei, Fang’s personal Douyin account — created by companies to boost AI actors’popularity — gained more than 470,000 followers. Her account posts content ranging from so-called “behind-the-scenes” footage during the show’s production to snippets of her supposed daily life, such as making breakfast.

Fang has been lauded by fans for having, unlike many AI characters, moles and blemishes, giving her an imperfect and realistic appearance. In “The Laid-off Girl,” she struggles with relatable Chinese workplace challenges, such as pressure to attend business dinners and getting bullied by her colleagues.

Domestic media reported that on Juliang Xingtu, Douyin’s influencer marketing platform, Fang Taozi’s advertising rates are 168,000 yuan ($24,900) per video for clips under 20 seconds, 208,000 yuan for videos between 21 and 60 seconds, and 258,000 yuan for videos over 60 seconds — significantly higher than ad rates charged by most human influencers.

Ma Lihong, a senior partner at Beijing DHH Law Firm, told domestic media that, despite AI avatars not being considered people under Chinese law and therefore not legally considered  endorsers, the video could still constitute false advertising.

Ma added that advertisers are responsible for the truthfulness of their content and that by making a first-person claim about experiencing a product, the AI character could be seen as fabricating user experience. As such, the brand and the ’s producer could potentially be in violation of the law.

Compounding the severity of the issue, colored contact lenses are classified as Class III medical devices under China’s regulatory system, reserved for items that pose the highest risk to consumers. Actors are prohibited from recommending such products in s, a rule aimed at preventing brands from misleading consumers.

This is not the first time Chinese brands have experimented with AI-generated figures in advertising. Major bottled water company Nongfu Spring made headlines last year for using AI-generated images in promotional posters, while companies ranging from yogurt brands to office chair suppliers have collaborated with various AI-generated actors to endorse products and use slogans. Tutorials on using AI-generated videos for livestream commerce have also become common.

Entertainment law expert Qiu Zhimiao said AI-powered endorsements will become increasingly common, and regulating them is a new frontier. As s endorsed by virtual influencers exist in a legal gray area, he said, there is a need for clearer regulations.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A screenshot of the AI actress Fang Taozi in the  promoting colored contact lenses. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018881/1,300 Meters Up, a Sichuan Soccer Hero Brings the Game Home
World.title: 1,300 Meters Up, a Sichuan Soccer Hero Brings the Game Home
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018881/1,300 Meters Up, a Sichuan Soccer Hero Brings the Game Home
World.content:
On a rain-washed weekend morning, mist clings to the peaks surrounding Ze’e Village in the southwestern Sichuan province. Over the sound of a rushing mountain stream, 24-year-old Jifu Lama leads a procession of children in matching kits. They navigate through rice paddies, along irrigation canals and over earthen mounds until they reach their destination: a soccer pitch carved out of a former cornfield.

Perched halfway up a mountain at an altitude of 1,300 meters, Lama’s pitch looks like a vibrant green terraced field folded into the sweeping landscape of Sichuan’s Daliangshan region. Standing in the center circle, the young coach directs his players — mostly children aged 6 to 13 from six neighboring Yi ethnic villages — to lace up their boots, arrange the cones and begin their warm-ups.

Ze’e Village is remote, accessible only by winding mountain roads, but the children’s imaginations stretch far beyond the peaks. During the buildup to the 2026 World Cup, the young athletes devoured match highlights on smartphones. Winning and losing are secondary to the star players: the children argue passionately over the goals scored by superstars like Cristiano Ronaldo, Kylian Mbappé, Lionel Messi and Harry Kane.

Seven-year-old Aluo, a first-grader with lightning-fast footwork, idolizes France’s Mbappé. His cousin, Yang Xiaojun, a skinny third-grader, became a die-hard Gareth Bale fan after watching a clip of the Welshman’s legendary bicycle kick.

When they score on this mountain pitch, the kids leap into the air, spinning to land in Cristiano Ronaldo’s iconic, arms-down “Siu” celebration.

For these children, soccer is bright spot in childhood marked by economic hardship. Local data shows rural per capita income in Daliangshan is around just 12,700 yuan ($1,770) a year. To make a living, parents migrate to factories in the southern Guangdong province, Wuhan in the central Hubei province, and the northern Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, returning only once a year for the traditional Yi New Year.

Raised by aging grandparents in households with multiple siblings, these “left-behind” children have few outlets for their energy. A piece of candy or a lucky draw at the school gate used to be the highlight of their week. Now, soccer offers them friendship, structure and a window to the outside world.

To keep them invested, Lama implemented a reward system. Players earn four points for every practice they attend, which they can exchange for free gear. That is how Hu Feifei, one of the girls who recently joined the squad, earned her jersey, socks and boots.

Hu remembers when the pitch was nothing but sand dumped over uneven soil. When it rained, they played in puddles and went home with scraped knees, but they were happy. Today, thanks to a corporate sponsor moved by the team’s story, they play on an artificial turf pitch that Lama proudly claims is “better than the ones in the county town.”

The sponsor discovered them because of Lama, who is no stranger to the spotlight. But his viral fame is a chapter of his life tinged with both pride and heartbreak.

Lama’s obsession began in middle school when a friend gifted him a Neymar Barcelona jersey. The self-described rebellious teen found his anchor in soccer. To play, he transferred to a vocational school with a pitch.

To master the game, he did the unthinkable and dropped out, hiked to an altitude of 2,000 meters, and built a wooden hut on a flat peak. There, with no electricity and relying on a wood fire to cook, he trained alone for days at a time. His goal was to become a professional soccer player within five years.

He documented his solitary, high-altitude drills on short-video platforms. The stark contrast between the primitive, breathtaking environment and the boy’s fluid footwork captivated the internet. He amassed hundreds of thousands of followers, drawing the attention of FIFA on the eve of the 2022 Qatar World Cup. At his peak, he was earning up to 6,000 yuan a month from his videos.

But soon this felt wrong, money was not why he played soccer. “It felt like I was using soccer to make a profit,” Lama says. “It betrayed my original love for the game.”

However, his online presence earned him a spot in professional tryouts. It was here that Lama’s dream collided with reality. “My technique was too poor, I couldn’t understand the tactics, and my receiving and passing were all wrong,” he said.

In May 2023, he finally earned a spot with Jingchuan Wenhui, a fourth-tier club in the Chinese Champions League. Stepping onto the pitch, the cheers of the fans made the experience feel unreal.

It lasted exactly 45 minutes. Half a match that Lama doesn’t dare to rewatch. “My muscles were constantly tense, and I felt I performed too poorly,” he said.

The experience made clarified the insurmountable chasm between himself and real professional players, he said he could “never keep up with the rhythm and physical confrontation.”

The failure was a brutal watershed moment. But instead of continuing to chase trials across the country, Lama packed his bags and looked back to the dirt fields of Ze’e Village.

Today, he serves as an unpaid, unofficial soccer coach for two local primary schools. He runs training sessions five days a week and spends his weekends driving his minivan across the mountains to ferry kids to and from practice.

The transition from viral star to grassroots coach hasn’t been easy. The internet money has dried up, and his public welfare coaching model is financially unsustainable. He is considering charging a modest annual fee of 1,200 yuan for new recruits this fall, but he agonizes over whether the cost will price out the very kids who need the game most. He regularly visits skeptical parents, trying to convince them that soccer isn’t a distraction, but a vital tool for development.

“I want these children to start changing from this generation,” Lama said. “I want them to learn manners and be driven.”

In a region where educational resources are sparse and academic struggles are common, Lama sees soccer as a safety net. His vision is already bearing fruit: four of his sixth-graders recently passed a specialized sports exam, securing them spots in a superior middle school in the county town.

Eventually, Lama plans to build a fully registered professional club. He has already chosen the name: Leke, the Yi word for plowshare.

It is a fitting moniker for a young man breaking tough ground. “I don’t even have a first team yet,” Lama said, looking out over the mist-covered pitch. “I’ve only just lifted my foot to take the first step, and it hasn’t even landed yet.”

This piece was originally published by Caixin Global. It is republished here with permission.

Reporter: Zheng Haipeng.

(Header image: Players from Jijia Primary School pose for a group photo, imitating the signature moves of their favorite soccer stars, Ze’e Village, Sichuan province, June 2026. Zheng Haipeng/Caixin)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018878/Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.title: Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018878/Targeted Online by Classmate’s Father, Shanghai Student Wins Damages
World.content:
A Shanghai court has ordered a father to pay 4,000 yuan ($590) in damages and legal fees after urging other parents in a group chat to ostracize his son’s classmate, domestic media reported last week.

According to a ruling by the Shanghai Pudong New Area People’s Court, the father was found to have infringed on the classmate’s right to reputation under China’s Civil Code. He was ordered to pay 2,000 yuan in emotional damages and 2,000 yuan in legal fees, as well as issue an apology to the boy.

A Beijing court handled a similar case in 2022, ordering two parents to apologize to a student after defaming them in a parent group on messaging app WeChat, widely used in China as a key channel for teachers and parents to exchange information and discuss student issues. However, they were not ordered to provide financial compensation.

The Shanghai dispute began after the father’s son, surnamed Zhang, was hit on the head with a tree branch by his middle school classmate, surnamed Zhao. After reviewing surveillance footage, teachers concluded that Zhao had not acted intentionally, domestic media reported.

Zhang’s father then attacked Zhao in a WeChat group of more than 80 parents. “This child has psychological problems,” he wrote in the group. “My son suffered a concussion after this student hit him with a stick.” He also claimed that the school was “well aware of this child’s mental health problems” and called on other parents to collectively demand that the school expel Zhao.

Zhao was subsequently isolated at school by his classmates and was unable to continue attending classes as normal. The boy later sued Zhang for infringing on his right to reputation.

Han Yini, the judge presiding over the case, told domestic media that the chat records from the parent group showed that Zhang’s remarks were “clearly derogatory and insulting” and “lacked sufficient factual basis.” The comments caused “panic” among other parents, some of whom demanded that Zhao’s parents provide a psychiatric assessment report of their son before he returned to school.

“This seriously damaged Zhao’s social reputation and placed significant stress on his studies, daily life, and friendships,” Han said.

“Student bullying includes not only physical conflict but also malicious exclusion and isolation through verbal or online means, which can harm minors both physically and psychologically,” said Zhang Jiawei, a judge specializing in juvenile and family cases at the court. He also called on schools to strengthen oversight and mediation.

School bullying has received growing attention in China in recent years. The revised Law on the Protection of Minors, which took effect in 2021, requires schools to establish mechanisms to prevent and address student bullying. In 2024, Chinese authorities launched a nationwide campaign targeting bullying and violence in schools.

Zhang added that when children have conflicts with others at school, parents should work with teachers to resolve them and, when necessary, seek help from educational authorities or judicial bodies.

“Every parent should understand that there are boundaries to what they can say and that infringement carries consequences. Respecting others is a prerequisite for protecting your own child,” Zhang said.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Kate3155/Getty Creative/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.title: Saving China’s Vanishing Fields of Knowledge
World.content:
Every summer, millions of Chinese high school students who have just completed the national college entrance examination, or gaokao, face a pivotal decision: which university and major to choose. At the same time, media outlets and social platforms fill with debate over which fields of study offer the best employment prospects and financial returns. Driven by pragmatism, students tend to favor majors that lead to well-paid or stable careers, such as computer science, software engineering, medicine, and accounting.

At the other end of the spectrum are disciplines that appear to have little practical value and remain unfamiliar to most people, including Western Xia studies, bamboo and wooden slip studies, silk manuscript studies, and Dunhuang studies. In recent years, these fields have come to be grouped under the poetic term “lengmen juexue,” often translated as “niche and endangered disciplines.”

The phrase combines two concepts. Lengmen, or “niche disciplines,” refers to traditional humanities fields with small research communities that attract limited scholarly attention and produce results slowly. Juexue, or “endangered disciplines,” refers to fields of exceptional cultural significance that require highly specialized expertise and risk disappearing as senior scholars retire. In other words, lengmen describes their circumstances, while juexue reflects their value. A true niche and endangered discipline must satisfy both conditions: it has only a small community of researchers while preserving an irreplaceable body of cultural knowledge at risk of being lost.

Many of these disciplines have a long history. Fields such as philology, Confucian classics, epigraphy, bibliography, ancient musicology, and calendrical studies were once central to Chinese scholarship but gradually became marginalized following the introduction of Western academic disciplines in the modern era. The term juexue itself dates back more than a thousand years. During the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127), the philosopher Zhang Zai (1020–1077) wrote in his “Hengqu Yulu” of the need “to ordain conscience for Heaven and Earth, to secure life for the people, to continue the lost teachings of past sages, and to establish peace for all future generations.”

Today, however, “niche and endangered disciplines” is more than a descriptive label. It has become an institutional framework within Chinese academia. In 2016, President Xi Jinping called for greater attention to marginal disciplines with high cultural value and significance for Chinese heritage during a speech at the Seminar on Philosophy and Social Sciences in Beijing. Quoting an old Chinese saying, he argued that resources maintained over the long term prove their worth when they are eventually needed.

That vision took institutional form in 2018, when the National Social Science Fund of China established a dedicated funding program for niche and endangered disciplines. Since then, the Ministry of Education, the Chinese Academy of History, and other institutions have launched related initiatives. One flagship funding program provides around 350,000 yuan ($52,000) for individual research projects and about 800,000 yuan for collaborative projects, placing these disciplines on a similar footing to other major National Social Science Fund initiatives.

These disciplines contribute little to GDP growth and seem far removed from everyday life. So why do the state and the academic community devote such significant resources to supporting them?

The answer lies in their role in helping Chinese civilization understand itself and sustain its continuity. Civilizations do not endure by chance. Their longevity depends not only on creating new knowledge but also on preserving and interpreting their past.

These disciplines address fundamental questions about China’s history. Why were oracle bone inscriptions written the way they were? How was the millennia-old “Book of Documents” passed down through the centuries? How did ancient Chinese societies observe the skies and develop calendars? What does the Library Cave at the Mogao Grottoes in Dunhuang reveal about cultural exchange? Such questions may seem remote, but they form the foundation of a civilization’s understanding of its own history.

These disciplines also safeguard cultural continuity. The longevity of the Chinese civilization has depended on generations of scholars who continuously compiled classical texts, interpreted ancient scripts, and preserved knowledge. Without this work, vast collections of cultural heritage might survive physically while becoming increasingly difficult, or even impossible, to understand.

These disciplines also shape China’s cultural narrative. Research into frontier history, ethnic writing systems, and Chinese texts preserved overseas extends beyond academic inquiry. It informs historical interpretation, cultural identity, and international exchange.

In short, niche and endangered disciplines preserve the historical memory of Chinese civilization. Once sustained by only a handful of scholars, they have become an important part of China’s broader cultural strategy.

So what qualifies as a niche and endangered discipline? There is no definitive list. Instead, the category has steadily expanded. It initially included fields such as oracle bone studies, Dunhuang studies, bamboo and wooden slip studies, and ancient script studies. More recently, it has broadened to encompass the history of ancient Chinese science and technology, ancient astronomy and calendrical studies, ethnic scripts, Chinese texts preserved overseas, frontier history and geography, and research on exchanges between China and other civilizations. Today, these disciplines are generally grouped into four broad categories: ancient scripts and extinct languages; traditional classics and endangered classical studies; ancient specialized histories and niche skills; and research on China’s frontiers and its exchanges with other ancient civilizations.

Why has the category expanded? Not because more disciplines have become obscure but because there is growing recognition that many specialized fields are indispensable to understanding Chinese civilization.

Take ancient astronomy and calendrical studies. Without them, it would be difficult to understand how ancient China developed its calendar, organized agricultural production, and structured political authority. Likewise, without research into historical ethnic writing systems, countless documents produced by frontier peoples would become unreadable. Moreover, dedicated funding programs provide specialized institutions and researchers with the long-term support needed to sustain this work.

State support has already produced significant results. The Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, for example, has published major works including “Heroic Epic and Oral Tradition” and “Translations of Sanskrit Literature.” These works preserve and interpret historical texts, making them accessible to modern scholars and readers. Meanwhile, digital technologies are increasingly being used to collate ancient texts, digitize documents, and recognize historical scripts, greatly improving research efficiency. Even so, significant challenges remain.

The greatest challenge is not funding but time. One scholar may spend three decades studying just a few dozen oracle bones. Another may devote an entire career to deciphering a script that disappeared more than a thousand years ago. A third may spend decades reconstructing an ancient calendar.

Mastering a niche and endangered discipline often requires decades of training, yet an entire field can disappear within a single generation. Early Chinese astronomy, for example, demands expertise in ancient astronomy and calendrical systems, the ability to decipher ancient scripts, and a deep understanding of history. The barriers to entry are therefore exceptionally high. Since the deaths of leading scholars such as Bo Shuren (1934–1997), Xi Zezong (1927–2008), and Chen Meidong (1942–2008), the field has weakened significantly, with few young researchers able to replace them. Sustained institutional support is therefore essential.

These disciplines also sit uneasily within a modern research system that rewards speed and measurable output. Their work progresses slowly, while public awareness remains limited and relatively few young people are willing to commit to careers that require decades of patient study.

Protecting niche and endangered disciplines therefore requires training and evaluation systems tailored to their unique characteristics. Only then can more students be encouraged to enter these fields, allowing scholars to devote themselves to the long-term work of preserving and expanding humanity’s understanding of China’s past.

Translator: David Ball; portrait artist: Wang Zhenhao.

(Header image: Visuals from International Dunhuang Programme and VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018870/China’s Henan Province to Enforce Paid Annual Leave
World.title: China’s Henan Province to Enforce Paid Annual Leave
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018870/China’s Henan Province to Enforce Paid Annual Leave
World.content:
China’s central Henan province issued a notice last week urging companies to ensure employees take their full paid annual leave and encouraging employer flexibility around workers leaving early on Fridays, domestic media reported Wednesday. The move was designed to encourage travel and spending on holidays and weekend getaways.

However, on Friday, local authorities said that the notice contained “inaccurate wording” and had “not undergone proper approval procedures,” and in response to public concerns, would be revised and reissued.

The original notice required employers to simplify leave approval procedures and called on company leaders to “lead by example” by taking time off themselves. It also clarified that all employees are entitled to the same paid annual leave regardless of whether they are permanent, temporary, dispatched, or contracted workers.

In addition, it encouraged employees to maximize their breaks by combining leave with weekends and public holidays, and said those with school-age children should receive priority when applying for leave during school breaks.

Henan is among several provincial-level regions that have introduced measures this year to better enforce paid annual leave, in line with China’s latest and first specific five-year plan on boosting consumption, approved by the State Council in July.

The Henan notice sparked heated discussion on social media, jumping to the trending topics list on microblogging platform Weibo. Some users voiced support and called for a nationwide rollout of the policy. Others took the opportunity to criticize a long-standing workplace culture in the country that promotes skipping leave to demonstrate dedication.

“I no longer have to lose pay to travel,” an employee who has worked at a state-owned enterprise in the Henan city of Luoyang for 10 years told Sixth Tone. “We were so excited when we saw the news that afternoon, and everyone cheered when our company issued (its own) notice the next day.”

She said taking time off previously meant losing a significant portion of her salary. “Now, (the notice) makes me feel more motivated to work,” she said. “People will complete their tasks more thoroughly before going on leave.” The employee added that she is already planning to combine her annual leave with the weeklong National Day holiday, at the beginning of October, for a longer break.

Two private-sector employees in Henan, however, told Sixth Tone that they had yet to receive any notice of a change in annual leave from their companies.

Similar notices have also been issued this year in the northern port city of Tianjin, the eastern provinces of Zhejiang and Anhui, the northwestern province of Shaanxi, and the southwestern province of Guizhou.

Many notices state they aim to change “unhealthy workplace norms,” while attempting to allay workers’ concerns that taking leave could affect their pay, performance evaluations, or chances for promotion.

In 2025, Lü Guoquan, a member of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference and then an official with the All-China Federation of Trade Unions, said only around 57% of China’s workers entitled to paid annual leave actually take it.

Under national regulations implemented in 2008, employees with one to 10 years of cumulative work experience are entitled to five days of paid annual leave; those with 10 to 20 years receive 10 days; and those with more than 20 years receive 15 days.

“To fundamentally change the situation, China also needs routine labor inspections, accessible channels for workers to defend their rights, and better job rotation systems to reduce operational pressure on employers,” Song Xiangqing, vice president of the Commerce Economy Association of China, told domestic business outlet Caijing.

In January, China’s Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security also announced that it would revise national regulations to promote better enforcement of the paid leave system.

“Paid leave is no longer simply about work-life balance or employee welfare,” state-run Guangming Daily wrote in a commentary published Thursday. “It has become part of the country’s strategy to boost consumption and expand domestic demand. Only with sufficient, uninterrupted, and predictable time off will people have both the time and willingness to spend.”

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Visuals from Horstgerlach/Getty Creative/VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018866/Too Many Cooks: China’s Culinary Titles Face a Credibility Test
World.title: Too Many Cooks: China’s Culinary Titles Face a Credibility Test
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018866/Too Many Cooks: China’s Culinary Titles Face a Credibility Test
World.content:
China’s industry associations are revoking hundreds of honorary designations that have increasingly been used as marketing tools.

In late July, the China Cuisine Association announced that all previously awarded titles — including “Chinese Culinary Master” and “Chinese Catering Service Master” — along with related certificates and uniforms, were now invalid. The association also revoked all honorary designations awarded to cities — such as the “capital of” and “hometown of” certain dishes. Local governments are now officially barred from using them in any form of publicity.

The revocation of the titles triggered renewed interest among social media users. This week, they questioned the reliability of the “National Stir-Fried Meat King” title awarded to restaurant chain Chef Fei, or Feidachu, after discovering it was conferred following an online public vote on photos and videos submitted by contestants.

The title has not yet been revoked, though, in response, the China Cuisine Association said they will “communicate after reviewing relevant materials,” domestic media reported.

Originally intended to recognize exceptional craftsmanship, “master” titles were once rare state honors. But in the early 2000s, industry associations across the tea, ceramics, and jewelry sectors, and many others, began creating their own titles, allowing businesses to charge a premium by creating the perception of higher-quality products and services. However, numerous shadowy practices also emerged around the honors, including honorary title certificates being openly sold on e-commerce platforms.

Since the beginning of this year, at least a dozen national and local industry associations covering sectors ranging from cosmetic surgery to jade carving and wedding services have revoked or abolished previously-conferred honorary titles containing words like “master.”

An increasing number of industry associations began nullifying their own honorary titles after the Social Work Department of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and the Ministry of Civil Affairs jointly released new guidelines on governing social organizations’ awards and commendations in mid-July.

The guidelines, which took effect on Aug. 1, imposed stricter eligibility requirements on organizations seeking to present awards. It also prohibits organizations from charging fees for recognition programs or partnering with, or outsourcing such activities to, for-profit entities.

China has gradually tightened oversight of awards and commendations organized by social organizations over the past decade, with its first regulations governing the practice taking effect in 2012.

Restrictions were tightened further in 2018, when award programs using national designations such as “China,” “Chinese,” and “national” became subject to stricter controls. In 2022, authorities required organizations seeking to launch honorary recognition programs to hold at least a 4A rating, the second highest on the country’s social organization rating scale.

Lu Zhen, a lawyer at the Shanghai office of Beijing-based Hylands Law Firm, told local media that rather than eliminating professional evaluations altogether, the regulations are intended to draw a clearer distinction between professional qualifications and commercialized honorary awards.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: An  for restaurant chain Chef Fei, or Feidachu, at a shopping mall in Beijing, May 23, 2024. VCG)

World.title: Apple trains its own AI model for China market with Alibaba’s support – sources
World.content:
Sources say Apple's AI model was developed in partnership with Alibaba Group and trained with the Chinese tech giant's support, Apple and Alibaba did not respond to requests for comment.

Apple has trained a large language model specifically for the China market, three people familiar with the matter said, a departure from the iPhone maker’s strategy of relying on third-party models to power AI features in the country.

The AI model was developed in partnership with Alibaba Group and trained with the Chinese tech giant’s support, the people said, declining to be named as the information is sensitive and not public.

Apple’s training of its own China-specific model has not been reported before. The company had previously leaned towards domestic partners’ models to bring generative AI to iPhones and other devices sold in China, where US models such as Anthropic’s Claude and OpenAI’s ChatGPT, which Apple pairs with its own technology in its home market, are not available.

Apple and Alibaba did not respond to requests for comment.

Apple Intelligence, the company’s suite of AI tools, is expected to launch in China in the coming months after an update to its iOS operating system, the people said.

A China-tailored model of its own would give Apple greater control over the AI experience in its most competitive overseas market, where it has lost ground to local rivals including Huawei that have raced ahead with AI-equipped handsets.

Apple’s planned rollout represents a unique dual-track strategy on AI deployment for a foreign firm in China, which would allow it to navigate steep regulatory hurdles that have limited access for many other US technology firms.

It would also make Apple the first foreign company approved by Beijing to offer a proprietary AI model in China, marking a rare collaboration by US and Chinese tech firms amid a widening trade and diplomatic rift between the two countries over AI.

Regulatory hurdles cleared but uncertainty remains

The move follows a lengthy regulatory process that ended last month, when the Cyberspace Administration of China, the country’s internet watchdog, registered Apple’s generative AI service, clearing the way for Apple Intelligence to reach Chinese iPhones for the first time.

Under that arrangement, Alibaba’s Qwen model is to be incorporated into the version of Apple Intelligence that ships with compatible iPhone, iPad, Mac and Vision Pro models in China, and the service was also set to incorporate technology from Baidu, Reuters reported in July.

Last week, Apple published a Chinese-language guide explaining how eligible Mac users in mainland China could connect Qwen to its Siri digital assistant and Writing Tools feature, a Mac-specific arrangement that could help it compete in China’s AI PC market. Apple has since deleted the guide, without providing an explanation.

Alibaba’s U.S.-listed shares climbed about 4% in premarket trading on news of the July registration, underscoring investor expectations that the tie-up could reshape China’s AI ecosystem.

Apple looks to AI for boost in China

Apple’s partnership with Alibaba was first confirmed in February 2025, when Alibaba chairman Joe Tsai, speaking at the World Governments Summit in Dubai, said Apple would use the Chinese company’s AI to power its phones in China.

“They talked to a number of companies in China. In the end they chose to do business with us,” Tsai said at the time. The rollout was subsequently delayed as Apple worked to adapt its features to Chinese regulations.

China remains critical to Apple’s fortunes, accounting for a significant share of its revenue. The absence of AI features on Chinese iPhones had been cited as a factor weighing on sales as consumers gravitated toward domestic brands offering built-in AI assistants.

It was not immediately clear what role Apple’s self-trained model would play alongside third-party Chinese models and how those are working together. – Rappler.com

World.title: Alex Eala gets chance for another payback as Ruse awaits in Cincinnati Open
World.content:
THINK. Alexandra Eala (PHI) reacts after losing a game against Belinda Bencic (SUI) during fourth-round play in the 2026 Canadian Open at Sobeys Stadium.

Alex Eala crosses paths with Elena-Gabriela Ruse again two years after the Romanian denied the Filipina what would have been her first main draw appearance in a Grand Slam

MANILA, Philippines – Another one of Alex Eala’s former conquerors stand in her way.

Eala begins her campaign in the Cincinnati Open in the United States against a familiar foe as she battles Romania’s Elena-Gabriela Ruse in the round of 64.

Their rematch comes two years after Ruse hacked out a 3-6, 6-1, 6-4 victory over Eala in the third qualifying round of the 2024 US Open, denying the Filipina what would have been her first main draw appearance in a Grand Slam.

Back then, Eala was still ranked outside the world top 150 at No. 153, while Ruse was at No. 122.

Eala, though, has seen a remarkable rise over the last two years as she now ranks No. 20 following impressive runs in her last three tournaments: a historic fourth-round stint in the Wimbledon Championships, a breakthrough WTA Tour title in the Washington Open, and a fourth-round outing in the Canadian Open.

With three players in the top 20 — Czech Republic’s Karolina Muchova, Canada’s Victoria Mboko, and Italy’s Jasmine Paolini — unable to compete due to injuries, Eala got seeded 17th — her highest in a WTA 1000 tournament — and earned a first-round bye.

Meanwhile, world No. 74 Ruse needed to beat Poland’s Magda Linette, 6-0, 6-3, to arrange a rematch with Eala.

If Eala gets her payback on Ruse, she will face either close friend Zeynep Sonmez of Turkey or world No. 10 Amanda Anisimova of the United States in the round of 32.

Eala has found success against past conquerors, beating each of her last seven opponents who previously defeated her as she topped Mexico’s Renata Zarazua, Australia’s Maya Joint, Poland Iga Swiatek, China’s Zheng Qinwen, Canada’s Leylah Fernandez, and USA’s Jessica Pegula and Alycia Parks.

The Filipina hopes to add Ruse to the list. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Measles-rubella vaccines are safe and effective, says DOH
World.content:
The Department of Health debunked posts circulating online spreading false information about the safety of the vaccine

Claim: The vaccine against measles (tigdas) and measles-rubella (tigdas hangin) being administered under the government’s “Ligtas Tigdas” campaign is not safe.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: Facebook user Maharaani Sona Shiloh, who has more than 350,000 followers, posted the claim on August 5. Her video has reached more than 2.4 million views, 38,000 likes, 4,200 comments, and 54,000 shares as of writing.

In the video, she labeled the Department of Health (DOH)’s nationwide “Ligtas Tigdas” program as the start of what she called the “neutralization of children.”

“Ang diskarte mga kapatid, ay kunwari maswerte ka na makakatanggap ka ng libreng bakuna kasi ito ay benepisyo bilang miyembro ng 4Ps,” she said.

(The strategy here is they’ll tell you you’re lucky to be among the recipients of the free vaccine, as a benefit for being a 4Ps member.)

She warned social media users not to have their children vaccinated, claiming that many have died due to the side effects of the vaccine.

“One in 30,000 children ay posibleng magkaroon ng febrile seizures. Mag-epilepsy sila, mangisay ba. Kirig hanggang mamatay. Brain shock, magkaroon ng brain dysfunction,” she added.

(One in 30,000 children can possibly have febrile seizures. They’ll have epilepsy, they’ll have spasms. Convulse until dead. [They can have] brain shock, brain dysfunction.)

She further listed other side effects of the vaccine that may lead to death and encouraged viewers to spread her video to save children from the effects of the vaccine.

The facts: The measles-rubella vaccines used by DOH for its program are confirmed safe for use.

The health department debunked the circulating post in a statement released on Facebook on August 7.

“Mali ang mga ulat na hindi ligtas o nakamamatay ang mga bakunang ito. Tinitiyak ng DOH na ligtas at epektibo ang mga bakuna sa tigdas at tigdas-hangin,” the statement read.

(Reports that these vaccines are unsafe or deadly are false. The DOH assures that the vaccines for measles are safe and effective.)

Typical side effects of vaccination, such as fever and pain from the injection site, are mild and temporary only, the health department said.

The DOH also addressed concerns over serious side effects of the vaccine.

“Nililinaw rin ng DOH na ang anumang naiuulat na malubhang sitwasyon ay masusing iniimbestigahan ng mga eksperto at hindi awtomatikong sanhi ng bakuna. Mas malaki pa rin ang panganib na dulot ng mismong sakit kaysa sa napakabihirang seryosong side effect nito,” it said.

(The DOH also clarified that any reported serious situations are thoroughly investigated by experts and are not automatically caused by the vaccine. The risk posed by the disease itself is still greater than its extremely rare serious side effects.)

According to DOH Eastern Visayas Regional Director Dr. Exuperia B. Sabalberino, there was no reason to worry as the vaccines have been in use around the world for five decades already to protect children against preventable diseases.

Ligtas Tigdas 2026: The DOH’s Measles-Rubella Supplemental Immunization Activity vaccination program began in Luzon and Visayas on August 10 and will run until August 28, 2026. The campaign aims to immunize children between the ages of six and 59 months who are at risk of infection.

The health department aims to achieve at least 95 percent vaccination coverage to build herd immunity and prevent outbreaks.

Measles is a highly contagious disease caused by a virus that can lead to life-threatening complications. While it can affect anyone, it is most common in children. Measles-rubella, also known as German measles, is a highly contagious disease caused by the rubella virus. According to health experts, measles-rubella vaccines greatly reduce risk of infection.

– Lourence Angelo Marcellana/Rappler.com

World.title: How much Northern Mindanao cities, provinces set aside for confidential funds
World.content:
Cagayan de Oro leads Northern Mindanao in confidential and intelligence fund allocations in 2023 and 2024, while Bukidnon has the lowest. With Iligan, Misamis Oriental and Misamis Occidental, the four account for nearly 80% of the region's allocations.

CAGAYAN DE ORO, Philippines – Cagayan de Oro was Northern Mindanao‘s biggest spender of confidential and intelligence funds (CIF) in 2023 and 2024, setting aside a total of P450 million during that period under Mayor Rolando Uy, Commission on Audit (COA) data showed.

At the other end was Bukidnon province, which set aside some P2.648 million over the same period under Governor Rogelio Neil Roque, the lowest among the region’s cities and provinces.

Along with Cagayan de Oro, Iligan City and the provinces of Misamis Oriental and Misamis Occidental were the three top CIF spenders, together accounting for nearly 80% of the over P1.1 billion in confidential and intelligence funds allocated by Northern Mindanao’s cities and provinces in 2023 and 2024.

Cagayan de Oro allocated a combined P450 million for CIF in 2023 and 2024; Iligan City, P94.5 million, Misamis Oriental, P210 million; and Misamis Occidental, P156 million. Together, the four accounted for more than P910 million of the region’s more than P1 billion total allocations during the two-year period.

Cagayan de Oro’s confidential fund rose to P250 million in 2024 from P200 million in 2023, a 25% increase.

Overall, cities and provinces in Northern Mindanao raised their confidential and intelligence fund allocations to P646.3 million in 2024 from P527.7 million in 2023. The figures exclude Northern Mindanao’s 84 municipalities, whose mayors are also allowed by law to maintain such funds.

Iligan City, the region’s second-biggest city spender, increased its allocation to P54 million in 2024 from P40.5 million in 2023 under Mayor Frederick Siao.

In Bukidnon province, Valencia City had a confidential fund of P22 million in 2023 and another P22 million in 2024 under then-mayor Azucena Huervas. The city had intelligence funds which ballooned to P11.9 million in 2024 from P6.584 million in 2023.

The COA report on Valencia also showed that the city government had P22 million in confidential fund cash advances that had remained unliquidated for 10 years.

El Salvador, one of Misamis Oriental’s component cities, increased its allocation to P14 million in 2024 from P10 million under Mayor Edgar Lignes.

In eastern Misamis Oriental, Gingoog City set aside P21 million in 2024 under Mayor Erick Cañosa. The COA report on Gingoog did not show an allocation in 2023.

Oroquieta City in Misamis Occidental nearly doubled its allocation to P20.329 million in 2024 from P10.484 million under Mayor Lemuel Meyrick Acosta.

Still in Misamis Occidental, Ozamiz City raised its allocation to P22.5 million from P20 million, while Tangub City increased its allocation to P15.997 million from P11.645 million.

Bukidnon’s capital, Malaybalay City, went the other way, reducing its allocation under Mayor Jay Warren Pabillaran to P900,000 in 2024 from P2.203 million in 2023.

Misamis Oriental was the biggest CIF spender among Northern Mindanao’s provinces, raising its allocation under then-governor Peter Unabia to P110 million in 2024 from P100 million in 2023.

Misamis Occidental kept its allocation at P78 million under Governor Henry Oaminal.

Lanao del Norte, under then-governor Imelda Dimaporo, slashed its allocation to P11.25 million from P15 million during the period, before she was succeeded by her son Khalid. The mother, who is now Lanao del Norte representative, and son traded positions in 2025.

The island province of Camiguin set aside P12 million for CIF in 2024, up from P10 million in 2023 under Governor Xavier Jesus Romualdo. In total, the small five-town province had P22 million in CIF during the 2023-2024 period.

The landlocked province of Bukidnon increased its allocation slightly to P1.395 million in 2024 from P1.253 million in 2023. Even so, its combined allocation remained the lowest among Northern Mindanao’s cities and provinces during that period.

The country has 18 administrative regions, 82 provinces, 33 highly urbanized cities, 116 other cities and 1,493 municipalities. The law allows governors and mayors to maintain confidential and intelligence funds, which they can spend at their discretion, subject to state auditing rules.

Critics, however, say the apparent laxity in auditing such funds and the lack of transparency surrounding them make such public money vulnerable to misuse and corruption. – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Video of Marcos and Romualdez laughing about ‘fooling’ the public is AI-generated
World.content:
The exchange never happened; two separate AI-detection tools flagged the video as likely containing AI-generated elements

Claim: President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and former House speaker Martin Romualdez were caught on video laughing together after “fooling” the public with Marcos’ statements against Romualdez during his State of the Nation Address (SONA).

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: A Facebook reel posted by the page “Canadian Tambay” purports to show Marcos and Romualdez in a private moment, laughing together in what appears to be an office setting.

The reel bears the caption “The masterminds of corruption. The flood control corruption.”

In the clip, Romualdez appears to tell Marcos, “Nabudol mo na naman ang mga tao ha, na kunwari ipapakulong mo ko, ang galing mo talaga.”

(You fooled the people again, huh, pretending you’ll have me jailed, you’re really good.)

The two are then shown bursting into laughter.

As of writing, the post has garnered over 1,900 reactions, 330 comments, and more than 1,000 shares. The post drew several comments criticizing the two officials.

The facts: The exchange between Marcos and Romualdez did not occur. No official Palace recording, press release, or credible news outlet has reported or documented such a moment, as the video is AI-generated.

AI detection tool DetectVideo AI assessed the clip as having an 80% likelihood of being AI-generated, with only a 7% probability the footage is authentic and 13% probability it’s manipulated rather than fully generated, rating its evidence confidence “High.”

A separate analysis using Sightengine returned an even higher 98% likelihood of the clip being AI-generated, with 0% detected face manipulation — suggesting the footage may be wholly synthetic rather than doctored real footage.

The Facebook post also contains no label or disclaimer indicating that the clip was created or altered using AI.

The fake exchange was referring to Marcos’s SONA remarks on July 27, where he stated that the Ombudsman is expected to file plunder and graft cases against Romualdez, his cousin, over alleged P56 billion in unexplained wealth tied to the flood control scandal.

“Masakit man sa akin ito, ngunit kailangan nating gawin ang tama. Hindi ako pangulo ng aking pamilya. Hindi ako pangulo ng aking kaibigan. Ako ay Pangulo ng Pilipinas, at ang tungkulin ko ay sa inyo: ang aking mga kapwa Pilipino,” Marcos said.

(Painful as this is for me, we have to do what is right. I am not the president of my family. I am not the president of my friends. I am the President of the Philippines, and my duty is to you, my fellow Filipinos.)

Blindsided: The two cousins, once considered close political allies, have grown increasingly estranged amid corruption scandals in the government. (READ: Biggest loser of SONA 2026: Martin Romualdez)

Romualdez has categorically denied all allegations of being one of the “masterminds” behind the flood control corruption. He released a statement in response to Marcos’ SONA remarks, saying that while this was hurtful for their family, he respects the decision of the president and reiterated that he was ready to prove his innocence.

“Ang tama ay ang sumunod sa proseso at hayaan ang ebidensya ang magsalita. Naninindigan akong wala akong ginawang anumang labag sa batas, at handa akong patunayan ito,” he said.

(The right thing to do is to follow due process and let the evidence speak for itself. I stand firm that I have not done anything against the law, and I am ready to prove this.) – Cyril Bocar/Rappler.com

Efren Cyril Bocar is a journalist from Llorente, Eastern Samar who graduated with a degree in English Language Studies at the Visayas State University. Cyril is also a graduate of the Aries Rufo Journalism Fellowship of Rappler for 2024.

World.title: Travis Kelce says ‘crazy’ wedding to Taylor Swift was ‘best night of my life’
World.content:
POWER COUPLE. Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce during their engagement in August 2025.

The football star makes his first public comments about his wedding to Taylor Swift

LOS ANGELES, USA – Travis Kelce made his first public comments about his star-studded wedding to Taylor Swift on Wednesday, August 12, calling it “the best night of my life” and expressing gratitude that “the AC was cookin'” during a New York City heat wave.

Kelce took questions from reporters during Kansas City Chiefs training camp in Missouri as the team prepares for the NFL season that starts in September. Most questions centered on football, but a couple of journalists tried to glean details about the private nuptials held at Madison Square Garden.

“It was a fun off-season, man,” Kelce said. “Wedding was the best night of my life, and I appreciate everybody who came out and celebrated and had fun with us.”

He added that it was “a crazy night” full of celebration.

The NFL star and the pop musician, both 36, married on July 3 in front of about 1,000 guests including celebrities such as Tom Cruise, Brad Pitt, Jennifer Lopez and Tom Brady, plus many of Kelce’s teammates. Comedian Adam Sandler officiated the ceremony.

Guests said the couple turned the famed sports venue — home of the New York Knicks — into a lavish garden setting.

“It’s kind of cool to live out my childhood dream of being in that venue, and the mecca of all sports venues, being able to get married there,” Kelce said.

“We can thank the owners of MSG for allowing us to get the opportunity to do that, knowing we wanted a private event and everything. It was perfect.”

He also voiced appreciation for the arena’s air conditioning.

“The AC was cookin’ baby,” he added. “That was the best part.” – Rappler.com
