World.title: ‘We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads’ — Pashinyan
World.content:
Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said there should be no situation in which anyone could say: “Armenia has nowhere to go and nobody needs it.” Four years ago, Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko made a similar statement.

According to Pashinyan, Lukashenko’s words actually reflect a “deeply rooted institutional perception” of Armenia, not only in Belarus but also in other countries that belong to the Russian-led Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU). The prime minister sees this as a “disrespectful perception”. He believes it developed from the following assumption:

“There is the Karabakh conflict, there is a conflict with Azerbaijan, there is a conflict with Turkey, and this hostility is insurmountable. So they have nowhere to go, and we can treat them however we want.”

However, Pashinyan said Armenia had managed to prove otherwise:

“We have demonstrated in practice that many countries need Armenia as a responsible partner in the international community and as a very important country. We have proved that Armenia is not a province, but a crossroads — together with the South Caucasus and the wider region.”

At a briefing, the prime minister again answered questions about Armenia’s choice between the EAEU and the European Union. He also discussed possible decisions on the management of Armenia’s railways, which Russia took over under a concession agreement in 2008. The Armenian government has effectively developed new proposals that would limit Russia’s role but would not yet terminate its concession.

“Before alternatives emerge, we need both the EU and the EAEU equally”

Russia continues to pressure Armenia over the need to choose between the EAEU and the EU. Armenian journalists therefore asked the government again about its position. Pashinyan said Russia expected Armenia to choose between “two alternatives”. However, the “second alternative” has not yet taken shape:

“We will certainly make this choice through a referendum in the future. But this will happen only after we first carry out the necessary institutional preparations and then formally apply for EU membership.”

According to Pashinyan, Armenia currently needs both the EU and the EAEU equally because the second alternative does not yet exist. He also said Armenia could eventually face not only a choice between these two options, but also a third approach:

“Perhaps a third initiative will emerge: neither the EAEU nor the EU. In other words, we do not need either structure. Who said that everyone must belong to some structure?”

Moreover, he said the government was considering many possible options, including “a fourth and fifth alternative”.

Returning to the issue of holding a referendum on EAEU or EU membership, he stressed:

“This choice must be a mature one because we do not yet know how realistic this path is or what the roadmap will look like.”

Without naming Russia, the prime minister said Armenia could not treat anyone’s interests with contempt or disregard. But it also could not put another country’s interests above its own national interests.

“That is why we are trying to discuss and resolve all issues patiently, without escalation or nervousness. We will discuss them for as long as necessary, until we find a solution that more or less satisfies both sides,” he said.

“We will not pursue the termination of the concession agreement”

Nikol Pashinyan once again said Yerevan wanted to resolve the issue of Armenia’s railway “in a friendly manner” without escalating the situation. He said both Armenia and Russia should consider each other’s interests and seek compromises.

This time, the prime minister outlined several possible scenarios for how the situation could develop:

“One of them could involve the Russian side selling its concession rights, either fully or partially. In other words, there could be certain shareholder configurations,” he said.

According to Pashinyan, Armenia does not want to terminate the concession agreement. It has always had that option and still does. However, the Armenian side prefers not to take such measures.

He said a possible solution for Yerevan would involve a Russian company selling its concession rights to a third party at market value.

At the same time, he noted that this approach might not be particularly acceptable to Russia’s partners.

He also said the Armenian government was working with experts to find an option that would at least partly address the concerns of both sides:

“[The experts] say that we could introduce a different management model. For example, Russia could retain part of its shares while transferring the rest. But the Russian side would have to retain a smaller stake. Otherwise, the problem would not be resolved.

There is another idea. The licence could be divided into two parts. At present, the railway infrastructure and its operation form a single package.”

Pashinyan explained the problems facing Armenia:

“The current situation prevents Armenia from seizing the historic opportunity to integrate our railway into the international rail network.”

He noted that countries responsible for the “lion’s share” of rail freight and which could become potential beneficiaries are looking for ways to bypass Armenia:

“They not only tell us this, but we can also see that they are showing no investment interest in this sector. As a result, we understand that the reason lies in the fact that our railway is under a Russian concession.”

Nikol Pashinyan added that this was why the government had raised the issue with its Russian partners in a friendly manner and proposed finding solutions.

Since 2008, Armenia’s railways have operated under a concession held by South Caucasus Railway. The company is a wholly owned subsidiary of Russian Railways. The agreement provides for a 30-year concession. However, since 2008, freight volumes have halved, some routes have stopped operating, and the required investments have remained on paper. Meanwhile, Armenia wants to fully unblock its borders, which requires restoring railway links to the borders with Azerbaijan and Turkey. Since the Russian company that operates Armenia’s railways has not undertaken to restore these sections, Armenia is looking for ways to implement the plans itself.

Pashinyan on EAEU membership and railway concession

World.title: Fuel supplies from Tbilisi-controlled territory to Abkhazia: humanitarian aid or move in Russia’s interests?
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Amid a severe fuel shortage in Abkhazia, the import of fuel from territory controlled by Tbilisi has sparked political controversy. The government says a private company delivered the shipment in full compliance with Georgian law, while the opposition and critics are calling for further clarification and answers to several questions: where did the fuel go, who brought it into Abkhazia, and for what purpose?

At a briefing on 12 August 2026, Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that fuel had reached Abkhazia from territory controlled by Georgia. He said the government had not organised the operation and that private companies had imported the fuel in accordance with the law.

According to ruling-party MP Rati Ionatamishvili, the shipment amounted to 3,000 tonnes of fuel, delivered to Abkhazia by several tankers. He said the shipment reached Abkhazia while fully respecting Georgia’s sovereignty and legislation.

Ionatamishvili criticised the opposition for its focus on the deliveries and dismissed as absurd suggestions that the operation aimed to supply Russia with several thousand tonnes of fuel. He said the 3,000 tonnes delivered to Abkhazia represented a negligible share of Russia’s annual fuel consumption. He added that presenting the issue in this way served a campaign aimed at undermining efforts to restore Georgian-Abkhaz relations.

Above all, the opposition is demanding details that the government has not yet provided.

According to Levan Samushia, one of the leaders of the Strong Georgia – Lelo alliance, the prime minister’s statement that the fuel was imported in compliance with the Law on Occupied Territories is not enough:

“Who supplied the fuel — in other words, where did it come from — and who was the recipient? Were Georgia’s laws and national interests respected?”

He said it was necessary to know which commercial entities were involved and what route the fuel took to reach Abkhazia.

Levan Samushia

Similar questions have also been raised by Berdia Sichinava, one of the leaders of the Gakharia – For Georgia party. However, he stressed that if the fuel shipment was genuinely humanitarian and did not violate the law, there was no problem with providing such assistance in itself.

“Georgia is involved in more than one such humanitarian project. For example, we fund medical treatment for our citizens from Abkhazia, we receive electricity from the Enguri Hydroelectric Power Plant, and people living in the occupied territory also receive it,” Sichinava said.

In his view, the main problem is the lack of transparency surrounding the process. Sichinava is demanding clarification on who imported the fuel, how large the shipment was, what procedures the cargo went through and where it was ultimately delivered.

Sichinava considers the way the fuel was ultimately used a particularly important question: did it go towards the needs of Abkhazia’s population and critical infrastructure, or was it eventually used in Russia-controlled areas to the south, including infrastructure linked to military activities?

“If the fuel entered occupied Abkhazia as a commercial rather than humanitarian shipment, and if it went through so-called customs procedures at the so-called border — which is actually the occupation line — this could raise serious concerns for our country’s territorial integrity and security,” Sichinava said.

Lasha Parulava, a member of the United National Movement, accused the government of serving Russian interests and betraying Georgia’s national interests.

He called Kobakhidze’s statement that the fuel deliveries complied with the Law on Occupied Territories cynical. Parulava also criticised the government’s policy towards Russia and noted that the fuel was supplied to Abkhazia amid a fuel shortage in Russia itself.

“This is not simply aiding the enemy, but a direct betrayal of national interests,” Parulava said.

Lasha Parulava

Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, believes the government may have authorised the operation in advance, although the public has not been told why, when or on what grounds it approved it.

Gvaramia points out that Russian military bases are deployed in Abkhazia and that the Russian military is facing fuel shortages.

In his view, these circumstances make it necessary to establish whether humanitarian or social considerations genuinely prompted the fuel shipment, or whether Russia ultimately used the cargo for military purposes.

Gvaramia argues that, in that case, the issue would go beyond the legality of economic activity in Georgia’s occupied territory. The situation could also involve the supply of goods of strategic importance to Russia.

Nika Gvaramia

Expert Gia Khukhashvili assesses the volume of fuel and the logistics of its delivery differently from the authorities. In his view, the “several tankers” mentioned by government officials actually represent a much larger shipment.

“Three thousand tonnes is a convoy of at least 100 fuel tankers,” Khukhashvili wrote.

He said fuel deliveries to Abkhazia could theoretically mark the beginning of a reintegration process. Under the current government, however, he described the decision as “an act of collaborationism and sheer greed”.

Tamta Mikeladze, director of the Social Justice Center, wrote:

“Amid Russia’s economic weakening, Abkhazia may need support from Tbilisi, and this crisis could provide an opportunity to transform the conflict.

Any step that could benefit the people of Abkhazia should not automatically be seen as serving Russia’s interests. That is precisely why full transparency is necessary: who makes the decision, what is its purpose, what mechanisms are in place to monitor the process so that it does not strengthen Russia’s military and economic interests, and what political strategy accompanies it?

Meeting humanitarian or civilian needs and strengthening Russia’s interests are not the same thing. However, a lack of transparency can blur the distinction and turn such actions into part of Russia’s game.

The particular problem with the Abkhaz issue is that a crisis can become an opportunity only if there is a political vision. Georgian Dream has no such vision. The party has yet to adopt either a de-occupation plan or strategic documents for rebuilding trust.

Irakli Kobakhidze has not even attempted to answer the questions raised above.

Given the deep mistrust of Georgian Dream and the complete lack of transparency surrounding its policies, concerns that something could happen that fundamentally and permanently contradicts our national interests are entirely understandable. However, accuracy and attention to nuance are crucial when formulating criticism.”Fuel supplies to Abkhazia (civil.ge)

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: EU annual report: “serious problems” in Azerbaijan and “serious restrictions” on fundamental freedoms
World.content:
European Union annual report

The EU says that the human rights and democracy situation in Azerbaijan in 2025 continued to be marked by “serious problems”. It highlighted restrictions on civil society and media freedom, concerns about the independence of the judiciary, and limited progress on structural reforms.

The overall situation in governance remained restrictive. This is according to the European Union’s Annual Report on Human Rights and Democracy in the World for 2025.

The report says legislative, administrative and judicial mechanisms “seriously restrict” the exercise of fundamental freedoms.

At the same time, the assessment notes progress in several areas. These include the criminalisation of child marriage, new measures to promote gender equality, and efforts to combat corruption.

The EU’s assessment of Azerbaijan in 2025 is critical but balanced.

Civil society under pressure

In 2025, civil society organisations continued to operate under restrictive conditions.

The EU notes that the 2017 Law on Non-Governmental Organisations remains in force. Registration, reporting and grant approval requirements continue to restrict the activities of independent organisations.

Local organisations reported persistent administrative pressure and increased scrutiny.

The departure of several UN agencies, including the United Nations Development Programme and UNICEF, also affected their operating environment. This reduced opportunities for international monitoring and assistance.

The EU says it continues to support civil society, independent media and human rights defenders, including through human rights monitoring and legal assistance programmes for vulnerable groups.

Concerns over the judiciary and the rule of law

According to the EU, problems related to the rule of law and judicial independence persist.

The assessment says courts lack sufficient independence when handling politically sensitive cases.

The report cites judgments by the European Court of Human Rights as an important indicator of the problems that remain.

In 2025, the ECHR issued 39 judgments in cases concerning Azerbaijan and found violations in 38 of them. Most cases involved the right to a fair trial, deprivation of liberty, freedom of expression and freedom of assembly.

The report also notes that Azerbaijan’s failure to implement ECHR judgments has affected the country’s relations with the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe.

Electoral system remains unchanged

The EU notes that Azerbaijan’s electoral system underwent no changes in 2025.

The country did not carry out major reforms aimed at implementing the long-standing recommendations of the OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights and the Council of Europe’s Venice Commission.

The report identifies the lack of progress in this area as one of the persistent challenges to Azerbaijan’s democratic development.

Progress in some areas

The EU report also notes a number of legislative changes.

In July 2025, Azerbaijan criminalised child marriage.

The authorities approved a National Action Plan on Gender Equality for 2026–2028 and amended the Law on Combating Corruption.

The amendments include provisions on whistleblower protection and corruption risk management.

At the same time, the EU notes that the implementation of these measures remains uneven.

Dialogue continues, reforms remain limited

Throughout 2025, the EU maintained regular contacts with the Azerbaijani authorities.

These included meetings with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, the Office of the Ombudsman and the State Committee for Work with Religious Organisations.

The discussions covered judicial reform, media freedom, the treatment of people in detention, the rights of religious minorities, gender equality and the fight against corruption.

The EU also raised concerns about individuals who had been arrested or barred from leaving the country for exercising their fundamental rights.

Human rights issues also featured in sectoral dialogues on public administration, justice and social policy.

However, despite the continued channels of engagement, the EU says that “progress on structural reforms remains limited”.

Media freedom and fundamental rights

Media freedom and freedom of expression remained among the areas closely monitored by the EU.

The report notes that throughout the year, the EU closely monitored developments concerning digital rights, freedom of expression and media freedom.

EU-funded programmes supported independent media, human rights monitoring, legal assistance, gender equality and children’s rights.

The EU continued to support civil society organisations and human rights defenders working under restrictive conditions.

Azerbaijan on international platforms

The EU continued to raise human rights concerns in Azerbaijan through international organisations.

At the UN, during the 80th session of the General Assembly’s Third Committee, the EU raised issues concerning the space for civil society, judicial independence and media freedom.

Cooperation with the Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights also continued, including preparations for Azerbaijan’s next Universal Periodic Review, scheduled for 2026–2027.

Within the Council of Europe, the EU supported mechanisms for implementing ECHR judgments and engaged with the Venice Commission and the Commissioner for Human Rights.

At the OSCE, the EU and its member states took part in discussions on media freedom and electoral standards, including restrictions affecting the work of the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights.

European Union annual report

World.title: ‘Even if nuclear power plant is shut down, Armenia will not face serious problems’: Reaction to Aliyev’s remarks
World.content:
Yerevan reacts to Aliyev’s AzTV interview

“Every nuclear power plant has an operating lifespan. Neither the Armenian government nor the Azerbaijani government, nor the government of any other country in the world, determines that lifespan,” Armenian ruling-party MP Arman Yeghoyan said in response to the Azerbaijani president’s remarks.

In an interview with AzTV, Ilham Aliyev said the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant was “outdated” and posed a potential threat to the entire region. He said “sooner or later it must be shut down”, after which “Armenia will face a full-scale energy crisis”.

At the same time, the Azerbaijani president said an energy corridor running through Armenia to Nakhchivan, then to Turkey and Europe, would “allow Armenia’s energy system to withstand a crisis”.

MP Arman Yeghoyan responded that “Aliyev has not made any revelation”. The maximum permitted operating period of the nuclear power plant expires in 2036, a fact that has long been known.

“And we have already announced that we are considering building a new nuclear power plant and are negotiating with several international partners,” the MP said.

Political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan believes Azerbaijan is trying to portray itself as a “generous country ready to help Armenia solve its problems”, despite the long-running conflict.

He noted that this was not the first such case. Baku had previously said that Azerbaijan could serve as a reliable partner for supplying energy resources to Armenia. Meliksetyan, however, said Armenia currently has a surplus of electricity. He stressed that even if the nuclear power plant shuts down, the country will not face serious problems.

“The claim that Armenia’s energy system will face a crisis after the Metsamor Nuclear Power Plant closes is not true,” the political analyst told JAMnews.

He said Armenia does not currently need additional sources of electricity. He noted that the project for a new nuclear power plant remains under discussion and that Armenia has opportunities to expand solar power.

In addition, the fifth unit of the Hrazdan Thermal Power Plant has roughly the same generating capacity as the nuclear plant. The only problem is that the nuclear power plant produces cheaper electricity.

Aliyev again refers to TRIPP as the “Zangezur Corridor”

During his visit to Nakhchivan, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev gave an interview to state broadcaster AzTV. Alongside the issue of the nuclear power plant’s closure, Aliyev discussed the 2020 Second Karabakh War. He called the trilateral statement of 9 November, which ended the fighting, “an act of Armenia’s capitulation”. He added that “there is no need to look for any humiliating or offensive meaning in this term; it is simply a reality”.

He then turned to the issue of transport links between mainland Azerbaijan and Nakhchivan. He stressed that this route had remained one of Baku’s strategic goals for many years.

“On 9 November, trilateral negotiations took place with the mediation of the Russian president. I insisted categorically that the statement we were about to sign must include a corridor linking mainland Azerbaijan with the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic. The Armenian side did not want to agree to this. But it did not have many alternatives. If the war had continued, we would of course have suffered losses as well, but Armenia’s losses would have been much greater. Its troops were, so to speak, surrounded, and their destruction had effectively become a possibility,” the president said.

Point 9 of the November [statement], which the leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and Russia signed, does not refer only to a road linking Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. It states: “All economic and transport links in the region shall be unblocked.” Moreover, the document does not contain the term “corridor”.

Aliyev went on to say that Armenia had delayed implementation of the relevant provision of the 9 November statement and had taken no practical steps to create the “Zangezur Corridor”.

According to him, Russia, the third signatory to the statement, either could not ensure its implementation or had other reasons for not doing so.

“Until August last year, this issue remained frozen. The situation changed when the United States became involved, around spring 2025. The implementation of the project known as TRIPP then began successfully,” Aliyev said, linking the Trump Route transit project to the idea of the “Zangezur Corridor”.

For several years, Baku had demanded that Armenia provide a “Zangezur Corridor” to connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan. The Armenian authorities repeatedly said they were ready to unblock all transport links, but refused to provide a “corridor”. The issue stemmed from the fact that Azerbaijan used the term “corridor” to refer to an extraterritorial route. Armenia, meanwhile, refused to give up sovereign control over its own territory.

On 8 August 2025, the sides reached an agreement in Washington, with the mediation of the US president, under which Armenia would provide a route while retaining its sovereign rights. The transit project therefore received the name “Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity” (TRIPP).

Aliyev also said that, as part of TRIPP, Azerbaijan had already prepared a project to build power transmission lines from mainland Azerbaijan to Nakhchivan through Armenian territory:

“As a result of our specialists’ survey of Armenian territory, we identified the points where the supporting pylons should be installed.”

The Azerbaijani president expressed hope that “Armenia will not delay this process”, saying it would also benefit the country.

“There is no infrastructure by that name in Armenia” — MP

Arman Yeghoyan, an MP from Armenia’s ruling Civil Contract party, said that documents signed by Armenia and Azerbaijan, including the peace agreement initialled in Washington, do not contain the term “Zangezur Corridor”.

“At the level of political narratives, you can say many things. But we are saying that there is no such concept or infrastructure with such a name or term on Armenian territory.”

The MP urged people to remember that Armenia is implementing the TRIPP project. The leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and the United States signed the declaration launching the project in Washington on 8 August 2025.

Comment

According to political analyst Samvel Meliksetyan, when the Azerbaijani side explains what it means by the “Zangezur Corridor”, it refers to the railway from Horadiz to Nakhchivan and then on to Turkey. He also noted that Aliyev used the name TRIPP in his interview.

The analyst said the meaning attached to the term “Zangezur Corridor” in 2022–2023 differs from what it means today. In his assessment, the project no longer involves an extraterritorial corridor:

“From a legal standpoint, TRIPP cannot become an extraterritorial corridor. But from a propaganda standpoint, Azerbaijan uses and will continue to use the term ‘Zangezur Corridor’, with some modifications.”

Meliksetyan stressed that the “Trump Route” project would proceed according to principles agreed with US mediation.

Commenting on Aliyev’s statement about building power transmission lines through Armenian territory, the political analyst said the sides were assessing the most suitable routes. He said the involvement of Azerbaijani specialists should not be interpreted as “acting on their own”.

“All the work is being carried out within the TRIPP framework. An electricity link will run through Armenian territory and connect the two parts of Azerbaijan. Azerbaijani specialists can only discuss where the link will enter Armenia from Azerbaijani territory and where it will re-enter Azerbaijan,” the expert explained.

Summing up his impressions of Aliyev’s interview, Meliksetyan said the Azerbaijani president had spoken in his characteristic style, seeking to highlight his “political achievements”.

The analyst said it was no coincidence that Aliyev focused on Nakhchivan’s economic and energy development, as well as its transport prospects. The president said Azerbaijan would finance the railway restoration itself, but also expressed interest in attracting international investors.

“Although Azerbaijan has repeatedly said that it has no financial problems, they certainly exist. Baku is trying to attract new investment to Nakhchivan through TRIPP to restore this section of the railway,” Meliksetyan said.

Yerevan reacts to Aliyev’s AzTV interview

World.title: Severe petrol shortages hit Abkhazia amid Russia fuel crisis following Ukrainian attacks — VIDEO
World.content:
Fuel shortages in Abkhazia

Severe fuel shortages continue in Abkhazia in the middle of the tourist season. All petroleum products are supplied exclusively from Russia, leaving one clear explanation: fuel shortages in Russia caused by Ukrainian drone attacks on oil and gas facilities.

The Abkhaz authorities are holding emergency talks with Moscow and say progress has been made. Reports say Russia has already arranged for 1,600 tonnes of AI-92 petrol to be sent to Abkhazia, with the first shipment expected to arrive in the coming days.

For now, petrol is available only at Rosneft and Podorozhnik filling stations.

Meanwhile, reports say petrol was supplied from territory controlled by Tbilisi

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed this:

“Amid the severe fuel shortage, a shipment was made to Abkhazia, but it was not supplied by the state, it was supplied by private businesses. If we continue to have the opportunity to ease the situation for the people living there, both Georgians and Abkhaz, we will continue to do so,” Kobakhidze said.

The Abkhaz news agency Apsnypress asked the Abkhaz government for comment following Kobakhidze’s statement and received the following response:

“Due to the circumstances caused by external factors, there is not enough motor fuel to meet Abkhazia’s needs. The authorities therefore decided to allow fuel supplies from alternative sources. Fuel market participants managed to arrange a shipment of petrol from Georgian territory. As is well known, Abkhazia also supplied fuel to Georgia from its territory in the post-war 1990s.”

Kobakhidze’s statement drew criticism from the opposition in Tbilisi. Opposition politicians said the fuel supplies to Abkhazia “could in fact mean supplies to Russian military bases”.

Economist and opposition politician Roman Gotsiridze said: “It is possible that the fuel could also have been transported to Russian territory. The company that made these deliveries will not escape sanctions.”

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Fuel shortages in Abkhazia

World.title: Georgian PM confirms “fuel was supplied to occupied Abkhazia from Tbilisi-controlled territory”
World.content:
Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze confirmed that petrol had been supplied from Tbilisi-controlled territory amid a severe fuel shortage in occupied Abkhazia. A journalist asked Kobakhidze about the issue.

Occupied Abkhazia has recently faced a severe fuel shortage, leading to significant restrictions on supplies of petrol and other petroleum products.

“We did not introduce this; it was introduced by private businesses,” Kobakhidze said at a briefing. He added that such measures were being taken in line with Georgia’s existing legislation, including the Law on Occupied Territories.

He said the Georgian government was ready to help ease the situation for people living in occupied Abkhazia where possible.

“If we can ease the situation, including for the population living in Abkhazia, we will do so, but we will act within the framework of the Law on Occupied Territories,” Kobakhidze said.

Kobakhidze also referred to the government’s “A Step to a Better Future” programme. According to him, it provides support for people living in the occupied territories, including the Abkhaz population.

Comment

Opposition Coalition for Change leader Nika Gvaramia reacted to Kobakhidze’s statement and called on the government to provide further clarification.

Gvaramia noted that Georgia’s Law on Occupied Territories generally prohibits direct unauthorised economic activity in Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region, although it provides certain exceptions, including for activities carried out for humanitarian purposes.

Gvaramia suggested that the fuel supplies in this case could have been intended for Russia’s “war machine”.

Nika Gvaramia: “We are dealing with an action that was presumably authorised by the government in advance. However, the public has not been told the grounds for such authorisation, or when and why it was issued.

“Given that:

— the Russian military machine is facing a severe fuel shortage, while Russian military bases are located in occupied Abkhazia;

— the Ivanishvili regime has repeatedly and deliberately stressed the need for cooperation with Russia;

— taking into account Georgia’s security and territorial integrity interests, as well as Western sanctions imposed on Russia, fuel supplies to territory controlled by Russia cannot be justified on legitimate humanitarian or socio-economic grounds,

“it becomes clear that the Ivanishvili regime has effectively acknowledged that, with its authorisation — and, in essence, by the regime itself — an action is being carried out that runs counter to Georgia’s sovereign interests. It:

violates Georgia’s Constitution;

violates Western sanctions imposed on Russia;

is aimed at assisting the Russian military machine by supplying strategically important products.”

Fuel supplies to Abkhazia

World.title: Teenager charged over $2m fire that destroyed multiple Melbourne shops
World.content:
A 16-year-old boy has been charged over a fire that caused $2 million worth of damage to a retail strip in inner Melbourne last month.

An alleged stolen car was used to ram a convenience store on Victoria Street, on the border of Abbotsford and Richmond, in the early hours of July 6.

The shop was then set alight, with the fire spreading through up to adjoining businesses.

Two women living in one of the businesses were forced to flee the fire.

Police at the time said the offenders fled on foot.

Dozens of firefigther battled the blaze through the early hours of the morning. (ABC News)

It took 80 firefighters an hour and a half to bring the fire under control.

Fire Rescue Victoria said up to 10 businesses were impacted by the fire.

The street was cordoned off for much of the day, with store owners unable to get in to check on their properties.

Detectives today arrested the teenager and charged him with arson, reckless conduct endangering life and car theft.

He has been remanded in custody to appear at a children's court at a later date.

World.title: Boxer dies more than a decade after fight leaves him with brain injury
World.content:
Prichard Colón, a former boxer who was left with severe brain damage after a fight more than a decade ago, has died aged 33.

His father, Richard Colón, confirmed his son's death in a Facebook post on Thursday.

The post did not detail the Puerto Rican boxer's cause of death.

World Boxing Organization (WBO) president Gustavo Olivieri posted a tribute to Colón on social media.

"Today, the WBO solemnly joins his family and all those who had the privilege of knowing, supporting, and loving him in mourning his passing," Mr Olivieri said.

What happened to Prichard Colón?

Colón was injured in a boxing match against Terrel Williams in Virginia in the US in October 2015.

Born in Florida, US, Colón kicked off his boxing career in Puerto Rico, where he won five amateur titles.

He was considered a "rising star" in the lead-up to the nationally televised match, ESPN reports.

Here's how a report from Reuters described the match at the time:

"An online video of the fight showed Williams, a 31-year-old fighter from Los Angeles, punching Colón in the back of the head in the seventh round, a shot that appeared to stun Colón, who was briefly examined in his corner. "Williams was penalised for the illegal punch. "Colón was then knocked down twice in the ninth round. "He was disqualified after the ninth round. "His corner mistakenly took off his gloves, thinking it was the final round and that the fight was complete."

After the match, Colón needed assistance to walk to his dressing room after the match.

He said he felt dizzy, vomited and then "passed out", according to a report from the Washington Post.

Colón was rushed to hospital where he underwent surgery to relieve pressure on his brain, spending seven months in a coma.

He was 23 years old.

Prichard Colon, left, and Terrel Williams during the fight. (Getty Images via AFP: Patrick Smith)

In 2016, the Virginia Department of Professional and Occupational Regulation determined there was no wrongdoing on the part of organisers of the fight, the Washington Post reported.

"No one action [or failure to act] can be identified that is so apparent or egregious to justify holding accountable any one person," the regulator said in a statement.

Signs of hope

In 2017, nearly two years after the fight, Colón was still in what doctors described as a persistent vegetative state, according to an article from ESPN.

He needed around-the-clock care.

At the time, his parents told the US broadcaster they hoped Colón would regain some brain function despite the challenges he faced.

"I do believe in miracles," his father said.

By 2019, Colón had made significant progress, according to another article by the Washington Post.

After months of therapy, he was able to communicate using facial gestures, verbal sounds and a computer that tracked his eye movements.

He could pedal on a recumbent bike, and his competitive spirit was driving him to take steps with assistance in a friendly rivalry with a fellow patient.

"He gets tired and impatient like anyone, and some of his days are better than others," Washington Post reporter Kent Babb wrote.

"What's clear is that he's made it this far, beyond where anyone thought he would, because of good coaching."

'Extraordinary fighting spirit'

News of the former boxer's death triggered an outpouring of grief in the boxing world.

"Prichard's life was defined by courage, perseverance, and an extraordinary fighting spirit," Mr Olivieri said.

"His story transcended the ring and deeply touched the boxing community, which stood by him throughout the years with respect, admiration, and hope."

The WBO paid tribute to Colón's "resilience" as well as "the unwavering love of his family".

Tributes to Prichard Colón were posted to social media after news of his death broke. (Facebook: World Boxing Organization-WBO)

ABC with Reuters

World.title: New mosque with capacity for 1,000 worshippers opens in cherry capital
World.content:
After years of planning, the small cherry growing town of Young in the NSW Riverina is now home to one of regional Australia's largest mosques.

With Muslims making up 10 per cent of the town's population of 11,000, they had long outgrown the old facility.

"The mosque was at the time already full on Friday prayers and we had people praying outside, it needed to happen," long-time worshipper Abdul Ghoneim said.

Gamel Kheir, from the Australian Lebanese Association, which owns the new mosque in Young. (Jostina Basta: ABC Riverina)

Gamel Kheir from the Australian Lebanese Association, which owns the mosque, said the previous facility was a makeshift one established in the 1990s.

The new build is five times larger and accommodates around 1,000 worshippers.

"[The Muslim community is] growing at an exponential rate that the old mosque just doesn't fit the community anymore," Mr Kheir said.

A group gathers outside of a newly built mosque in Young. (Jostina Basta: ABC Riverina)

"It proves that for the Muslim community, as we enter into our fourth and fifth generation here, is not living in enclaves anymore.

" We are actually expanding into Australia and we are part of the fabric of multicultural Australia and Young is testimony to the fact that multiculturalism is alive and succeeding. "

'Attracting' worshippers to the country

Abdul Ghoneim, who left Sydney to settle in Young 10 years ago, said he was not the only one who escaped city life to live in a tighter-knit community.

Abdul Ghoneim moved to Young 10 years ago. (Jostina Basta: ABC Riverina)

"A lot of the communities from overseas have come from villages," he said.

"The pressures of the city, people want to get out."

Hilltops Council mayor Brian Ingram said construction of a new mosque, alongside the existence of an Islamic school, had become a major drawcard for Muslim families.

Mayor of Hilltops Council Brian Ingram at the opening of the mosque in Young. (ABC Riverina: Jostina Basta)

"[It's] played a big part in drawing more of the community here because they knew they would have somewhere to follow their beliefs and their cultures," he said.

"And that's not available in a lot of regional areas in NSW."

Mr Kheir said much of Young's Muslim community is of Lebanese descent, but also included people from South-East Asia and Egypt.

He said the mosque had become more than just a place of worship.

"That's what makes it so beautiful about Young, is they find solace in being one community," Mr Kheir said.

A 'thriving' community, despite challenges

A woman and two girls standing inside the mosque at Young. (Jostina Basta: ABC Riverina)

Cr Ingram said the Muslim community was largely embraced.

"They're really endeavouring to be part of what I call our community, one community," he said.

The mosque has also become known for its community outreach, delivering free meals across the Hilltops region and outreach days for people to ask questions about Islam.

But the journey has not been without controversy, with Cr Ingram acknowledging some national headlines had cast a "dark shadow" in Young.

So-called ISIS bride Mariam Raad was arrested in Young in 2023, accused of willingly entering Syria to be with her Islamic State husband.

She was later discharged conditionally.

Earlier this year, principal Sheikh Abdulghani Albaf of a local Islamic school stood down after the NSW Education Standards Authority (NESA) deemed he did not "meet the fit and proper requirements" after posting comments about Zionism on social media.

The Supreme Court ruled last month that NESA had failed to provide him with procedural fairness.

"It brings with it some doubt in the community and sets those tongues wagging," Cr Ingram said.

"But day to day, we haven't got a problem."

Mr Ghoneim said the actions or views of individuals should not be used to define an entire community.

"If there's one person that has done something wrong, we can't paint the whole community with the same brush," he said.

" We're trying to focus on the positives and just bring happiness to the wider community. "

For Mr Kheir, the opening of a new mosque represented a significant milestone, not just for those who worship there today, but for the generations expected to follow.

He said it could become a place where the Muslim community could continue to grow, while remaining connected to the broader Hilltops region.

"There's no taboo questions we are shying away from answering," Mr Kheir said.

"We open our doors to all."

World.title: Australia's Grace Kim makes fast start at LPGA event
World.content:
Australian golfer Grace Kim has continued her hot run with a stellar opening round at the LPGA Tour's Portland Classic.

Fresh off two straight top-10 finishes, Kim is just one stroke behind Colombian leader Mariel Galdiano after the first round at the Columbia-Edgewater Country Club.

Playing an all-out attack, the major champion collected seven birdies and an eagle to finish the day in a seven-way tie for second.

The world number 38 also needed only 24 putts, the fewest of any player in the field.

Kim started with a three-birdie stretch after starting her round on the 10th hole.

"Having that three-birdie start is just a nice feeling to kick-start things," the 25-year-old said.

"A lot of us out here are pretty straight, fairways and greens.

"But in terms of holing all those putts, knowing that the greens roll quite true … it's really nice to just put a stroke on it and see where it would normally go."

Kim is in a batch at 6-under, including Augusta National women's amateur champion Maria Jose Marin, Arpichaya Yubol and Olivia Cowan.

The 20-year-old Marin landed five-straight birdies on the front nine.

"I reached a flow state that I haven't reached in a while," she said.

"After the British Open I didn't play my best golf, and I think getting that confidence back with this round is all that I needed."

One shot behind them and tied for ninth is Australian Robyn Choi (67), who sprang to life on the back nine.

After going out in even par with a birdie and bogey, Choi stormed home with four consecutive birdies beginning on the 12th. She then added another on the 17th to rocket up the field.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Fellow Australian Steph Kyriacou (72) had a solid round of even par, but will have to play well with the cut projected to be around 1-under.

American pacesetter Galdiano's opening 65 featured nine birdies.

Galdiano, a 28-year-old from Hawaii, is making her fourth LPGA Tour start of the year.

"Every start on the LPGA means a lot to me, so just enjoy the moment, really," she said.

AAP

World.title: Breaking: Angry WA premier lashes 'east-coast clowns' on explosive GST report
World.content:
An angry Roger Cook has lashed as "east coast clowns" the people who authored an explosive report into GST distribution and branded it an "attack" on Western Australians.

Western Australia was the only state or territory to benefit from 2018 changes to how the goods and services tax is carved up, according to a new Productivity Commission interim report into the reforms.

The GST distribution is supposed to help each state and territory provide services and infrastructure to the same standard.

"However, as a result of the [2018] reforms, Western Australia received enough GST revenue to meet 113 per cent of its assessed fiscal needs in 2024-25 — compared with 98 per cent for all other states," the interim report said.

Premier Roger Cook said any changes to the GST distribution would unfairly punish WA for its success "simply to prop up other lazy states".

The WA premier argued that Western Australia and its mining industry prop up the rest of the country. (ABC News: Benjamin Gubana)

He said the Productivity Commission's report was "an attack on every hard working Western Australian".

"It's a sign that these east coast clowns simply do not understand Western Australia, they have no Western Australian representative, and no idea," Mr Cook said.

The report said WA's mining boom drove up the state's ability to fund itself, meaning it received less GST, while the GST formula also meant WA was caught short when mining royalties fell after the global financial crisis.

"This produced a sentiment among many Western Australians that the state was 'losing' its revenue," the commission's interim report said.

The interim report found WA had more money than was needed as part of the deal. (AAP: Joel Carrett )

The commission said political pressure from the WA government at the time partially influenced the 2018 reforms.

'Dodgy, deceitful, dumb'

The Productivity Commission has proposed three potential options for change, stating the "first-best response" would be a return to the pre-2018 system, while addressing issues caused by mining revenue "directly and transparently".

Premier Roger Cook and WA Treasurer Rita Saffioti held a blistering media conference on Friday after the report was made public. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Mr Cook described the commission's proposed options as "dodgy, deceitful, and quite frankly dumb".

"I'm angry, Western Australians are angry, and we have a right to be," he said.

Mr Cook said he spoke with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese today.

Escape plan from 'costly' WA GST deal The Productivity Commission finds the WA GST deal is a "costly mistake" that has led to "perverse" outcomes, and recommends it be scrapped.

"The Prime Minister told me the arrangements in place for Western Australia will remain," Mr Cook said.

"And, this report, a product of the Morrison Liberal government's legislation, does not reflect the federal government's position.

"But we're taking nothing for granted. We are going to fight to keep Western Australia the strongest economy in the nation."

Speaking this morning before the interim report was released, Mr Albanese assured WA would get a "fair deal".

"You will get your fair share, because your work and what you contribute to the national economy really counts," he said.

The Productivity Commission argued the GST was intended to provide an equal quality of services across Australia, rather than punish or incentivise state developments.

"Where a state receives a smaller share of the GST pool, it reflects a need for less support to deliver this level of services," the interim report said.

WA Treasurer Rita Saffioti joined the premier in condemning the report on the GST carve-up. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

The media conference, held by the WA premier and treasurer, was evacuated after the fire-alarm went off at Dumas House.

"Yeah, while we're gone, they're going to take our GST," Treasurer Rita Saffioti quipped.

World.title: Woman involved in fraudulent visa scheme with former MP avoids jail
World.content:
A woman who helped to run a fraudulent visa scheme with former Wagga Wagga MP Daryl Maguire has avoided jail.

Maggie Ning Logan, also known as Maggie Wang, was sentenced in the NSW District Court on Friday to an aggregate prison term of two years and 10 months and 240 hours of community service over two charges relating to her involvement in the crime.

Judge Frank Veltro ruled the sentence could be served in the community, meaning Logan is unlikely to spend any time behind bars.

In his sentencing remarks, Judge Veltro said the 57-year-old aided migration agent Monica Hao in lodging 19 visa-related documents to the Commonwealth that contained false or misleading information.

He told the court Logan met Maguire, who was found guilty of conspiracy last month over his involvement in the scheme, through the NSW Parliament's Asia Pacific Friendship Group in 2012.

In a letter read to the court during a previous hearing, Logan said she had poor mental health and low self-esteem at the time.

She cited the death of her former partner, Sydney barrister Roger Quinn, in a 2010 car accident and said she struggled with her work as an administrative officer with NSW Police.

"I wanted to hold onto something that would give me a sense of importance," Logan told the court.

The letter said Maguire was complimentary of her and his invitations to eat at Parliament House made her "feel important".

"I wanted to please Mr Maguire, I didn't want to disappoint him," Logan said.

" I felt desperate to rebuild my life. "

'Psychologically vulnerable'

The court heard Logan's role in the scheme was to liaise with businesses that were recruited to sponsor Chinese nationals on work visas, but the applicants either never showed up or worked less than the visa allowed.

Logan was paid between $60,000 and $80,000 for the work she performed, and received a $5,000 cash payment for each successful application lodged.

Maggie Logan in NSW Parliament. (Supplied: ICAC)

Judge Veltro described Logan, who moved from China to Australia in 2002 with university degrees in biomedical research and accounting, as "psychologically vulnerable" at the time of the offences.

The court heard she had diagnoses of post-traumatic stress disorder and a major depressive disorder.

Judge Veltro said her mental state contributed to the offending, but noted the conduct remained serious.

"The honesty of documents is fundamental," he said.

"[The offending] was designed to undermine the integrity of the visa system.

" It was a sustained and deliberate pattern of conduct. "

Court accepts genuine remorse

The court was told Logan did not devise or instigate the scheme, which became public during an Independent Commission Against Corruption inquiry between 2018 and 2023.

Judge Veltro said Logan's culpability was less than that of Maguire and Ms Hao's. Ms Hao was a close personal friend of Logan's and left Australia in 2021.

He said Logan had shown genuine remorse and contrition and had "demonstrated significant progress in rehabilitation since offending".

Judge Veltro imposed the prison term for two counts of causing delivery, document with false statement, Migration Act. The offence carries a maximum penalty of 10 years' jail.

He said a full-time custodial sentence would likely threaten Logan's recovery and imposed an intensive corrections order allowing her to serve the sentence in the community.

Maguire is due to be sentenced for his role in the scheme in October.

His legal team has told the ABC they intend to lodge an appeal over the guilty verdict.

World.title: Woman worried about relative's neo-Nazi views criticises support hotline
World.content:
A woman concerned about her young relative's neo-Nazi beliefs has criticised the Commonwealth's flagship violent extremism helpline, saying the service provided vague and unhelpful information during her time of need.

Funded by the federal government, Step Together is a national violent extremism prevention and disengagement program that is administered by the NSW Department of Communities and Justice.

The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion this week heard evidence about the service, which includes a hotline and website providing advice on how to support people at risk of becoming involved with violent extremism.

One woman, who cannot be identified, said she called the Step Together hotline after becoming concerned about a young relative displaying far-right extremism and neo-Nazi beliefs.

She told the commission she was seeking information about community-led services or psychologists with specialist expertise, but was instead directed to her state's police-led intervention program.

The royal commission has been sitting in Sydney to examine deradicalisation programs in Australia. (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

She said she left the call "feeling [her] needs were not being met".

"I was directed to a police intervention program which I didn't feel was appropriate as a first step, to introduce the young person or his family, to a police program," she said.

"That's just escalating it to a point that would not be helpful right now. I don't believe we need the police right now, I hope we don't need the police.

"To say, your child has this issue, let's go to the police, I don't think anyone would want to do that at all. For me that's a last port of call."

'We don't adopt a practice of direct referral'

The NSW Department of Communities and Justice's Heather Jackson told the commission there were limited specialist services available in some jurisdictions, and Step Together did not refer callers to community- led countering violence extremism programs of individuals counsellors.

"Outside our government partners, we don't identify particular services," she said.

"We don't adopt a practice of direct referral … we'd have to endorse that service or believe in that service."

She said if the woman were to call again today, she would be met with the same response.

The anonymous woman was also critical of the Step Together website, saying it was difficult to navigate and did not contain the information she was looking for.

"There is little or no information about the specific groups or patterns of behaviour, including those associated with far-right extremism or neo-Nazi beliefs, which I found troubling," she said.

"To help educate my young relative's family and myself about the Australian and international groups from which he'd been obtaining information … I really had to independently research myself."

The woman said some of the information on the website appeared to be "misrepresenting" the social and personal harms of someone who had radicalised but was not violent.

"Your child could be acting out in all manner of ways, but if they're not blowing something up … this website's not for you," she said.

Ms Jackson earlier this week said work was underway to refresh the website and raise awareness about the service.

'Moral dilemma' for families

The woman said, "out of [her] frustration", she went on to seek alternative support through the community-led initiative Exit Australia, which connected her to an interstate psychologist with relevant expertise.

She said the most valuable advice the psychologist gave was around family support, and how to "manage the moral dilemma" of trying to help someone who had concerning beliefs.

"I got to the point where I didn't believe I could hang in there with the young relative," she said.

"As this psychologist and Exit and other people have shared, as best you can, stick with them … and that is really, really challenging.

"But I got great support and advice about how to manage that."

Clients 'quite happy' with police-run programs, inquiry told

The inquiry also heard from radicalisation researcher Adrian Cherney, who was asked by the commission to assess whether Australia's countering violent extremism programs were consistent with best practice criteria.

Counsel assisting Zelie Heger SC put to Professor Cherney from the University of Queensland that some people may be "deterred" from engaging with a program if it was police-led.

Professor Cherney conceded such a response was possible.

Adrian Cherney is a professor in the School of Social Science at the University of Queensland. (ABC News)

But he said he did not find evidence of police involvement acting as a deterrence in his review of countering violent extremism programs in Australia.

"To some degree, clients were quite happy for police to be managing the program," he said.

Professor Cherney said police-led interventions may also be useful in challenging participants' negative attitudes towards law enforcement.

The inquiry has adjourned and will return for its final hearing block on Monday.

World.title: Further charges laid against former CFMEU boss John Setka
World.content:
Police have laid further charges against former construction union boss John Setka, as part of their investigation into allegedly threatening and harassing emails sent to CFMEU administrators.

The 61-year-old was arrested at his Footscray home on Friday morning.

He has since been charged with using a telecom communications device to menace, using a telecom communications device to offend and two charges of committing an indictable offence while on bail.

Victoria Police allege the harassing and offensive comments were made online on Monday.

Former union boss John Setka was arrested by police at his home in Footscray. (Supplied: Victoria Police)

Mr Setka was first arrested by investigators in November last year, and charged with seven counts of using a telecom communications device to menace, harass and offend.

He was charged again in February this year with using a carriage service to harass and commit an indictable offence whilst on bail.

Police said they would allege additional threats were also made, and Setka was served with an intervention order in July.

Mr Setka was arrested by officers from what Victoria Police has dubbed Taskforce Hawk, which is investigating alleged criminal behaviour linked to the state's construction industry.

He stood down as the head of the Construction, Forestry, Maritime and Energy Union (CFMEU) in Victoria in July 2024, after 12 years in the job.

The Albanese government later placed the union into administration following allegations it had engaged in bullying, corruption, and criminal infiltration.

World.title: Farage began a political farce. Binface missed his chance
World.content:
Analysis WorldEuropeWorld politics Farage began a political farce. Binface missed his chance David Crowe August 14, 2026 — 3:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

London: Nigel Farage will no doubt see his return to the UK parliament as a victory for common sense after the voters of Clacton endorsed him at a byelection he forced upon them. In fact, the outcome is a victory for English farce. And that is not only because the Reform UK leader ended up in a battle for votes with a man who wears a garbage bin on his head. That joke isn’t funny anymore: Binface may have gone global, but Farage will be going back to parliament. Marija Ercegovac There were few surprises when the results were declared at about 6am on Friday local time (3pm AEST) after a very long count because the ballot paper had 34 candidates – ranging from members of the Official Monster Raving Loony Party to the Everyone is God Party and more than a dozen little-known independents. Farage won with 22,239 votes. His main rival, Count Binface, secured 9455 votes.



Turnout was lower than at the general election just over two years ago. Back then, 58.7 per cent cast ballots. This time, 44.4 per cent did so. Voting is not compulsory in the UK, and many voters were clearly unimpressed with the need for this election. Farage won a slightly higher number of votes than the 21,225 he received last time. So, given the lower turnout, he gained a higher percentage of the vote. Last time, it was 46 per cent. This time, it is 62.7 per cent, although it will take time to see all the results because of the sheer number of candidates. Farage in Clacton-on-Sea on Thursday. Getty Images That is a win, of course. But Farage boycotted the vote count and avoided the traditional moment when candidates appear on stage together – when he might have ended up standing alongside Binface. He claimed police warned of a campaign to disrupt the result, but he also complained about the photo opportunity. “I’m damned if I’m going to stand on a stage having won a resounding victory, a ringing endorsement of all that I’ve tried to fight for and you’ve tried to fight for, and be demeaned and humiliated by nobodies,” he told supporters before the final tally was announced.



That just highlighted the farcical nature of the outcome. In a sense, both candidates got what they wanted. Farage gained the formal endorsement of Clacton, an electorate on the English coast north-east of London that he has held for just over two years. Binface, the creation of comedy scriptwriter Jonathan Harvey, gained global attention for his brand of humour. Count Binface poses for the media during the byelection count in Clacton-on-Sea. Bloomberg Even so, nobody really shone. The campaign had its moments of comedy, thanks to Binface and his space warrior outfit, but it was hardly memorable. The Binface routine was a visual gag without any witty lines, even though podcasters and media commentators gave the comic candidate plenty of opportunity. In the end, the joke was fairly humdrum in a nation that has given the world so much biting political satire – not least Monty Python’s the People’s Front of Judea.



So, while there was farce, it was mostly scripted by Farage himself. The Reform UK leader called a referendum on his future early last month by staging a dramatic press conference at which he announced his resignation from parliament. Then he said he would stand for his own seat again. It was a massive display of pique. Farage was simply fed up with media scrutiny of his financial arrangements and seemed to think a byelection could work like a circuit-breaker – or perhaps a distraction such as those that have often helped US President Donald Trump change the conversation. It hasn’t worked. Farage merely highlighted his weakness. Everyone can see he is highly sensitive about his ties to wealthy donors like investor Christopher Harborne, who gave him £5 million ($9.7 million), and crypto millionaire George Cottrell, an aristocrat known as “Posh George” and a long-time supporter of Reform.



This guarantees more scrutiny. The parliamentary inquiries into his donations are expected to resume. Voters knew the byelection was unnecessary, and they knew Farage was putting his own constituency through a waste of time and money. The major political parties contributed to the farce by choosing not to field candidates, and thereby depriving Farage of the serious contest he wanted. Tactically, this made sense. At a deeper level, however, it showed that the Conservative Party did not have the courage to take on Farage in a seat he won from them in 2024. The Conservatives, under leader Kemi Badenoch, are still recovering from that rout at the general election after 14 years in power.



The bigger contest lies ahead. If the inquiries into Farage and his finances go against him, he may be forced to fight for his seat at another byelection. The Conservatives would have a chance to knock him off in a deadly serious campaign over donations and favours. The mere prospect of removing Farage from parliament, and beheading Reform UK, has his enemies salivating. Related Article Analysis

UK politics Alien space warrior v right-wing populist: The UK election that is beyond a joke The mainstream view, conveyed in most of the media, is that Farage has peaked. This is reflected in a change in coverage from one summer to the next. One year ago, the more conservative parts of the media would report his every utterance as major news. This year, the same outlets are openly sceptical about his fortunes. Voters have drifted away from Reform since Farage said he would quit parliament. In early July, 25 per cent said they would vote for Reform. At the start of this week, it was 22 per cent, according to YouGov. Taken in isolation, these numbers are cited as proof Reform is on the decline.



The bigger factor, however, is the bounce for Labour since Andy Burnham became prime minister. The party has risen from 20 per cent to 24 per cent, according to YouGov. But this is a polling honeymoon, and everyone knows they end. Burnham has barely begun to wrestle with the intractable problems of the UK government. He marks his fourth week in the job this Monday. There is no point extrapolating a result in Clacton in 2026 to the rest of the country when the general election is not due until 2029. A lot depends on whether voters really care about the financial support Farage receives from mysterious crypto investors.



Many will engage instead with his argument that Britain is broken, simply because it resonates with their daily experience, regardless of the chatter in Westminster. Asylum seekers continue to cross the English Channel in small boats. Migration is still too high for many voters. Everyday costs are rising. The nation is still debating whether to cut taxes and welfare spending, or do the opposite. Loading There is, in other words, a long way to go before Britain reaches a decisive contest between Burnham, Badenoch and Farage. A minor farce in Clacton is only a small step along the way. Get a note directly from our foreign correspondents on what’s making headlines around the world.

World.title: Sobering markdown: Canva slashes valuation by $10b as AI reality bites
World.content:
TechnologySoftware Sobering markdown: Canva slashes valuation by $10b as AI reality bites David Swan Updated August 14, 2026 — 3:37pm ,first published 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney design giant Canva has cut its internal valuation by a fifth, telling staff an independent assessment now values the business at $43.9 billion, a cut of more than $10 billion from its most recent valuation a year ago. The markdown delivers a sobering reality check for Australia’s largest privately owned company and biggest tech hopeful. For years, Canva has been the undisputed darling of the local start-up scene, carrying the expectations of an entire industry as it grew into a genuine global heavyweight. Canva co-founders Cliff Obrecht, Melanie Perkins and Cameron Adams. Bloomberg Its biggest Australian backer has moved, too. Blackbird Ventures has marked the company down to $US34.9 billion ($49.5 billion) after a fresh independent valuation, a cut of about $10 billion from the $US42 billion price set in a share sale which Canva arranged a year ago. Updated fund valuations went to Blackbird’s investors on Friday. The number Canva gave staff is a 409A valuation, an independent price US tax rules require before a private company can hand shares to employees. It is designed to sit below what investors would pay because staff shares cannot easily be sold.



Canva will use it to price this year’s share grants to its roughly 5500 employees, due within a fortnight. Many hold options once expected to make them millionaires when the company floats. Canva co-founders Cliff Obrecht and Melanie Perkins seated next to Microsoft founder Bill Gates and partner Paula Hurd at the Australian Open in January. Louis Trerise Behind both revisions is the fear that AI will cannibalise the software platforms it was meant to enrich. Anyone who can write a decent prompt can now ask a chatbot to generate a poster or a pitch deck, which is close to Canva’s core business. Investors have already punished the listed companies in that position. Adobe is down about 23 per cent over 12 months and HubSpot about 45 per cent. Figma, which listed to a rapturous reception a year ago, is down about 68 per cent. Canva’s own business has weakened, with the company telling investors this month it now expects revenue growth of 20 per cent this year, down from earlier guidance of 30 per cent. It grew 38 per cent in 2025 and 45 per cent the year before.



Its monthly active users then fell below 208 million in the first week of August, flat year-on-year for a month that is historically its weakest. Canva said the dip reflects northern hemisphere school holidays and a user base that skews more heavily towards education. Related Article Exclusive

Software Canva billionaire has found her next big challenge: democracy Canva said the internal assessment was shaped as much by market conditions as by its own performance, and would have fallen regardless of the revenue downgrade. Blackbird partner Rick Baker said his firm’s revaluation followed Canva’s recent results and forecasts. “The Canva valuation was completed in line with our valuation policy, by our independent valuers on a mark-to-market basis, and our updated fund valuations were sent to investors today,” Baker told this masthead. Canva’s answer to the AI threat is that it is an AI company that happens to do design. It has bought a string of AI start-ups, built its own design model and says it has cut the cost of serving AI products by 90 per cent.



Canva co-founder and chief operating officer Cliff Obrecht said the company was built for a longer horizon than its critics allow. “We’ve always been focused on building a generational company, and that means making deliberate decisions for the long term rather than optimising for short-term valuations,” he said. “Being private gives us the freedom to make big bets and think with a much longer time horizon rather than simply managing quarter to quarter. “We’ve seen markets move in both directions over the years.” Baker said he shared that view. “We back Canva’s judgment to think long term,” he said. “This will unlock the ability to deliver AI at real scale with unit economics that actually stack up. The Canva AI product is looking great and early signs from users are strong, and that gives me a lot of optimism in what’s next.”



Canva said its core business remains strong, pointing to a ninth consecutive year of profitability on a free cash flow basis and revenue growth of 25 per cent in the most recent quarter. The immediate casualty appears to be the company’s float. Canva had long been expected to list on the Nasdaq, a debut that would have ranked it among the 10-largest companies on the ASX had it happened here. Those plans are understood to have been shelved over the valuation concerns. Multiple Australian super funds hold Canva through Blackbird and Airtree funds, meaning millions of Australians own a slice of the company through their superannuation without ever having opened it. The regulator, APRA, criticised funds for being slow to mark Canva down during the 2022 tech downturn. The Business Briefing newsletter delivers major stories, exclusive coverage and expert opinion.
