World.title: A toddler got on a 10.30pm flight. You’ll never guess what happened next
World.content:
LifestyleLife & relationshipsFamily business Opinion A toddler got on a 10.30pm flight. You’ll never guess what happened next Michelle Cazzulino Writer August 14, 2026 — 3:30pm

August 14, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Occasionally you come across parents whose life decisions are so unambiguously stupid that you feel like hacking out your own fallopian tubes and using them to choke yourself into blissful unconsciousness. Regrettably I flogged mine on the Dark Web after the birth of my fourth child, but I promise you, the urge is still strong. Seatbelt, what seatbelt? Getty Images/iStockphoto Anything – and I do mean anything – to separate myself from the pair of breeder imbeciles who determined last week that the best use of their time was to board a plane in Canada with their (allegedly) uncontrollable toddler, who in turn refused to sit in a chair and allow his or her seatbelt to be fastened before take-off. The entire flight, a red eye, was cancelled as a result. Trigger alert: what I’m about to say involves a spirited defence of a budget airline. Don’t worry, the warning is for me, not you. I swore after Jetstar announced last week’s new raft of passenger baggage charges that I’d drink acid before I said a kind word about it or operators of its ilk. #bottomsup. Anyway, back to Porter Airlines, and the incident in question, which happened on August 6, on a flight that was scheduled to leave the Canadian city of Victoria at 10.30pm and land in Toronto at 6.04am.



Alas for all concerned – the pilots, the crew, the other 97 passengers, the ground staff and assorted other airline workers who spent the next few hours untangling a gargantuan administrative snarl – that never happened. By the time all parties established that the toddler wasn’t for turning on the matter of wearing the seatbelt, a decision was made to return to the terminal and disembark the child and the parents. But according to a Porter Airlines spokesman, that meant that, in fact, everyone had to leave the aircraft because it was impossible to remove the family and refile the paperwork before the airport closed at 12.30am. Insert some corporate blather about how Porter Airlines was very sorry that 97 entirely blameless people had to spend the night on horrible plastic airport chairs or wherever, but hip-hip hooray they all made it to Toronto a-bit-late-but-still the next day. Truly. Maybe I spoke too soon about defending budget airlines. The strangest part of this episode has been the reaction it has unleashed online, and the sheer number of people willing to throw shade on the airline for not nixing the flight sooner and/or form a healing circle in solidarity with the Porter Airlines parents. Perhaps part of the reason relates to the post-flight comments made by fellow passenger Aryeh Kozuch, who should forthwith be nominated for sainthood for his take on the situation: “[The toddler] just kept hiding under their seat. If they got forced into [being] strapped in, they just kind of slid out underneath.



“This was a child that was in a tube with 150 people … They’re obviously terrified, and their response was to try and hide under the seat in front of them. That’s so different than a kid running around and screaming.” Related Article Opinion

Streaming I brought the kids on a scenic train trip. My optimism was soon derailed Michelle Cazzulino Writer Different, yes. Entirely predictable, coming from an exhausted, bewildered toddler? Also, yes. To recap, the flight was supposed to leave at 10.30pm, or, to a very small and overtired person, half past why-am-I-still-awake-time-to-morph-into-a-psychopath o’clock. There’s been no word, to date, on how he or she spent the earlier part of the evening, but the odds are it went something along the lines of: queue up through customs, eat rubbish from a diabolical cross-section of airline retailers, try unsuccessfully to nod off, terrorise managers of duty-free shops, try unsuccessfully to nod off, locate departure lounge, try unsuccessfully to nod off, board plane. It’s weirdly tiring. I know because it looks uncannily like my pre-flight routine, and I won’t see early childhood again unless I’m reincarnated.



It’s not difficult to imagine the dialogue that led to the toddler being dragged onto the flight in the first place. You can practically draw the speech bubbles above the parents’ silly heads.

Parent 1: “It’s a night flight – [he or she] will sleep the whole eight hours!” Parent 2: “… and that way, we’ll get a flying start on whatever the hell there is to do in Toronto at 6.04am!” A kinder, more tolerant soul than yours truly (possibly one who’s not still smarting from a five-hour delay that resulted in a 2.30am arrival at New York’s LaGuardia Airport last month, which had nothing at all to do with a toddler) might say I’m being a bit harsh on the parents here. But speaking as someone who can still recite every word of Paul the Police Car, years after having read it at 10-minute intervals on a trip back from Fiji with a two-year-old and a busted in-flight entertainment system, you’ve got to pick your battles when it comes to travelling with children. A budget flight at 10.30pm is no place for the young. Or the young at heart. Or the faint of heart. Or the simple of mind. Thank you and have a pleasant onward journey.



Michelle Cazzulino is a Sydney writer. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: Roosters complained about ground announcer helping Panthers
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 Roosters complained about ground announcer helping Panthers Christian Nicolussi August 14, 2026 — 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Sydney Roosters officials lodged a complaint with the NRL ground manager on Thursday night after they spotted former Panthers player Josh Mansour giving unsolicited advice to Penrith players during the game. Mansour was working at CommBank Stadium as a ground announcer, but dropped the microphone and shouted advice towards Panthers players including winger Tom Jenkins. Loading Under NRL rules, only trainers can pass on coaching messages during stoppages in play. One NRL official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity, confirmed the Roosters had approached the ground manager about Mansour’s actions. The same official said Mansour was being “over-exuberant and encouraging” rather than tactical, and stopped when asked to do so.



Mansour, who spent nine seasons at the Panthers culminating in the 2020 grand final, said he had been playing it for laughs, though some members of the Roosters bench did not see the funny side. The NRL felt no need to take the matter further. “It was no big deal, I actually thought it was comical when they asked me to stop,” Mansour said. Penrith winger Tom Jenkins admits he was happy to get advice from the ground announcer, Josh Mansour, in Friday night’s clash against the Roosters. Getty Images “It’s not like I was sitting there with some big tip sheet of information about the Roosters players. I was calling out stuff like any fan would. “The reason the Roosters may have piped up when they did was because their side started to look like they were on the ropes. They thought I was giving them an edge. I thought it was hilarious. It was all fun.”



Jenkins was glad to have an experienced former winger like Mansour giving him feedback in real time. “‘Sauce’ [Mansour] is funny, he’s such a competitor, he always has been, and you can obviously see he still is that [competitor]; I love him,” Jenkins said. “They thought I was giving them an edge. I thought it was hilarious.” Josh Mansour “He’s got a lot to tell me, he was a great winger. He was doing exactly what your teammates or trainers would do, and that’s tipping you up on little things, and seeing things you maybe don’t see. “In saying that, the boys are good at communicating with each other, seeing what’s coming, and how they’re looking. It’s part of the game. [You welcome] any advantage you can get.”



Mansour had been impressed at how Jenkins had held his own against the aerial threat of Roosters opposite Mark Nawaqanitawase. “He knew when to contest, and backed off when he didn’t have the momentum when he had to catch,” Mansour said. He also believed Nawaqanitawase “had the wheels starting to fall off late in the game”, which is why the Panthers attacked down that edge, and Jenkins came up with some crucial tackles. Sauce of irritation: Former Panther Josh Mansour was working as a ground announcer at CommBank Stadium. Getty Images The NRL was reviewing a number of contentious calls from the game, including the decision to force the Panthers to drop the ball out after five-eighth Daly Cherry-Evans appeared to have knocked the ball on in the in-goal. Referee Adam Gee asked bunker official Ashley Klein to review the matter more than once. The12-6 victory saw the Roosters move to the top of the ladder, and raised further questions about Penrith’s ability to go all the way with co-captain Isaah sidelined due to a pectoral injury.

World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: Complainant ‘C’ felt ‘uncomfortable’ in bedroom at former 2GB broadcaster’s farm, court told
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day eight of Alan Jones’ lengthy criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. My colleagues Clare Sibthorpe and Harriet Alexander will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

The NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court building will hear today from complainant “C”, the second of six men who have accused the former 2GB host of unwanted touching and kissing over a 20-year period.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Friday. Peter Rae

Jones denies the claims and is entitled to the presumption of innocence.

In the first week of the trial, the court heard allegations that Jones indecently assaulted “J”, a young athlete, starting with unwanted kissing and progressing to touching. On the Crown’s case, “J” was aged between 17 and 21 at the time of the nine alleged indecent assaults.

The defence case is that the alleged incidents didn’t happen.

This week, the older brother of “J” and the complainant’s ex-girlfriend gave evidence about what they said he told them about the alleged assaults, and his mother and his former coach gave evidence yesterday.

His mother testified that “J” initially told her that Jones had not touched him, before telling her the following year that he had lied. She said that she was in shock when “J” made the disclosure, and she told her son she should have protected him.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Sylvia Park workers and locals nervous to go back after man shot by police
World.content:
People working at Sylvia Park Shopping Centre are feeling shaken after a man carrying a stolen air rifle was fatally shot by police as he approached the mall yesterday.

Serving waffles from the Eggloo food truck inside the mall, Cherry Zhao faces the doors where just outside, the man, identified as Hapai Otene, was fatally shot

"I just see the police there and I hear the gun and it was really smelly. I just sit down, you know I was really scared and didn't know what was going on."

She crouched down and was on the phone to her manager when police officers locked down the shopping centre.

"The police say put down your phone and close the door...I just stay inside for one and a half hour."

Zhao works alone most week days and said she felt lucky to be unscathed.

She felt a bit nervous coming to work today but said she was pleased to see more security guards and police.

"I'm quite scared I'm not joking," she said.

RNZ / Marika Khabazi

The manager of a bar at the shopping centre, Seri Jackman, said he was not working yesterday but a coworker called him when they saw police.

"One of the managers just called me and was telling me police are here. It's scary to think about but it could happen anywhere. I'm just glad that [there] wasn't that much damage."

Lanie Lidasan, a local who moved from the Philippines just a month ago, was surprised there had been a shooting in an area she thought was safe.

"I'm so nervous to come back right now but I have to buy medicine. I feel safe right now because there's lots of police inside."

Police on Thursday at Sylvia Park Mall after the incident. RNZ / Kim Baker Wilson

On Friday, Superintendent Sunny Patel said a scene examination has been completed and a post-mortem examination is underway.

"I understand the events that unfolded have shaken people that were there at the time, and the wider community. There will be an increased police presence around Sylvia Park Shopping Centre over the coming week to provide reassurance for the public."

Later on Friday evening Patel identified the man as Hapai Otene, aged 33, saying the post-mortem examination and formal identification processes were complete.

"I'm aware there is much discussion about the events that occurred, and it's important that for all parties concerned that we allow due process to be carried out. There are several detailed investigations underway, and these will take time to reach their conclusion."

RNZ understands the father of five had four previous convictions for firearms offences and was sentenced to four years in prison in 2023 for aggravated robbery.

In response to questions from RNZ, Corrections director of communities, partnerships and pathways Simon Chaplin said Corrections' thoughts were with those impacted by the incident at Sylvia Park.

RNZ / Marika Khabazi

"Corrections can confirm this person was subject to community detention and supervision.

"Their community sentence included a 7pm-7am curfew where electronic monitoring was used to verify that they were at their home address during the hours of this curfew. They were not in breach of this curfew at the time the Sylvia Park incident occurred."

On Thursday afternoon police had received information about the theft of an air rifle in Penrose, which resulted in a chase across Auckland.

Gun City owner David Tipple, where police say Otene stole the air rifle from, told RNZ staff chased him after the theft but he had "succeeded in driving off in a car".

World.title: Flights cancelled, delayed as fog restrictions hit Auckland Airport
World.content:
Fog restrictions are in place at Auckland Airport.

By 7.20am, several domestic regional flights had been cancelled as well as some arrivals.

A number departing had been delayed as well as arriving.

Of the main trunk domestic flights, one to Christchurch had been delayed, as had an arrival from Dunedin.

International flights have not been affected by the fog.

The airport said passengers are advised to check its website for the latest flight information.

Wellington seafog

MetService said seafog and low clouds in Wellington Harbour could disrupt flights.

A southerly wind has pushed a low cloud shelf into the city over the past few hours.

Meteorologists said as temperatures cool in the evening, a thick bank of mist could sink to surface levels.

The weather agency said there was still a probability of fog around the airport, which could disrupt flights.

But it said exact conditions were difficult to predict.

The cloud bank was expected to last through the afternoon to the early hours of Saturday morning.

Meteorologist Alwyn Bakker earlier said the southern coast of Wellington would be most exposed - including the harbour and airport.

"So you get that sea fog when sea surface temperatures and air temperatures are very close together.

"So with a southerly the air is cooled down, the sea takes a little bit longer to cool down water - it hangs on to heat better than air essentially."

He said low visibility might impact flights, depending on how much moisture builds in the air.

"Basically, planes like to see the ground before they land."

World.title: Philip Polkinghorne denies direct accusations he killed wife Pauline Hanna during inquest
World.content:
Philip Polkinghorne has denied killing his wife as the accusation was put directly to him at her inquest.

Polkinghorne was cleared of Pauline Hanna's 2021 murder at a trial two years ago but chose not to give evidence there.

On Friday, he got into the witness box at the Coronial inquest into Pauline Hanna's death where police lawyer Alysha McClintock accused him directly.

"You laid her out and you go about making it look like she killed herself," she said.

Polkinghorne answered with an emphatic "no."

McClintock accused Polkinghorne of attacking Hanna after an argument, incapacitating her so she could not fight back, killing her, and making it look like a suicide.

At each step Polkinghorne said "no" or "wrong".

Earlier in the hearing, he admitted he had lied several times since Hanna's death about some of the circumstances surrounding it, but denied it was to cover-up killing Hanna.

McClintock said there would be no other reason to lie.

"If Pauline had killed herself and all you had to do is explain how you found her, we shouldn't have all these lies," McClintock said.

McClintock asked Polkinghorne about a statement from sex worker Madison Ashton, who he'd been in a relationship with.

In it, Ashton said Polkinghorne told her Hanna had broken into their house and killed herself.

Polkinghorne denied saying that, and denied messaging Ashton the day his wife died.

He was grilled about his wife's use of the sleeping pill zopiclone, some of which were his.

Coroner Tania Tetitaha asked him if he had ever been in trouble with the Medical Council for prescribing medicines for himself.

He denied that until McClintock produced a 2018 letter from the council that warned him about self prescribing, including for zopliclone.

"I apologise, I had forgotten about that," he said.

A message from Ashton showed he had spoken to her about the council's letter.

"No biggie, I'll use a false name in the future," he said in the message.

Today, he said the message was "very flippant and inappropriate."

Pauline Hanna's family were able to put questions to Polkinghorne for the first time under oath

Her brother Bruce Hanna spent the time asking about the position of Pauline's arms when she was found.

Through a lawyer, her sister Tracey asked about why Polkinghorne had been searching for information about her injuries in the days after her death.

The purpose of the inquest is to establish the circumstances surrounding Pauline Hanna's death, including whether it was self inflicted.

Several details are suppressed.

World.title: Deadly Tauranga landslides public submission process extended
World.content:
The public submissions process for the inquiry into the fatal Tauranga landslides has been extended for another three weeks.

A government inquiry was launched in February into the January landslides, which killed eight people.

Six people died at Mt Maunganui Mauao when severe storms and record rainfall sent mud and debris onto the campsite below. A landslide also fell onto three properties in Welcome Bay Road in Pāpāmoa, killing a further two people.

Public submissions for the Inquiry opened last month.

The inquiry chair, former Supreme Court judge Sir Mark O'Regan, said the inquiry had already received a high calibre of submissions, and further contributions were welcome.

"We have received thoughtful and informative submissions from people with a wide range of knowledge, experience and perspectives," he said.

"Those submissions are already valuable in helping the Inquiry build a fuller picture of the circumstances surrounding these tragic events and the lessons that can be learned from them. Extending the submissions period will allow more people to share information that may assist the Inquiry's work."

The inquiry has been tasked with investigating how the landslides occurred, and whether relevant agencies took appropriate steps to manage any risk.

Submissions will now close on 4 September. Video and drone footage, photos, rain gauge measurements, and information relevant to the Inquiry's terms of reference could be uploaded to a portal.

World.title: China denies espionage, foreign interference in NZ
World.content:
The Chinese Embassy rejects a new report by New Zealand's top spy agency that includes what it says are multiple "false allegations against China".

In its fourth Security Threat Environment report released on Thursday, the New Zealand Security Intelligence Service said China was the sole nation pursuing espionage in New Zealand "at scale".

The report also said China continued to be the "most active" nation among several others involved in foreign interference activity in New Zealand.

In a statement on Friday, the Chinese Embassy said the NZSIS report included baseless and fabricated accusations.

"Its false allegations against China either smear normal exchanges and cooperation as so-called espionage or interference, or are entirely groundless and fabricated out of thin air," the statement said.

"We firmly oppose this and will never accept it."

The embassy said the China-New Zealand relationship was one of mutual benefit, with progress having been made in areas such as trade, people-to-people exchanges, tourism and international education in recent years.

It said the Chinese community in New Zealand had played a positive role in this process.

Since China's implementation of a unilateral visa-free policy for New Zealand, a growing number of New Zealanders had visited China and the goodwill towards China as well as support for China-New Zealand relations continued to grow, the embassy said.

"That this report is released at this particular juncture is no coincidence - it forms part of a new wave of attacks, slander and vilification against China orchestrated by certain international forces, and may well itself be a product of foreign interference," the statement said.

It claimed "anti-China forces" were seeking to drive a wedge between the people of both countries, creating a chilling effect on the public, undermining mutual trust and obstructing the growth of the relationship.

"Our message to those forces and individuals attempting political machinations is this: do not sacrifice the hard-won, mutually beneficial China-New Zealand relationship for selfish gain, and do not act against the interests of New Zealand and its people," the embassy said.

"Serving as a pawn for anti-China forces will ultimately backfire.

"Manufacturing distractions in foreign relations will not solve New Zealand's own problems - it will only prove counterproductive. We urge these forces and individuals not to quench their thirst with poison, and not to lift a rock only to drop it on their own feet."

World.title: Victim Support confirms terms of reference for independent investigation into workplace culture
World.content:
The country's lead agency supporting victims of crime and trauma has confirmed the terms of reference for an independent investigation into its workplace culture, confidence in leadership and workplace complaints processes.

The external review came after reporting by RNZ over claims of a "toxic" and "bullying" workplace culture, four years after an investigation into similar allegations.

RNZ spoke to several current and former workers who raised concerns about the culture at Victim Support. One person described it as a "very unsafe environment".

The agency's chief executive James McCulloch earlier said the agency "does not accept that these claims reflect Victim Support today".

Do you know more? Email sam.sherwood@rnz.co.nz

However, in a u-turn last month Victim Support announced it had agreed to commission a review of the organisation's workplace culture, confidence in people leadership and the processes for resolving workplace concerns.

On Friday, Victim Support announced it had confirmed the terms of reference for the review.

"The Board commissioned the review to provide objective assurance on the organisation's current workplace culture, including assessing employee confidence in leadership, speaking-up processes and whether there are recurring or systemic issues that need to be addressed."

Every current employee would have the opportunity to participate in the review, Victim Support said.

The Board had appointed Charlotte Stevens as Independent Reviewer and Samantha Turner as Independent Peer Reviewer.

"The Independent Reviewer will select a random sample of employees from across different roles, functions, locations and lengths of service. Any employee who is not selected will also be able to request a confidential interview, make a written submission or participate through another mechanism established by the reviewer.

"Participation will be voluntary and confidential, and information will be anonymised and reported in themes."

The Independent Reviewer would determine the methodology and may seek further information or interviews where needed.

"The review will also consider employee survey results, workforce and exit data, previous independent reviews, organisational policies and other relevant evidence.

"The Independent Peer Reviewer will provide additional quality assurance. The Independent Reviewer will retain sole responsibility for the final findings and recommendations."

Board Chair Rob Marshall said the terms of reference had been designed to give staff confidence in the process.

"The Board wants a clear, independent and evidence-based assessment of Victim Support's workplace today," Board Chair Rob Marshall said.

"We want our people to be able to participate openly and with confidence in the process. The Independent Reviewer will follow the evidence, identify what is working well and where improvements may be needed. We will take their findings and recommendations seriously - the wellbeing of our people and the quality of support we provide to victims are closely connected."

Victim Support said the review was focused on the agency's current workplace culture.

"Relevant historical information, including previous reviews, exit information and workforce data, will also be considered where it helps understand changes over time.

"The review is not an investigation into individual employment matters or allegations."

World.title: New bidding round opens at site of declined Golden Bay mining permit
World.content:
New bidding round opens at site of declined Golden Bay mining permit

Almost three months after declining a controversial gold mine proposal on public conservation land in Golden Bay, the Crown is accepting new mineral permit applications for the area.

New Zealand Petroleum and Minerals has opened the Sam's Creek site in the Upper Tākaka Valley to a competitive application process that would enable Siren Gold and rival companies to apply for prospecting, exploration or mining permits.

Siren Gold announced in May that its application had been unsuccessful following exploration drilling that began in 2022.

The news was welcomed by some Golden Bay locals who fought staunchly against the mine, fearing potential harm to the Te Waikoropupū Springs.

Some activists locked themselves to the main drilling rig in protest.

Protesters occupy the drilling site in Sams Creek, in the Upper Tākaka Valley. Supplied / Timothy Firkin

At the time its application was declined, Siren Gold said its exploration permit had also expired and it was assessing the next steps.

"If the land becomes available for permitting again, the decision does not preclude the company from applying for a further permit," the company said.

On Friday New Zealand Petroleum and Minerals confirmed it had opened applications for the 20-square-kilometre area.

"The land previously covered by exploration permit 40338 (Sam's Creek) and exploration permit 54454 (Barrons Flat) has been designated as newly available acreage for both metallic and non-metallic minerals," it said.

Applications were open until 9 October.

World.title: Ex-politician Kiri Allan says public service bloated, slow and overpaid
World.content:
Former Labour cabinet minister Kiri Allan has come out swinging against the public service saying it is bloated, slow, and overpaid.

In her new memoir, Go Hard or Go Home, she is scathing of the sector and doubled-down on her position on Friday, calling for an overhaul on Midday Report.

Kiri Allan on overhauling the public service Midday Report Download MP3 16m

Public Service Commissioner Sir Brian Roche declined to comment.

Allan said there were "exceptional people" throughout the public service and her comments weren't an attack on individuals, but on the system.

She said in the private sector, the incentive to work hard was to "put food on the table" the next day, and maintained the problems she saw with the public sector were particularly acute in upper management.

"What I found with senior bureaucrats is that they're often more political than politicians. They know they're going to out-survive politicians.

"And they just sometimes need to bide their time, say 'Yes minister, absolutely minister.'"

Allan said it was "problematic" for the country's political system, and different from some systems overseas.

She said she also believed in "devolution" and thought taxpayer dollars were overly centralised and wanted to see more money and resources in the hands of communities.

"Because of the policies that our government's provide, there ends up being a lot of gatekeeping in the centre in terms of getting those resources out."

Allan said she ran into this during her time as conservation minister, claiming getting millions of dollars to community groups under the Jobs for Nature programme was a "ridiculous process" that took a couple of years.

She said in another instance, resolving who had cultural rights over whale bones took four years.

The Department of Conservation declined to comment.

Allan said she did not agree with the ACT Party's policy to slash the public sector, but said an overhaul was needed.

World.title: Fraser officially enters Carlton coaching race after mid-year turnaround
World.content:
Josh Fraser has presented to the Carlton hierarchy after officially entering the club's process to find its full-time coach.

After a stunning run of 10 wins from 12 matches since becoming interim coach when Michael Voss left the club in May, Fraser has Carlton on the cusp of the most unlikely finals appearance.

Although he has delivered a perfect on-the-job audition, Fraser was still required to pitch to the Blues' coaching panel on Wednesday.

Loading...

Untried assistants Jaymie Graham (Fremantle), Corey Enright (St Kilda) and James Kelly (Geelong) have been through the process, with Fraser only formally putting his hand up this week.

"A fortnight ago, the club came to me and asked me to be a part of this coaching process," Fraser said today.

"Then this week, I was in a position to go back to the club and accept that offer to go through the process.

"I presented to the coaching panel this week."

At his first press conference when taking over from Voss, Fraser was adamant he was not interested in being Carlton's coach beyond this season.

But after a wildly successful 12 weeks in charge, buoyed by enthusiastic fans, Fraser could not turn down the opportunity.

"I have said, previously, that I've been ambitious to be a senior coach," Fraser said.

"I've been fortunate to be able to sit in the chair and consolidate some of my thinking; get some opportunity exposure to the role that otherwise you wouldn't normally get.

"It's been something that's been crystallising in my mind and my thoughts.

"Really confident that I'm ready to assume the responsibility of being a senior coach.

"There are 19 jobs to be a senior (AFL) coach.

"I'm as excited about this group as a lot of our Carlton supporters will be."

Joyous Blues fans were chanting "we want Fraser" as the Blues steamrolled St Kilda on Sunday night to put themselves in the box seat to earn a spot in the wildcard round.

If they defeat the Western Bulldogs, who will be without superstar captain Marcus Bontempelli on Sunday, the Blues will lock in their spot in the top 10.

It has been one of the more remarkable in-season turnarounds in AFL history, with Carlton 1-8 when Fraser took over.

"It can disrupt the club at times, when there's a significant change, like when you lose a coach, and you bring another coach in mid-season," Fraser said.

"That speaks to the culture that's been here, but I'm grateful for all the support I've had around me."

AAP

World.title: Live: Bangladesh opener scores maiden Test century as Aussies flounder
World.content:
He was in deep discussion with some of the Australian staff as that last over was underway.

FOUR! Lovely sweep from Shanto - it wasn't perhaps as well struck as he would have liked, a bit top-edgy as Shanto had to reach for it. But he gets enough contact to make it to the rope.

Quick single now from Shanto, as he chips the ball towards mid on.

Solid defence from Mushfiqur, as Lyon comes around the wicket to the right hander. There's a bat pad and slip in place.

World.title: EPL side walks off as Spanish club kicks penalty into open net
World.content:
Fulham's preseason match against Málaga turned out to be not too friendly after the English club walked off and coach Álvaro Arbeloa was shown a red card for complaining to the referees.

The match had finished 2-2, after the La Liga side Málaga FC equalised in the 90th minute.

At full-time, the Premier League outfit walked off the pitch while Málaga stayed on, believing a penalty shootout should decide the winner.

Malaga striker Jauregi then kicked a penalty into an open net before celebrating in front of the home fans.

In a post on X, Fulham said both teams had agreed before the match that no penalty shootout would follow a draw.

"We can confirm that prior to the match, both teams agreed that there would not be a penalty shootout in the event of a draw," Fulham wrote on X.

On their club website, Malaga said it believed a shootout was on the cards.

"Although a penalty shootout had been scheduled, Fulham left the pitch, claiming that a shootout had not been included in the contract," the La Liga club said.

World.title: Payne's fame began as a joke. Now his shirt has sparked a bidding war
World.content:
Just a few months ago, few soccer fans outside New Zealand and Australia knew Tim Payne's name. Now they are bidding thousands of dollars for the jersey off his back.

The shirt Payne wore in his debut for Club Olimpia, a Paraguayan soccer powerhouse, has become a coveted piece of match-worn memorabilia since the club put it up for auction online five days ago.

With bidding set to close, the leading offer has climbed above 21 million in Paraguay's currency, the guarani, equivalent to around $5,000.

Viral Kiwi star meets Argentine influencer who boosted following to 5M New Zealand soccer player Tim Payne has met social media influencer Valen Scarsini after the Argentine encouraged his fans to follow the unheralded All Whites player.

It is the latest development in the unlikely rise of the 32-year-old defender, who entered the World Cup with just over 4,000 followers on Instagram and emerged as one of the tournament's biggest social media sensations.

Before representing New Zealand at the World Cup, Payne spent most of his career out of the limelight, playing for low-profile clubs in New Zealand before playing 143 A-League matches for Wellington. He also spent two years with England's Blackburn Rovers but never made a major appearance because of work-permit problems.

Then Argentine soccer influencer Valen Scarsini, known online as El Scarso, went searching for what he called the World Cup's "least-known soccer player".

Scarsini settled on Payne, whose Instagram account had 4,715 followers at the time, and encouraged his more than 2 million followers across Instagram, TikTok and YouTube to follow Payne, flood his posts with supportive comments and mention his name everywhere.

Loading Instagram content

Within days, Payne's following skyrocketed, eventually topping 5.4 million — more than the entire population of his native New Zealand. The surge in online fame helped carry Payne to Paraguay, where he signed with national club champion Olimpia on a one-year deal in June, ending a seven-year stint with Wellington Phoenix.

Payne gave legions of new fans another reason to cheer him during his August 2 debut against Asunción club Rubio Ñu, scoring minutes after coming off the bench to help Olimpia win 5-0.

Now the signed jersey from that match is drawing the sort of interest usually reserved for far more established names — though the leading offer remains a far cry from the millions of dollars paid for jerseys worn by Argentine superstar Lionel Messi and other soccer greats.

"I know exactly what it means to wear these stripes and play in this shirt, and that's why I want to give it to a true Olimpista (Olimpia fan)," Payne said in a video launching the auction.

AP

World.title: Brian To'o is still just the beginning for the PNG Chiefs
World.content:
After a week in the spotlight following the biggest decision of his career, Brian To'o went back to work.

His showing in the Panthers' 12-6 loss to the Roosters was typical of the To'o we've come to know.

The future Papua New Guinea Chief did not bring up his 100th try for the Panthers but did churn through 17 runs for 162 metres to go with five tackle busts and two line breaks. For some wingers that's a big night but for To'o it's the standard.

'Can't compete': Super coaches weigh into PNG Chiefs debate Two of the NRL's most successful modern coaches weigh into the debate about the concessions afforded to the league's forthcoming PNG franchise.

The performance came in the days following confirmation of To'o's move to the Papua New Guinea Chiefs and it shouldn't have been a surprise.

There are good reasons To'o has become the premier winger of his time, and having such a high baseline is one of them.

Continued excellence on his part, for both the rest of this season and his final year with Penrith in 2027, is as close to a given as you'll find anywhere in rugby league.

He is the best player the Chiefs have signed but that may not remain so. Not since the Broncos filled their boots with Queensland-based stars for their inaugural season in 1988 has an expansion team signed so much established talent.

Zac Lomax will return to rugby league with the Chiefs. (Getty Images: Brendon THorne)

Of the six players to commit to the Chiefs, four have played State of Origin in the past two years. Some clubs go decades without signing one or two players who fit such a criteria.

The other two are the greatest try-scorer the Australian game has ever known and one of England's top front-rowers.

Unless Joseph Manu was just in Port Moresby on holiday, it seems likely they'll add the Golden Boot winner from the most recent World Cup to the list before long.

They have achieved all this without really entering the cut and thrust of the transfer market in earnest. Officially, the Chiefs cannot talk to any NRL free agents for the 2028 season until November 1 this year.

Manu has been linked with an NRL return with the Chiefs. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

Each of the signings they've made within the NRL have come because a club granted permission for the player in question to negotiate early or because the player activated something in their contract that allowed them to do so.

They've done all this while the luxury compound they're building is still a hole in the ground and before they have a logo or a jersey. To'o himself hasn't even been to Papua New Guinea before.

They're yet to land any young legs but if these are the players they can sign through the activation of obscure clauses and arcane options and the like, imagine what they can do in the jungle of true free agency when they have the biggest and sharpest teeth via their mountain of government funding?

With local products like Gairo Voro, Morea Morea and Finlay Glare, all of whom are enjoying standout seasons with London Broncos and will eventually take up development contracts with the club, to fill out the other end of the roster, the Cheifs can keep aiming high.

The floodgates have yet to truly open but already the ripples of the league's new money-monster are clear to see.

Hudson Young, fresh off a career-changing State of Origin series, is in the Chiefs' sights and despite the Raiders offering just about everything they've got to a player who has found a home in Canberra, fans there are turning as green as their jerseys because they know there's a chance they'll be money-whipped.

Young is the latest player to come into PNG's sights. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The spectre of similar moves loom over a sport addicted to transfer gossip and sank into Thursday's top-of-the-table clash because after the start they've made, no player seems out of reach for the Chiefs.

Not Sam Walker, who turned down the Roosters first contract offer midweek and has the chance to secure untold riches over the final stages of this season, a chance he has surely enhanced after a mature performance that helped put the Tricolours on top of the ladder.

Not Liam Martin, who rattled Cody Ramsey with the best shot of the night or Spencer Leniu, who struggled to find the fire against his former club and looks like he'd benefit from a change of scenery.

Not even Nathan Cleary, who tried every trick he knew but could not break down a resolute Roosters defensive line.

As impossible as it seems to picture him playing rugby league in anything but a Penrith jersey, even he is in play.

Through their tax-free contracts and the legitimacy that comes with signing established stars, the Chiefs have the capability to tip the entire league on its head.

They can pay a battler like a prince, a prince like a king and a king like a god and given they've already shown a taste for the finer things in assembling their roster, there's little reason to expect it won't continue.

Their advantages warp the salary cap beyond recognition and each signing they make is further proof of concept that the gold rush is real.

General manager of football Michael Chammas says he wears it as a badge of honour that clubs are beginning to gripe at the advantages PNG have been given and well may he, given how those clubs, blinded by the glittering of gold, let a Chief into the henhouse.

Why Luai's move to PNG has changed everything Jarome Luai's decision to sign with Papua New Guinea is a showcase of the economic power behind the Chiefs and marks the start of the greatest rugby league gold rush since Super League.

It is hard to begrudge any player for taking what's on offer, like it's hard to begrudge the way Chammas and the Chiefs are going about it. They're playing by the rules they've been given and they're playing by them well.

Ever since Jarome Luai was announced as their first signing, their power has become more and more real and it continues to solidify with every signing they make. Now, they are securing a firm foothold on the high side of an uneven surface.

To'o is the latest, but not the last and rugby league is only just beginning to reckon with the power of what the NRL has created with its concessions to the Chiefs and how it alters the competitive balance of the league.

They have turned the dial as far as it will go and are now waiting to see what happens next, as is their way, and it is happening hard and fast all around us.

The downpour of money is a monsoon that shows no sign of breaking, even as rival clubs get swamped.

And stars like To'o who have been swept along are still just the start. Expect plenty more to dive in.

World.title: Teen Italian star breaks world record for second time this week
World.content:
Italian teenage swimming sensation Sara Curtis has broken the world 50m backstroke world record again, just a day after eclipsing the global mark of Australian great Kaylee McKeown.

The 19-year-old Curtis ‌won gold in 26.56 seconds in the final of the European Championships in Paris on Thursday, local time, clipping another 0.07 seconds off the time of 26.63 she had set in Wednesday's semifinals.

That time had obliterated the three-year-old mark of five-time Olympic champion McKeown, who had clocked 26.86 when winning a World Cup race in Budapest in 2023.

Teenager breaks Kaylee McKeown backstroke world record Italian teenager Sara Curtis has set a new world record in the women's 50m backstroke, beating the mark previously held by Australian great Kaylee McKeown.

It continued the historic week for the Savigliano-born Curtis, who has a Nigerian mother and Italian father, as she becomes the first Black swimmer to hold an individual long-course world record.

Mary-Ambre Moluh, from ​France, finished ‌half a second behind Curtis ​to take the silver, while Britain's Lauren Cox took ​bronze.

"I'm happy I managed it again. It's absurd, another crazy feat," Curtis told Italian TV station Rai 2.

It ​was the ​third medal in Paris for ‌the University of Virginia star, who also took bronze in 100m freestyle and silver in ​the 4x100m freestyle relay.

The teenager had been inching towards the ​world ​record all year, having ​broken the Italian and ‌European records earlier in the season.

"From the moment I set off for Virginia, that's all I thought about, the record. A dream and ​an immense goal," she admitted.

But it has been a tough spell for McKeown, who had to pull out of both the recent Commonwealth Games and the current Pan Pacific Championships because of glandular fever.

The 25-year-old is determined to get back into top shape for the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, where Curtis shapes to be one of the pool stars.

Great Britain's Filip Nowacki claimed the European 200m breaststroke gold, continuing his terrific rise.

The 18-year-old was fresh from winning gold for Jersey at the Commonwealth Games, only the second ever for his little Channel Island home.

AAP

World.title: Four-goal Austin gives Dees perfect start to new AFLW era
World.content:
Melbourne's new dawn in the AFLW has begun with a win, with recruit Mia Austin kicking four goals to give Demons coach Tom Wilson victory in his first match in charge.

Hawthorn tested last year's preliminary finalists at Princes Park on Thursday night, and went into the final quarter level.

But the Dees kept the Hawks scoreless in the final term to secure a 19-point round one triumph.

AFLW double-header season opener left fans with 'lots of mixed feelings' The AFLW opened its 2026 season with a double-header at Docklands Stadium.

The contest was the first time Melbourne's women have not been coached by Mick Stinear, who is now in charge at Geelong, with Wilson taking over to start his AFLW coaching career.

Liv Purcell returned from the knee reconstruction that kept her to only two games last season and she was best afield, racking up 32 possessions and nine tackles.

Recruited from Carlton, Austin was outstanding and looks the ideal replacement for Eden Zanker, now at Fremantle.

Melbourne captain Kate Hore also starred, but goal kicking let her down and she finished with a wasteful 1.4.

The Hawks rallied after a slow start as they unveiled their key-forward double act, with former Gold Coast player Jacqueline Dupuy joining All-Australian Aine McDonagh.

Dupuy took nine marks and kicked a goal, while McDonagh made a strong start with three majors.

Hawthorn defender Jenna Richardson, who took 11 marks, and ruck Lucy Wales impressed.

With Hore, Tayla Harris and Purcell firing, the Dees threatened to kill off the game early.

Melbourne kicked the first three goals of the game and were up by 23 late in the opening term.

But Dupuy kicked her first for the Hawks to keep them within 17 points at the first change.

The game flipped in the second, as Dupuy and McDonagh fired in attack. Hawthorn kicked three goals to one and only trailed by seven points at the main break.

Jacinta Hose's long-overdue AFLW debut ended in more pain for the Demons' ruck when she was forced out of the game in the second quarter with an ankle injury.

Hose was drafted in 2023, but two knee reconstructions have stalled her career.

When McDonagh kicked the only goal of the third quarter, the Hawks led for the first time in the game and scores were tied at the final change.

But Austin kicked her fourth goal at the start of the last quarter and Elizabeth McNamara added another a couple of minutes later to steady for Melbourne.

While Shelley Heath goaled 11 minutes into the term, the Demons had a three-goal break and the game was over.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Cherry-Evans confirms NRL exit in shock call after Roosters win
World.content:
Daly Cherry-Evans has given himself every chance to book-end his NRL career with a second premiership after confirming 2026 will be his last season in Australia.

The Sydney Roosters star announced today he would finish in the NRL at season's end, before moving to the English Super League for a one-year swan song at Hull FC.

His exit will bring the curtain down on one of the NRL's most storied careers, after debuting at Manly in 2011 before his shock Sea Eagles exit at the end of last season.

At the age of 37, Cherry-Evans is the second-most-capped player in NRL history and has a string of records, including the most 40-20s ever kicked, most golden-point winners and most field goals in the NRL era.

He also captained both Queensland and Australia, helping lead the Maroons to three series wins and claiming a Clive Churchill Medal in 2013.

Cherry-Evans led the Maroons to three series victories as captain. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

His announcement comes despite him showing last night he is still playing as well as ever, scoring both of the Roosters' tries in a 12-6 win over Penrith.

After beginning his career with a premiership as a rookie halfback at Manly in 2011, Cherry-Evans now has the Roosters in first with a second title looking a real possibility.

"I still have a real desire to play and compete, so the opportunity to join Hull FC and experience the Super League is something I'm genuinely excited about," Cherry-Evans said.

"But there's still plenty of football to be played this season, and that's where my focus is.

"We've got a lot we still want to achieve as a team here at the Roosters, and I'm determined to give my all and play my part in that."

Rumours of Cherry-Evans' Super League move had come as something of a shock earlier this week.

Hull will be coached next season by Steve McNamara, who is a long-time friend and former assistant of Roosters' coach Trent Robinson.

The former Queensland halfback shocked Manly last March when he announced he would leave the club after 15 seasons there.

He insisted today he had no ill feelings towards the Sea Eagles, where he remains the most-capped player in the club's history.

"Manly will always hold a special place for me and my family," he said.

Roosters force first NRL lead change in five months There's a new name at the top of the NRL ladder for the first time since March after the Roosters outlasted Penrith in a possible grand final preview.

"I spent more than 15 years there, made lifelong friendships and was fortunate to experience so much throughout my time at the club.

"Coming to the Roosters this year gave me the opportunity to challenge myself in a completely new environment, and I've loved being part of this club."

Cherry-Evans' Roosters arrival has prompted the Tri-colours to deploy promising playmaker Hugo Savala in the centres this season.

Robinson described coaching Cherry-Evans as a "gift" after his side climbed to first and moved to within touching distance of the minor premiership.

"You talk about external motivation, but to watch someone care about the way that he plays the game and goes about it," Robinson said.

"Maybe two or three years ago at a charity function, I almost bought his boot for a couple of thousand dollars, but one of my mates got it before me.

"I feel like a guy plays with a spirit… I really enjoy watching him play, and I've said that, but I've enjoyed watching him come and want to improve his game."

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

Tech.title: Trump declares 100 percent tariffs on many drones and all aircraft parts
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

DJI ban: how the world’s biggest dronemaker is getting shoved out of the US

The United States has already banned future foreign drones from entering the United States unless their companies kiss the ring — as well as routers, robots, and Roombas. Now, President Donald Trump is targeting existing drone imports and parts, too. He’s going to try to make them cost a lot more.

In a presidential action, he’s declared a whopping 100 percent tariff on imports of drones with thermal cameras, drones weighing over 25kg (57 pounds), and any kind of part for any kind of unmanned aircraft weighing over 25kg — you can read the full list here. For all other drones, including tiny sub-250-gram “Mini” consumer drones, he’s declared a 25 percent tariff.

In Trump fashion, these tariffs have a huge loophole: if a company commits to making some of their drones or aircraft parts in the United States, they don’t have to pay tariffs. Trump suggested he’d make similar deals when he threatened a 100 percent tariff on computer chips last year.

And Trump is giving the EU, Japan, Liechtenstein, South Korea, Switzerland, and Taiwan a lower rate of 15 percent, and a rate of 10 percent for the UK, “provided that substantially all hardware, software, and technology originates from within these countries and the United States.”

Stated reasons for the new tariffs include:

“many U.S. commercial manufacturers that produce UAS domestically are highly dependent on foreign sources for critical UAS components, such as motors, electronic speed controllers, lithium-ion batteries, and docking stations, which creates unacceptable national security vulnerabilities.”

“products pose an information technology security risk because their software allows data to be sent back to the manufacturer in a foreign country.”

“there are concerns as to whether the U.S. industry can produce UAS and UAS components at the required speed and scale to adequately support national security operations and activities, including during a surge for wartime or armed conflict, or in a manner to sustain long-term economic competitiveness.”

Trump is also dangling a carrot, not just wielding a stick. The proclamation states that he’s authorizing the Secretary of Commerce to create a new program “to incentivize new investment in U.S. production facilities to produce UAS and UAS components.” That could be interesting, but last we checked, the government’s drone incentives were aimed towards drones for war.

The Supreme Court already ruled earlier this year that Trump’s global tariffs were illegal; the US Court of International Trade ruled against them too, though Trump continues to announce more.

As of today, it appears that Trump’s tariffs are enriching corporate America at the expense of everyday citizens. First, companies raise their prices so that you pay the cost of tariffs instead of them. Then, those companies get gigantic refunds from the government when the tariffs are declared illegal. Finally, they profit. Companies do not pass those refunds along to you, even though you paid for them, and they do not lower their prices either.

The tariffs aren’t the US government’s only attempt to target larger foreign drones in the US. The FCC recently threatened to retroactively ban “military-grade” drones using definitions that would also catch drones for farmers, first responders, and light shows in the same net.

Tech.title: ‘That is not acceptable’: Judge orders Google to make rival app store installs easier
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

One month after Epic Games and Google seemingly stopped fighting over the future of Android app distribution, they were back in a San Francisco courtroom today — where Judge James Donato just ordered Google to make it easier to install rival app stores on Android.

It’s been nearly three years since a jury unanimously decided that Google had an illegal monopoly over Android apps, and almost two years since Judge Donato decided the best way of undoing that monopoly would be to crack open Android app distribution. Donato ordered Google to carry rival Android app stores inside its own Google Play Store, and to provide rivals with complecte access to Google’s full catalog of apps, for several years.

But Epic argued that Google is still making it too difficult to install rival app stores, showing the entire courtroom a live demo of how many steps it currently takes — and Judge Donato agreed that some of those steps were unnecessary “anticompetitive friction” and ordered Google to remove them.

First, Epic’s lawyer Yonatan Even showed that if you search Google’s Play Store for the term “store for apps,” no third-party app stores appear, only physical stores. “Wait, why did Walmart come up?” Judge Donato asked. “That’s not good,” he exclaimed.

These are my own screenshots, not the live demo shown in court, as no photography is allowed there. Images: Google

“That is not acceptable, that has to be fixed. I want every possible variation that’s even only 70 percent properly phrased,” Donato ordered. Google’s counsel agreed to make it happen.

Similarly, Judge Donato bristled when he saw that users have to press a “view” button before they can press an “install” button when choosing to install a third-party app store, and so that will change too. “You don’t get that when you’re looking at Apple Music,” he noted.

“Make that install, not view,” Donato ordered, and Google agreed to do so.

Later, Epic showed that when you search for “app store,” or even if you search directly for Aptoide, the first rival store to make it into the Google Play Store, Google doesn’t surface a normal list of apps — it shows you a new banner you have to click through to a dedicated third-party app store page.

That’s not just a problem for brand-new app stores, argued Even. Big, established companies like Amazon might decide not to launch app stores because they’d be losing the ability to appear in normal appstore search results.

Judge Donato ordered Google to fix that one, too, telling the company that it didn’t make any sense. “Why doesn’t it say ‘are you looking for music’ when you type in ‘music store’?” he asked.

Google’s attorney replied that Epic and Google had already agreed that app stores are a special category of apps that have advanced permissions. But Donato said the warning on the third-party app store page itself was sufficient to address that — there’s no need to ask a user whether they really want the thing they searched for, whether it’s a game store or a glass of water.

“We all know that when you go to a Google store or an Apple store and you type in the name of your app, you’re going to get one thing you were looking for and ten things you don’t want,” said the judge, explaining that he doesn’t think average users will be confused when they get what they’re asking for.

“Take off the ‘are you looking for’ screen, there’s no purpose for that. There’s a friction there that has no purpose whatsoever,” Donato said.

The judge wants these changes fast. “Have it done by a week from today,” he told Google. “If there’s some problem with that, let me know.‘

Tech.title: The fight over Flock and other ALPRs
Tech.content:
There are over 120,000 of Flock’s automatic license plate reader (ALPR) cameras installed all over the US. Flock’s cameras, and others like them, use AI to identify and track vehicles based on their license plate number, make, model, color, and other info, networked together to track vehicles and people’s movements throughout the day and across the country.

Dozens of communities have canceled contracts for the cameras or turned them off, including Los Angeles, as officials have pushed for more limits on the data they collect, who has access to it, and how it can be used in the future. Earlier this year, Amazon-owned Ring canceled a partnership with Flock after online backlash.

Tech.title: Microsoft’s Clippy-like Mico character is no longer the face of Copilot
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Microsoft Copilot will no longer show its emotive yellow blob, Mico, when you use the chatbot’s voice mode. In a support page, Microsoft says it’s going to move Mico to its Learn Live platform, where the avatar will have “more to react to,” as reported earlier by GeekWire.

Mico launched in Copilot’s voice mode last October, with Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman pitching the avatar as a way to give the chatbot an “identity.” The blob would react to what you say in real-time, complete with facial expressions and animations.

Mico joins the long list of virtual helpers that Microsoft has retired over the years, like Clippy, Cortana, and Rover. “Mico helped us learn about warmth, expressiveness, and how people want to talk with AI,” Microsoft’s support page says. “Those learnings are shaping Copilot going forward.” Microsoft is removing Mico from Copilot “in waves.”

The change is part of Microsoft’s plans to merge its Copilot and Microsoft 365 Copilot apps. It also comes just months after an AI reshuffling that put Jacob Andreou in charge of Copilot, while Suleyman turned his attention to developing new AI models.

Tech.title: Netflix is closing two game studios
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Netflix plans to shut down two of its gaming studios, as reported by Game File and Variety, as it makes a bigger shift toward party games and titles streamed to TVs.

One of the studios being shut down is Night School Studio, creators of the Oxenfree series. Netflix bought Night School in 2021, and it just released a horror experience called Unhinged for TVs and launched a mobile game in 2025 tied to Black Mirror. The other studio that’s set to close is Helsinki-based Moonloot Games, which was created in 2022.

Netflix’s big push into TV-based games kicked off late last year and was a pivot from a mobile-focused approach that featured prestige indie titles. But Netflix has let many of those indie hits leave its mobile lineup as it focuses instead on four pillars of kids, party, narrative, and “mainstream” games.

“As we continue to prioritize these areas, we see an opportunity to be more focused in our execution, so we are making organizational changes to the business to match those priorities,” Netflix spokesperson Chrissy Kelleher tells The Verge. Netflix is also eliminating “some” additional roles in its games business, according to Kelleher. The cuts include Tara Voelker, who says she was the “single accessibility person” on the gaming team.
